paragraphs: The paper models how a visual system can learn a pattern's true direction of motion from incomplete local measurements. A detector viewing a moving edge can register the motion component perpendicular to that edge, leaving the full direction ambiguous. This is the aperture problem: individual edge measurements do not directly specify the motion of the whole pattern.

The authors use a multilayer feedforward network trained with a Hebb rule. Input patterns contain randomly oriented contours moving in a particular direction. The input units are assigned direction and speed sensitivities resembling those of neurons projecting from visual area V1 to MT, so the network begins with biologically motivated component-motion signals.

After exposure to many patterns, training continues until most weights saturate. A proportion of second-layer units acquire responses that solve the aperture problem and resemble pattern-direction-selective neurons in MT. The result shows that learning from varied moving contours can produce a more complete motion representation from component-sensitive inputs, with the reported capability emerging in some units.
summary.tldr: Hebbian learning produces units that recover pattern motion from locally ambiguous edge-motion signals.

title: Learning the Solution to the Aperture Problem for Pattern Motion with a Hebb Rule

abstract: A digital realisation of two-dimensional self-organising feature maps is presented. The method is based on subspace classification using an n-tuple technique. Weight vector approximation and orthogonal projections to produce a winnertakes-all network are also discussed. Over one million effective binary weights can be applied in 25ms using a conventional microcomputer. Details of a number of image recognition tasks, including character recognition and object centring, are described.

paragraphs: The paper presents a digital implementation of two-dimensional self-organizing feature maps. Its method uses subspace classification through an n-tuple technique, organizing classification around selected groups of input components. The focus is on realizing the map computationally, connecting a neural representation with operations suitable for a conventional microcomputer.

The authors also discuss approximating weight vectors and using orthogonal projections to produce a winner-take-all network. These mechanisms address how information is represented and how one response is selected from competing responses. Together, they form part of the implementation approach for turning a feature-map model into a workable digital system.

The reported implementation can apply more than one million effective binary weights in 25 milliseconds on a conventional microcomputer. This figure describes the computational capacity of the implementation, rather than a recognition accuracy. The paper also describes image recognition tasks, including character recognition and object centering. These applications connect the implementation techniques to concrete uses involving both image identity and position.
summary.tldr: A digital self-organizing-map implementation applies over one million effective binary weights in 25 milliseconds and supports image recognition tasks.

title: Digital Realisation of Self-Organising Maps

abstract: Three methods for improving the performance of (gaussian) radial basis function (RBF) networks were tested on the NETtaik task. In RBF, a new example is classified by computing its Euclidean distance to a set of centers chosen by unsupervised methods. The application of supervised learning to learn a non-Euclidean distance metric was found to reduce the error rate of RBF networks, while supervised learning of each center's vari(cid:173) ance resulted in inferior performance. The best improvement in accuracy was achieved by networks called generalized radial basis function (GRBF) networks. In GRBF, the center locations are determined by supervised learning. After training on 1000 words, RBF classifies 56.5% of letters correct, while GRBF scores 73.4% letters correct (on a separate test set). From these and other experiments, we conclude that supervised learning of center locations can be very important for radial basis function learning.

paragraphs: Radial basis function networks classify examples using their distances from a collection of centers. In the version considered here, those centers are initially selected without using the desired outputs. The paper asks which parts of this distance-based representation benefit most from supervised learning, testing three modifications on the NETtalk task.

Learning a non-Euclidean distance measure reduces the network's error rate, indicating that the ordinary geometric distance is not always the most useful measure for classification. Learning each center's variance produces inferior performance. The strongest improvement comes from generalized radial basis function networks, which use supervised learning to determine the center locations themselves.

After training on 1,000 words, the standard RBF network correctly classifies 56.5% of letters in a separate test set, while the generalized version reaches 73.4%. These results support the paper's conclusion that center placement can be especially important. Using the desired outputs to decide where centers belong changes the reference points underlying the network's predictions and substantially improves accuracy in this experiment.
summary.tldr: Supervised learning of RBF center locations substantially improves test accuracy on NETtalk.

title: Improving the Performance of Radial Basis Function Networks by Learning Center Locations

paragraphs: This paper analyzes stochastic learning by tracking probability distributions over network weights. Instead of following one particular training run, it describes how an ensemble of possible runs evolves. The authors derive equations of motion for these weight-space densities using theoretical techniques from statistical physics.

They study equilibrium distributions through a diffusion approximation and give expressions for special cases of the least-mean-squares algorithm. A central result is that equilibrium generally does not follow a thermal, or Gibbs, distribution determined by the objective function alone. It depends on an effective potential that also incorporates diffusion effects arising from stochastic learning.

The paper additionally derives an exact expression for the time evolution of the density when weight updates are proportional to the sign of the gradient. Together, these results connect update rules to both transient behavior and eventual distributions. Their significance is that understanding where stochastic learning spends its time requires accounting for its fluctuations, alongside the objective it is trying to minimize.
summary.tldr: Weight-distribution dynamics show that stochastic-learning equilibria depend on diffusion effects as well as the objective being minimized.

title: Weight Space Probability Densities in Stochastic Learning: I. Dynamics and Equilibria

abstract: Recent physiological research has shown that synchronization of oscillatory responses in striate cortex may code for relationships between visual features of objects. A VLSI circuit has been de(cid:173) signed to provide rapid phase-locking synchronization of multiple oscillators to allow for further exploration of this neural mechanism. By exploiting the intrinsic random transistor mismatch of devices operated in subthreshold, large groups of phase-locked oscillators can be readily partitioned into smaller phase-locked groups. A mUltiple target tracker for binary images is described utilizing this phase-locking architecture. A VLSI chip has been fabricated and tested to verify the architecture. The chip employs Pulse Ampli(cid:173) tude Modulation (PAM) to encode the output at the periphery of the system.

paragraphs: This paper develops a VLSI circuit for exploring the idea that synchronized neural oscillations can encode relationships between visual features. The hardware rapidly brings multiple oscillators into phase alignment. Such synchronization provides a mechanism for linking signals through their timing, reflecting the physiological motivation from oscillatory responses in visual cortex.

The architecture also allows a large synchronized group to split into smaller synchronized groups. It does this by exploiting intrinsic random differences between transistors operated in the subthreshold regime. Device variation therefore becomes a resource for organizing oscillator groups, supporting the separation of feature groupings within the same architecture.

The authors describe a multiple-target tracker for binary images that uses this phase-locking mechanism. They also fabricated and tested a chip to verify the architecture, giving the proposal a hardware realization. The chip encodes output at the system's periphery using pulse amplitude modulation. Together, the circuit and tracking application connect a proposed neural feature-linking mechanism to an implemented system that can represent multiple synchronized groups.
summary.tldr: A tested VLSI architecture uses synchronized oscillator groups to link features for multiple-target tracking.

title: VLSI Phase Locking Architectures for Feature Linking in Multiple Target Tracking Systems

paragraphs: This paper develops a statistical account of overtraining and asks how much early stopping improves generalization. The analysis concerns realizable stochastic neural networks trained with Kullback-Leibler loss. These conditions define the setting of the theoretical conclusions, including the assumption that the learning model can represent the process being learned.

In the asymptotic regime, the authors find only a small generalization benefit from early stopping, even when the best stopping time is available. They also analyze stopping based on cross-validation and address how examples should be divided between training and testing to obtain optimal performance. This connects the stopping decision with the cost of reserving data to make it.

The paper reports a different conclusion in the non-asymptotic region: cross-validated early stopping decreases generalization error within the studied setting. Large-scale simulations agree closely with the analytical findings. The main lesson is that the benefit of early stopping depends on the statistical regime, and that evaluating cross-validation requires considering both its stopping guidance and the allocation of examples.
summary.tldr: A statistical analysis finds small asymptotic gains from early stopping but benefits from cross-validated stopping in the studied non-asymptotic regime.

title: Statistical Theory of Overtraining - Is Cross-Validation Asymptotically Effective?

paragraphs: The paper examines whether reinforcement learning can work reliably when function approximation is needed to generalize across continuous states. Earlier experiments had reported failures on several control problems. The authors revisit all of those tasks and add a substantially larger one, reporting positive results throughout their evaluation.

Two major differences distinguish their approach: they use sparse coarse coding through CMAC function approximators, and they learn online. Sparse coarse coding represents situations through a limited set of active features, allowing shared parameters to support generalization. The earlier work used mostly global approximators and offline learning, making representation and learning procedure central to the comparison.

The authors also test the suggestion that learning should rely on actual outcomes through rollouts, corresponding to the full-return setting of temporal-difference learning. In their experiments, this consistently performs substantially worse. The findings support using function approximation with reinforcement learning and challenge a blanket preference for full-return methods. They are empirical evidence of robust performance on these tasks, against a background of limited convergence theory.
summary.tldr: Online reinforcement learning with sparse coarse coding succeeds on previously troublesome control tasks and outperforms full-return learning in the reported experiments.

title: Generalization in Reinforcement Learning: Successful Examples Using Sparse Coarse Coding

abstract: Real-valued random hidden variables can be useful for modelling latent structure that explains correlations among observed vari(cid:173) ables. I propose a simple unit that adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to its input before passing it through a sigmoidal squashing func(cid:173) tion. Such units can produce a variety of useful behaviors, ranging from deterministic to binary stochastic to continuous stochastic. I show how "slice sampling" can be used for inference and learning in top-down networks of these units and demonstrate learning on two simple problems.
originalAbstract: Real-valued random hidden variables can be useful for modelling latent structure that explains correlations among observed vari(cid:173) ables. I propose a simple unit that adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to its input before passing it through a sigmoidal squashing func(cid:173) tion. Such units can produce a variety of useful behaviors, ranging from deterministic to binary stochastic to continuous stochastic. I show how "slice sampling" can be used for inference and learning in top-down networks of these units and demonstrate learning on two simple problems.

paragraphs: Hidden variables can explain why observed quantities vary together. This paper proposes a belief-network unit that allows those hidden variables to take real values, expanding the kinds of latent structure the network can represent. The aim is to combine useful stochastic behavior with a simple construction for individual units.

Each unit adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to its input and then passes the result through a sigmoidal squashing function. This order of operations produces a range of behaviors, including effectively deterministic outputs, binary stochastic outputs, and continuous stochastic outputs. A single unit design can therefore express different forms of hidden-variable behavior within the network framework.

The paper shows how slice sampling can support inference and learning in top-down networks built from these units. Inference concerns hidden-variable values associated with observations, while learning adjusts the model to the data. Demonstrations on two simple problems show learning with the proposed construction. The contribution brings together a flexible stochastic unit and a sampling method that makes networks of those units usable for latent-structure modeling.
summary.tldr: Adding Gaussian noise before a sigmoid creates flexible belief-network units that can be trained and used for inference with slice sampling.

title: Continuous Sigmoidal Belief Networks Trained using Slice Sampling

abstract: We present new algorithms for parameter estimation of HMMs. By adapting a framework used for supervised learning, we construct iterative algorithms that maximize the likelihood of the observations while also attempting to stay "close" to the current estimated parameters. We use a bound on the relative entropy between the two HMMs as a distance measure between them. The result is new iterative training algorithms which are similar to the EM (Baum-Welch) algorithm for training HMMs. The proposed algorithms are composed of a step similar to the expectation step of Baum-Welch and a new update of the parameters which replaces the maximization (re-estimation) step. The algorithm takes only negligibly more time per iteration and an approximated version uses the same expectation step as Baum-Welch. We evaluate experimentally the new algorithms on synthetic and natural speech pronunciation data. For sparse models, i.e. models with relatively small number of non-zero parameters, the proposed algorithms require significantly fewer iterations.

paragraphs: The paper introduces hidden Markov model training algorithms that seek higher observation likelihood while also keeping each update close to the current model. Closeness is measured using a bound on relative entropy between two HMMs. This makes the relationship between successive parameter estimates an explicit part of the training procedure.

The algorithms resemble Baum-Welch training but replace its maximization, or parameter re-estimation, step with a new update. They retain a step similar to its expectation step, and an approximate version uses the same expectation step as Baum-Welch. The abstract reports only negligible additional computation per iteration for the proposed methods.

Experiments use synthetic data and natural speech pronunciation data. For sparse models, meaning models with relatively few nonzero parameters, the new algorithms require significantly fewer iterations. The practical benefit is therefore strongest in the stated sparse setting: the update rule reduces the number of training rounds while adding little work to each round, connecting an entropy-based notion of model distance to improved iterative estimation.
summary.tldr: Entropy-based HMM updates require significantly fewer iterations for sparse models while adding negligible per-iteration computation.

title: Training Algorithms for Hidden Markov Models using Entropy Based Distance Functions

abstract: We have constructed an inexpensive video based motorized tracking system that learns to track a head. It uses real time graphical user inputs or an auxiliary infrared detector as supervisory signals to train a convolutional neural network. The inputs to the neural network consist of normalized luminance and chrominance images and motion information from frame differences. Subsampled images are also used to provide scale invariance. During the online training phases the neural network rapidly adjusts the input weights depending up on the reliability of the different channels in the surrounding environment. This quick adaptation allows the system to robustly track a head even when other objects are moving within a cluttered background.

It uses real time graphical user inputs or an auxiliary infrared detector as supervisory signals to train a convolutional neural network. The inputs to the neural network consist of normalized luminance and chrominance images and motion information from frame differences. Subsampled images are also used to provide scale invariance. During the online training phases the neural network rapidly adjusts the input weights depending up on the reliability of the different channels in the surrounding environment. paragraphs: This paper describes an inexpensive motorized video system that learns to follow a person's head. Its central challenge is deciding which visual evidence remains trustworthy as the surroundings change. A moving object in the background, for example, makes motion alone an unreliable guide to the target.

A convolutional neural network combines normalized brightness and color images with motion information obtained from differences between video frames. It also receives subsampled images, which help it handle changes in the head's apparent size. Training signals come either from real-time graphical input supplied by a user or from an auxiliary infrared detector. These signals guide the network toward the intended target.

During online training, the network rapidly changes the weights assigned to its input channels according to their reliability in the current environment. The reported outcome is robust head tracking despite clutter and other moving objects. The useful design principle is adaptive combination of several visual cues: the system can change which information it emphasizes as conditions change.
summary.tldr: A motorized head tracker learns to combine brightness, color, and motion cues while adapting to their changing reliability.

title: A Neural Network Based Head Tracking System

This type of data arises naturally in many ap(cid:173) plication ranging from computational linguistics and information retrieval to preference analysis and computer vision. In this paper, we present a systematic, domain-independent framework of learn(cid:173) ing from dyadic data by statistical mixture models. Our approach covers different models with fiat and hierarchical latent class struc(cid:173) tures. We propose an annealed version of the standard EM algo(cid:173) rithm for model fitting which is empirically evaluated on a variety of data sets from different domains.

paragraphs: This paper studies observations attached to pairs of objects drawn from two finite sets. Each observed pair contains one object from each set. This structure appears across language, information retrieval, preference analysis, and computer vision, motivating a learning framework organized around the paired nature of the data.

The authors propose a domain-independent approach based on statistical mixture models. It includes both flat and hierarchical latent-class structures, allowing the hidden organization used to explain observations to take different forms. The shared framework brings these alternatives together under the same general view of learning from pairs.

For model fitting, the paper introduces an annealed version of the standard expectation-maximization algorithm and evaluates it empirically on datasets from multiple domains. The contribution connects a common data structure, a family of latent-class models, and a corresponding fitting method. Its cross-domain evaluation reflects the central aim: to study dyadic observations through a reusable statistical framework rather than a separate formulation for every application.
summary.tldr: A mixture-model framework with annealed EM learns from paired-object observations across multiple application domains.

title: Learning from Dyadic Data

abstract: We generalize a recent formalism to describe the dynamics of supervised learning in layered neural networks, in the regime where data recycling is inevitable, to the case of noisy teachers. Our theory generates reliable predictions for the evolution in time of training- and generalization er(cid:173) rors, and extends the class of mathematically solvable learning processes in large neural networks to those situations where overfitting can occur.
originalAbstract: We generalize a recent formalism to describe the dynamics of supervised learning in layered neural networks, in the regime where data recycling is inevitable, to the case of noisy teachers. Our theory generates reliable predictions for the evolution in time of training- and generalization er(cid:173) rors, and extends the class of mathematically solvable learning processes in large neural networks to those situations where overfitting can occur.

paragraphs: The paper studies how supervised learning unfolds in layered neural networks when the available training data must be reused. Repeated exposure to a restricted dataset makes the evolution of learning important: fitting the examples already seen and performing well beyond those examples are distinct outcomes that can change differently during training.

The authors extend an existing mathematical framework to include noisy teachers, meaning that the source of supervision contains noise. Their theory predicts how both training error and generalization error develop over time. Tracking both quantities makes it possible to describe the learning process in terms of its changing fit to training data and its changing ability to generalize.

The stated contribution is an expansion of the learning processes that can be solved mathematically for large neural networks. The extended framework includes situations in which overfitting can occur, and the authors describe its predictions as reliable. This makes the theory relevant to the combination of reused data and noisy supervision, where training progress alone does not fully describe learning quality.
summary.tldr: An extended theory predicts training and generalization dynamics for large networks learning from reused data and noisy teachers.

title: Dynamics of Supervised Learning with Restricted Training Sets and Noisy Teachers

abstract: A neural model is described which uses oscillatory correlation to segregate speech from interfering sound sources. The core of the model is a two-layer neural oscillator network. A sound stream is represented by a synchronized population of oscillators, and different streams are represented by desynchronized oscillator populations. The model has been evaluated using a corpus of speech mixed with interfering sounds, and produces an improvement in signal-to-noise ratio for every mixture.
originalAbstract: A neural model is described which uses oscillatory correlation to segregate speech from interfering sound sources. The core of the model is a two-layer neural oscillator network. A sound stream is represented by a synchronized population of oscillators, and different streams are represented by desynchronized oscillator populations. The model has been evaluated using a corpus of speech mixed with interfering sounds, and produces an improvement in signal-to-noise ratio for every mixture.

paragraphs: The paper presents a neural model for separating speech from interfering sounds. The central problem is deciding which parts of a mixed acoustic input belong to the same sound stream. Its approach uses the timing relationships among neural oscillators as a way to represent those groupings.

The model contains a two-layer network of oscillators. Oscillators representing one stream synchronize with one another, while populations representing different streams remain out of synchrony. In this representation, coordinated activity identifies elements as belonging together. Differences in coordination allow separate streams to coexist in the network without being represented as a single combined source.

The authors evaluate the model on a corpus containing speech mixed with interfering sounds. They report an improvement in signal-to-noise ratio for every mixture tested, indicating that speech becomes stronger relative to interference according to that measure. The finding supports oscillatory correlation as a useful grouping mechanism for the evaluated mixtures, with synchronized populations providing the link between the neural representation and sound separation.
summary.tldr: A neural oscillator network groups sound streams through synchrony and improves signal-to-noise ratio for every tested speech mixture.

title: An Oscillatory Correlation Frame work for Computational Auditory Scene Analysis

abstract: Incorporating prior knowledge of a particular task into the architecture of a learning algorithm can greatly improve generalization performance. We study here a case where we know that the function to be learned is non-decreasing in two of its arguments and convex in one of them. For this purpose we propose a class of functions similar to multi-layer neural networks but (1) that has those properties, (2) is a universal approximator of continuous functions with these and other properties. We apply this new class of functions to the task of modeling the price of call options. Experiments show improvements on regressing the price of call options using the new types of function classes that incorporate the a priori con(cid:173) straints.
originalAbstract: Incorporating prior knowledge of a particular task into the architecture of a learning algorithm can greatly improve generalization performance. We study here a case where we know that the function to be learned is non-decreasing in two of its arguments and convex in one of them. For this purpose we propose a class of functions similar to multi-layer neural networks but (1) that has those properties, (2) is a universal approximator of continuous functions with these and other properties. We apply this new class of functions to the task of modeling the price of call options. Experiments show improvements on regressing the price of call options using the new types of function classes that incorporate the a priori con(cid:173) straints.

paragraphs: The paper examines how known properties of a target function can be built into a learning model. The setting assumes that the function is non-decreasing in two inputs and convex in one. These are structural constraints on how predictions may change as inputs vary, giving the learner information beyond the observed training values.

The authors propose a function family resembling multilayer neural networks that satisfies these properties by construction. They also establish a universal approximation property for continuous functions with the specified and other stated properties. This matters because incorporating constraints should still leave the model flexible enough to approximate the relevant class of functions, rather than forcing one narrow functional shape.

The application is regression for call-option prices. Experiments show improved price prediction when the proposed function classes incorporate the prior constraints. The findings support using known monotonicity and curvature properties as part of model architecture in this setting. The approximation result concerns functions within the constrained class, while the empirical result concerns the option-pricing task studied.
summary.tldr: Neural-network-like function classes that enforce known monotonicity and convexity improve call-option price regression in experiments.

title: Incorporating Second-Order Functional Knowledge for Better Option Pricing

abstract: In memory consolidation, declarative memories which initially require the hippocampus for their recall, ultimately become independent of it. Consolidation has been the focus of numerous experimental and qualita(cid:173) tive modeling studies, but only little quantitative exploration. We present a consolidation model in which hierarchical connections in the cortex, that initially instantiate purely semantic information acquired through probabilistic unsupervised learning, come to instantiate episodic infor(cid:173) mation as well. The hippocampus is responsible for helping complete partial input patterns before consolidation is complete, while also train(cid:173) ing the cortex to perform appropriate completion by itself.

paragraphs: The paper models memory consolidation: the process through which declarative memories initially dependent on the hippocampus for recall become accessible without it. The authors aim to give a quantitative account of a process that had received extensive experimental and qualitative modeling attention but comparatively little quantitative exploration.

In the model, hierarchical cortical connections initially encode semantic information learned through probabilistic unsupervised learning. During consolidation, these connections also come to encode episodic information. This gives the same cortical hierarchy a changing role, extending what it represents as memories become established.

The hippocampus contributes both to current recall and to the development of later cortical recall. Before consolidation is complete, it helps reconstruct full patterns from partial inputs. It also trains the cortex to perform the appropriate reconstruction independently. The proposed mechanism therefore connects the immediate usefulness of hippocampal pattern completion to the gradual emergence of cortical self-sufficiency. It offers a computational account of how dependence on the hippocampus could diminish as cortical representations change.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical cortical model explains consolidation through hippocampal pattern completion that also trains the cortex to recall memories independently.

title: Hippocampally-Dependent Consolidation in a Hierarchical Model of Neocortex

abstract: Neural activity appears to be a crucial component for shaping the recep- tive ﬁelds of cortical simple cells into adjacent, oriented subregions alter- nately receiving ON- and OFF-center excitatory geniculate inputs. It is known that the orientation selective responses of V1 neurons are reﬁned by visual experience. After eye opening, the spatiotemporal structure of neural activity in the early stages of the visual pathway depends both on the visual environment and on how the environment is scanned. We have used computational modeling to investigate how eye movements might affect the reﬁnement of the orientation tuning of simple cells in the pres- ence of a Hebbian scheme of synaptic plasticity. Levels of correlation be- tween the activity of simulated cells were examined while natural scenes were scanned so as to model sequences of saccades and ﬁxational eye movements, such as microsaccades, tremor and ocular drift. The speciﬁc patterns of activity required for a quantitatively accurate development of simple cell receptive ﬁelds with segregated ON and OFF subregions were observed during ﬁxational eye movements, but not in the presence of saccades or with static presentation of natural visual input. These re- sults suggest an important role for the eye movements occurring during visual ﬁxation in the reﬁnement of orientation selectivity.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how eye movements might help refine the orientation preferences of cortical simple cells. These cells develop adjacent regions receiving different ON- and OFF-center inputs. Because visual experience depends on both the scene and how the eyes scan it, the authors examine movement as part of the developmental input.

Their computational model uses Hebbian synaptic plasticity and measures correlations among simulated cells while natural scenes are scanned. The scanning conditions represent saccades and the smaller movements that occur during fixation, including microsaccades, tremor, and drift. Static presentation of natural input provides another condition.

They did not appear under the modeled saccadic or static conditions. This result suggests that the small movements occurring during fixation may contribute to refinement of orientation selectivity. Its force comes from the comparison within the modeling framework, rather than a direct demonstration of developmental causation in animals.
summary.tldr: Simulations suggest that fixational eye movements supply activity correlations that can support refinement of cortical orientation selectivity.

title: Eye movements and the maturation of cortical orientation selectivity

abstract: Narayanan and Jurafsky (1998) proposed that human language compre- hension can be modeled by treating human comprehenders as Bayesian reasoners, and modeling the comprehension process with Bayesian de- cision trees. In this paper we extend the Narayanan and Jurafsky model to make further predictions about reading time given the probability of difference parses or interpretations, and test the model against reading time data from a psycholinguistic experiment.
originalAbstract: Narayanan and Jurafsky (1998) proposed that human language compre- hension can be modeled by treating human comprehenders as Bayesian reasoners, and modeling the comprehension process with Bayesian de- cision trees. In this paper we extend the Narayanan and Jurafsky model to make further predictions about reading time given the probability of difference parses or interpretations, and test the model against reading time data from a psycholinguistic experiment.

paragraphs: A sentence can support more than one grammatical structure or interpretation. This paper investigates language comprehension through a model that treats readers as Bayesian reasoners. In that framework, competing interpretations have probabilities, giving the model a way to express preferences among possible readings rather than merely selecting a grammatical analysis.

The authors extend an earlier account that represented comprehension using Bayesian decision trees. Their contribution is to make further predictions about reading time from the probabilities of different parses or interpretations. This connects two aspects of comprehension: which interpretation a reader favors and how long processing takes. Reading time therefore becomes an observable quantity against which the probabilistic account can be checked.

The extended model is tested against reading-time measurements from a psycholinguistic experiment. The supplied abstract establishes this link between probabilistic interpretation and experimental testing, without specifying the outcome of the comparison. The contribution is a more directly testable account of comprehension, connecting uncertainty about sentence meaning with the timing of human reading.
summary.tldr: An extended Bayesian model links the probabilities of sentence interpretations to reading-time predictions tested against human data.

title: A Bayesian Model Predicts Human Parse Preference and Reading Times in Sentence Processing

abstract: In this paper we show how the generation of documents can be thought of as a k-stage Markov process, which leads to a Fisher ker(cid:173) nel from which the n-gram and string kernels can be re-constructed. The Fisher kernel view gives a more flexible insight into the string kernel and suggests how it can be parametrised in a way that re(cid:173) flects the statistics of the training corpus. Furthermore, the prob(cid:173) abilistic modelling approach suggests extending the Markov pro(cid:173) cess to consider sub-sequences of varying length, rather than the standard fixed-length approach used in the string kernel. We give a procedure for determining which sub-sequences are informative features and hence generate a Finite State Machine model, which can again be used to obtain a Fisher kernel. By adjusting the parametrisation we can also influence the weighting received by the features . In this way we are able to obtain a logarithmic weighting in a Fisher kernel. Finally, experiments are reported comparing the different kernels using the standard Bag of Words kernel as a baseline.

paragraphs: This paper connects several ways of comparing text by treating document generation as a staged Markov process. From that probabilistic model, the authors derive a Fisher kernel that can reconstruct n-gram and string kernels. The connection provides a common modeling perspective on methods that otherwise appear as separate definitions of document similarity.

That perspective also suggests how to make string kernels more flexible. Their parameters can reflect the statistics of the training collection, and the underlying process can include subsequences of different lengths. The authors give a procedure for identifying informative subsequences and constructing a finite-state machine from them, which then supplies another Fisher kernel.

The parameterization also controls how strongly individual features contribute, including a construction that yields logarithmic feature weighting. Experiments compare the resulting kernels with one another and with a bag-of-words baseline. The contribution is a probabilistic route for understanding, adapting, and extending sequence-based text kernels, including both the selection of features and the weights those features receive.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic Fisher-kernel view unifies text kernels and enables corpus-dependent weighting and informative subsequences of varying lengths.

title: String Kernels, Fisher Kernels and Finite State Automata

abstract: Machine learning techniques are increasingly being used to produce a wide-range of classiﬁers for complex real-world applications that involve nonuniform testing costs and misclassiﬁcation costs. As the complexity of these applications grows, the management of resources during the learning and classiﬁcation processes be- comes a challenging task. In this work we introduce ACT (Anytime Cost-sensitive Trees), a novel framework for operating in such environments. ACT is an anytime algorithm that allows trading computation time for lower classiﬁcation costs. It builds a tree top-down and exploits additional time resources to obtain better esti- mations for the utility of the different candidate splits. Using sampling techniques ACT approximates for each candidate split the cost of the subtree under it and fa- vors the one with a minimal cost. Due to its stochastic nature ACT is expected to be able to escape local minima, into which greedy methods may be trapped. Ex- periments with a variety of datasets were conducted to compare the performance of ACT to that of the state of the art cost-sensitive tree learners. The results show that for most domains ACT produces trees of signiﬁcantly lower costs. ACT is also shown to exhibit good anytime behavior with diminishing returns.

The results show that for most domains ACT produces trees of signiﬁcantly lower costs. ACT is also shown to exhibit good anytime behavior with diminishing returns.

paragraphs: A classifier can incur costs both when obtaining information and when making an incorrect prediction. When those costs differ across tests and mistakes, choosing a decision tree requires more than optimizing predictive accuracy. This paper introduces ACT, an algorithm that lets additional learning time be exchanged for lower classification costs.

ACT builds a tree from the top down. For each possible split, it uses sampling to estimate the cost of the subtree that would follow, then favors the split with the lowest estimated cost. Extra computation improves these estimates. This gives split selection a view of downstream consequences, and the authors expect its randomness to help it escape local minima that can trap greedy approaches.

Across the evaluated datasets, ACT produces significantly lower-cost trees in most domains than the compared state-of-the-art cost-sensitive learners. It also exhibits the intended anytime behavior: additional computation helps, with diminishing returns. The findings support treating the learning-time budget as a practical control over the eventual tree's classification costs.
summary.tldr: ACT uses extra computation to estimate downstream decision-tree costs more accurately, producing lower-cost trees in most evaluated domains.

title: Anytime Induction of Cost-sensitive Trees

abstract: We present a novel paradigm for statistical machine translation (SMT), based on joint modeling of word alignment and the topical aspects underlying bilingual document pairs via a hidden Markov Bilingual Topic AdMixture (HM-BiTAM). In this new paradigm, parallel sentence-pairs from a parallel document-pair are coupled via a certain semantic-flow, to ensure coherence of topical context in the alignment of matching words between languages, during likelihood-based training of topic-dependent translational lexicons, as well as topic representations in each language. The resulting trained HM-BiTAM can not only display topic patterns like other methods such as LDA, but now for bilingual corpora; it also offers a principled way of inferring optimal translation in a context-dependent way. Our method integrates the conventional IBM Models based on HMM --- a key component for most of the state-of-the-art SMT systems, with the recently proposed BiTAM model, and we report an extensive empirical analysis (in many way complementary to the description-oriented of our method in three aspects: word alignment, bilingual topic representation, and translation.

paragraphs: HM-BiTAM jointly models word alignment and the topics underlying paired documents in two languages. Word alignment identifies which words correspond across languages. The paper's central idea is that these correspondences should reflect the topical context of the documents, rather than being learned without the semantic connections between their sentence pairs.

The model couples parallel sentence pairs through a semantic flow that maintains topical coherence. Likelihood-based training learns both topic-dependent translation lexicons and topic representations for each language. The construction combines HMM-based IBM translation models with the bilingual topic admixture approach, connecting a conventional alignment component with explicit bilingual topic modeling.

The trained model can display topic patterns in bilingual collections and provides a principled approach to context-dependent translation inference. The authors report an extensive empirical analysis covering word alignment, bilingual topic representation, and translation. The contribution is a unified account of these three tasks, in which document context helps organize the relationship between words and their translations.
summary.tldr: HM-BiTAM jointly learns bilingual topics and word alignments so that translation can account for coherent document-level topical context.

title: HM-BiTAM: Bilingual Topic Exploration, Word Alignment, and Translation

abstract: We present the Gaussian Process Density Sampler (GPDS), an exchangeable generative model for use in nonparametric Bayesian density estimation. Samples drawn from the GPDS are consistent with exact, independent samples from a fixed density function that is a transformation of a function drawn from a Gaussian process prior. Our formulation allows us to infer an unknown density from data using Markov chain Monte Carlo, which gives samples from the posterior distribution over density functions and from the predictive distribution on data space. We can also infer the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process. We compare this density modeling technique to several existing techniques on a toy problem and a skull-reconstruction task.
originalAbstract: We present the Gaussian Process Density Sampler (GPDS), an exchangeable generative model for use in nonparametric Bayesian density estimation. Samples drawn from the GPDS are consistent with exact, independent samples from a fixed density function that is a transformation of a function drawn from a Gaussian process prior. Our formulation allows us to infer an unknown density from data using Markov chain Monte Carlo, which gives samples from the posterior distribution over density functions and from the predictive distribution on data space. We can also infer the hyperparameters of the Gaussian process. We compare this density modeling technique to several existing techniques on a toy problem and a skull-reconstruction task.

paragraphs: The Gaussian Process Density Sampler is a generative model for estimating an unknown probability density within a nonparametric Bayesian framework. It constructs the density by transforming a function drawn from a Gaussian process prior. This connects uncertainty about the density to a prior over functions rather than selecting one fixed density shape in advance.

The model is exchangeable, meaning that the ordering of observations does not determine their joint distribution. Its generated samples are consistent with exact, independent sampling from a fixed density produced by the construction. This sampling property concerns the generative model and is distinct from the procedure used to infer the density after observing data.

For inference, the authors use Markov chain Monte Carlo to obtain posterior samples of density functions and predictive samples in the data space. The method can also infer Gaussian-process hyperparameters. Comparisons with existing techniques on a toy problem and a skull-reconstruction task demonstrate its application. The output includes uncertainty over possible densities as well as a distribution for future observations.
summary.tldr: The Gaussian Process Density Sampler supports Bayesian density estimation through a GP-based generative construction and MCMC inference.

title: The Gaussian Process Density Sampler

abstract: Models for near-rigid shape matching are typically based on distance-related features, in order to infer matches that are consistent with the isometric assumption. However, real shapes from image datasets, even when expected to be related by almost isometric" transformations, are actually subject not only to noise but also, to some limited degree, to variations in appearance and scale. In this paper, we introduce a graphical model that parameterises appearance, distance, and angle features and we learn all of the involved parameters via structured prediction. The outcome is a model for near-rigid shape matching which is robust in the sense that it is able to capture the possibly limited but still important scale and appearance variations. Our experimental results reveal substantial improvements upon recent successful models, while maintaining similar running times."

paragraphs: Matching nearly rigid shapes often relies on distances, because a near-isometric transformation approximately preserves them. Real image data also contain noise and some changes in appearance and scale. The paper argues that these variations can matter even when the shapes are expected to be close to an isometric match.

The authors introduce a graphical model with parameters for appearance, distance, and angle features. They learn all of these parameters through structured prediction, allowing the model to combine several kinds of evidence when choosing a correspondence. The resulting formulation is intended to capture the limited but consequential variations that distance-focused matching can overlook.

Experiments show substantial improvements over recent successful models while keeping running times similar. The reported robustness concerns the scale and appearance variations addressed by the formulation; the setting remains near-rigid shape matching. The contribution is a learned combination of visual and geometric evidence that improves matching in the evaluated cases without a corresponding increase in reported runtime.
summary.tldr: Learning appearance and geometry jointly improves near-rigid shape matching while retaining similar experimental running times.

title: Robust Near-Isometric Matching via Structured Learning of Graphical Models

abstract: Automatic speech recognition has gradually improved over the years, but the reliable recognition of unconstrained speech is still not within reach. In order to achieve a breakthrough, many research groups are now investigating new methodologies that have potential to outperform the Hidden Markov Model technology that is at the core of all present commercial systems. In this paper, it is shown that the recently introduced concept of Reservoir Computing might form the basis of such a methodology. In a limited amount of time, a reservoir system that can recognize the elementary sounds of continuous speech has been built. The system already achieves a state-of-the-art performance, and there is evidence that the margin for further improvements is still significant.

In this paper, it is shown that the recently introduced concept of Reservoir Computing might form the basis of such a methodology. In a limited amount of time, a reservoir system that can recognize the elementary sounds of continuous speech has been built. The system already achieves a state-of-the-art performance, and there is evidence that the margin for further improvements is still significant.

paragraphs: This paper explores reservoir computing as a possible foundation for a different approach to speech recognition. Its motivation is the difficulty of reliably recognizing unconstrained speech, despite gradual progress in existing systems. The authors investigate whether a reservoir-based system can perform strongly on phoneme recognition, the task of identifying the elementary sounds within continuous speech.

The work presents a system built in a limited amount of time using large hierarchical reservoirs. The reported achievement is state-of-the-art performance on recognizing these elementary speech sounds. This establishes a concrete result for phoneme recognition and supplies evidence for considering reservoir computing in the broader search for alternative speech-recognition methods.

The authors also report evidence that substantial room for further improvement remains. Their broader conclusion is deliberately prospective: reservoir computing might provide the basis for a methodology capable of advancing speech recognition. The demonstrated phoneme result supports that possibility, while the claim about further progress remains an indication of potential rather than an already achieved solution to unconstrained speech recognition.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical reservoir system achieves reported state-of-the-art phoneme recognition, supporting reservoir computing as a promising direction for speech recognition.

title: Phoneme Recognition with Large Hierarchical Reservoirs

abstract: We develop a theory of online learning by defining several complexity measures. Among them are analogues of Rademacher complexity, covering numbers and fat-shattering dimension from statistical learning theory. Relationship among these complexity measures, their connection to online learning, and tools for bounding them are provided. We apply these results to various learning problems. We provide a complete characterization of online learnability in the supervised setting.
originalAbstract: We develop a theory of online learning by defining several complexity measures. Among them are analogues of Rademacher complexity, covering numbers and fat-shattering dimension from statistical learning theory. Relationship among these complexity measures, their connection to online learning, and tools for bounding them are provided. We apply these results to various learning problems. We provide a complete characterization of online learnability in the supervised setting.

paragraphs: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding which supervised learning problems can be learned online. Its approach is to define complexity measures suited to online learning and connect those measures to learnability. The goal is a general account of what makes a learning problem manageable in this setting, rather than an algorithm for a single application.

The proposed measures include online analogues of Rademacher complexity, covering numbers, and fat-shattering dimension from statistical learning theory. These provide different mathematical ways to describe the richness of a learning problem. The authors establish relationships among the measures and supply tools for bounding them, making the definitions usable in theoretical analyses.

The framework is applied to several learning problems and yields a complete characterization of online learnability in the supervised setting. This means the contribution goes beyond giving isolated sufficient conditions: it provides a characterization of when learning is possible within that setting. The relationships and bounding tools support applying that general result to particular problem classes.
summary.tldr: Online analogues of statistical complexity measures provide a complete characterization of supervised online learnability.

title: Online Learning: Random Averages, Combinatorial Parameters, and Learnability

abstract: Many practical modeling problems involve discrete data that are best represented as draws from multinomial or categorical distributions. For example, nucleotides in a DNA sequence, children's names in a given state and year, and text documents are all commonly modeled with multinomial distributions. In all of these cases, we expect some form of dependency between the draws: the nucleotide at one position in the DNA strand may depend on the preceding nucleotides, children's names are highly correlated from year to year, and topics in text may be correlated and dynamic. These dependencies are not naturally captured by the typical Dirichlet-multinomial formulation. Here, we leverage a logistic stick-breaking representation and recent innovations in P\'{o}lya-gamma augmentation to reformulate the multinomial distribution in terms of latent variables with jointly Gaussian likelihoods, enabling us to take advantage of a host of Bayesian inference techniques for Gaussian models with minimal overhead.

paragraphs: Categorical and multinomial models describe discrete outcomes, but many such outcomes are related across time or position. The paper points to dependencies among neighboring DNA nucleotides, the popularity of children's names across years, and changing or correlated topics in documents. The usual Dirichlet-multinomial formulation does not naturally express these kinds of dependence.

The authors combine a logistic stick-breaking representation with Pólya-gamma augmentation. Together, these constructions reformulate the multinomial distribution using latent variables whose likelihoods have a jointly Gaussian form. The key change is in the mathematical representation of the model: discrete observations become compatible with inference machinery developed for Gaussian models.

This compatibility opens access to a broad collection of Bayesian inference techniques with minimal additional overhead. The contribution is a reusable modeling and inference construction for dependent discrete data. Its importance lies in connecting two kinds of statistical machinery: the categorical distributions needed to represent observations and the Gaussian methods available for expressing and analyzing structured latent relationships.
summary.tldr: Logistic stick-breaking and Pólya-gamma augmentation make dependent multinomial models accessible to Gaussian Bayesian inference techniques.

title: Dependent Multinomial Models Made Easy: Stick-Breaking with the Polya-gamma Augmentation

abstract: Super resolving a low-resolution video is usually handled by either single-image super-resolution (SR) or multi-frame SR. Single-Image SR deals with each video frame independently, and ignores intrinsic temporal dependency of video frames which actually plays a very important role in video super-resolution. Multi-Frame SR generally extracts motion information, e.g. optical flow, to model the temporal dependency, which often shows high computational cost. Considering that recurrent neural network (RNN) can model long-term contextual information of temporal sequences well, we propose a bidirectional recurrent convolutional network for efficient multi-frame SR.Different from vanilla RNN, 1) the commonly-used recurrent full connections are replaced with weight-sharing convolutional connections and 2) conditional convolutional connections from previous input layers to current hidden layer are added for enhancing visual-temporal dependency modelling. With the powerful temporal dependency modelling, our model can super resolve videos with complex motions and achieve state-of-the-art performance. Due to the cheap convolution operations, our model has a low computational complexity and runs orders of magnitude faster than other multi-frame methods.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a network for increasing video resolution by using information across frames. Processing each frame independently discards temporal relationships, while conventional multi-frame approaches often extract motion information at substantial computational cost. The authors use a bidirectional recurrent convolutional network to model those relationships efficiently.

The architecture changes the connections used in a conventional recurrent network. Shared convolutional connections replace fully connected recurrent links, and additional conditional convolutional connections connect previous inputs to the current hidden layer. These changes are intended to strengthen the modeling of visual information across time. Bidirectional recurrence allows temporal context to be considered in both sequence directions.

The authors report that the resulting model handles videos with complex motion and achieves state-of-the-art performance. They also report low computational complexity and speeds orders of magnitude faster than other multi-frame methods, attributing the efficiency to inexpensive convolution operations. The stated contribution is a combination of temporal modeling and computational efficiency, addressing both reconstruction quality and the cost of using multiple frames.
summary.tldr: A bidirectional recurrent convolutional network uses temporal context for video super-resolution with reported gains in quality and speed.

title: Bidirectional Recurrent Convolutional Networks for Multi-Frame Super-Resolution

abstract: We present a new affine-invariant optimization algorithm called Online Lazy Newton. The regret of Online Lazy Newton is independent of conditioning: the algorithm's performance depends on the best possible preconditioning of the problem in retrospect and on its \emph{intrinsic} dimensionality. As an application, we show how Online Lazy Newton can be used to achieve an optimal regret of order $\sqrt{rT}$ for the low-rank experts problem, improving by a $\sqrt{r}$ factor over the previously best known bound and resolving an open problem posed by Hazan et al (2016).

paragraphs: Online optimization involves making decisions as information arrives, with performance assessed through regret relative to a comparison strategy. This paper introduces Online Lazy Newton, an affine-invariant algorithm. Its central theoretical property is that its regret does not depend on the conditioning of the problem as originally presented.

Instead, the guarantee reflects the best preconditioning that could have been chosen after seeing the problem, together with its intrinsic dimensionality. Preconditioning concerns how the problem is represented for optimization. The result therefore ties performance to favorable underlying structure rather than requiring the initial representation to expose that structure well.

The paper applies the algorithm to the low-rank experts problem and obtains optimal regret of order square root of rT, where r represents rank and T the number of rounds. This improves the previously best known bound by a factor of square root of r and resolves the stated open problem. The application gives a concrete consequence of the broader invariance result: low-dimensional structure yields a sharper regret guarantee.
summary.tldr: Online Lazy Newton gives conditioning-independent regret guarantees and achieves optimal square-root-of-rT regret for low-rank experts.

title: Affine-Invariant Online Optimization and the Low-rank Experts Problem

abstract: We study online reinforcement learning in average-reward stochastic games (SGs). An SG models a two-player zero-sum game in a Markov environment, where state transitions and one-step payoffs are determined simultaneously by a learner and an adversary. We propose the \textsc{UCSG} algorithm that achieves a sublinear regret compared to the game value when competing with an arbitrary opponent. This result improves previous ones under the same setting. The regret bound has a dependency on the \textit{diameter}, which is an intrinsic value related to the mixing property of SGs. Slightly extended, \textsc{UCSG} finds an $\varepsilon$-maximin stationary policy with a sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\left(\text{poly}(1/\varepsilon)\right)$, where $\varepsilon$ is the error parameter. To the best of our knowledge, this extended result is the first in the average-reward setting. In the analysis, we develop Markov chain's perturbation bounds for mean first passage times and techniques to deal with non-stationary opponents, which may be of interest in their own right.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning in two-player zero-sum stochastic games with an average-reward objective. Both the learner and an adversary influence immediate payoffs and state transitions. Learning therefore requires handling an opponent's behavior as well as uncertainty about the environment.

The proposed UCSG algorithm achieves sublinear regret relative to the game's value against an arbitrary opponent, improving previous results in the same setting. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated shortfall grows more slowly than the interaction horizon. The bound depends on the game's diameter, a quantity related to its mixing behavior, so the guarantee reflects how the dynamics allow movement through the game.

An extension finds a stationary policy that is within an error tolerance of the maximin objective, with sample complexity polynomial in the inverse tolerance up to logarithmic factors. The analysis develops perturbation bounds for Markov-chain mean first passage times and techniques for handling nonstationary opponents. These tools support guarantees in a setting where the adversary need not maintain a fixed behavior throughout learning.
summary.tldr: UCSG achieves sublinear regret in average-reward stochastic games against arbitrary opponents and can be extended to learn approximately maximin stationary policies.

title: Online Reinforcement Learning in Stochastic Games

abstract: Reasoning plays an essential role in Visual Question Answering (VQA). Multi-step and dynamic reasoning is often necessary for answering complex questions. For example, a question "What is placed next to the bus on the right of the picture?" talks about a compound object "bus on the right," which is generated by the relation . Furthermore, a new relation including this compound object is then required to infer the answer. However, previous methods support either one-step or static reasoning, without updating relations or generating compound objects. This paper proposes a novel reasoning model for addressing these problems. A chain of reasoning (CoR) is constructed for supporting multi-step and dynamic reasoning on changed relations and objects. In detail, iteratively, the relational reasoning operations form new relations between objects, and the object refining operations generate new compound objects from relations. We achieve new state-of-the-art results on four publicly available datasets. The visualization of the chain of reasoning illustrates the progress that the CoR generates new compound objects that lead to the answer of the question step by step.

paragraphs: Answering a question about an image can require several connected reasoning steps. A description may first identify an object through its relationship to something else, then use that refined object to ask about another relationship. The paper argues that methods limited to one step or fixed relations cannot adequately support this changing reasoning process.

Its chain-of-reasoning model alternates between two operations. Relational reasoning constructs new relationships among objects, while object refinement uses those relationships to create compound objects. These compound objects capture descriptions that depend on context, providing the material for the next reasoning step. The model can therefore update both what it reasons about and the relationships it considers.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on four public visual question answering datasets. Visualizations show compound objects being formed progressively as the model approaches an answer. These findings connect prediction performance with an inspectable sequence of intermediate refinements, illustrating how the proposed model handles questions whose interpretation develops over multiple steps.
summary.tldr: A visual question answering model repeatedly updates objects and their relationships to support dynamic, multi-step reasoning.

title: Chain of Reasoning for Visual Question Answering

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms can attain excellent sample efficiency, but often lag behind the best model-free algorithms in terms of asymptotic performance. This is especially true with high-capacity parametric function approximators, such as deep networks. In this paper, we study how to bridge this gap, by employing uncertainty-aware dynamics models. We propose a new algorithm called probabilistic ensembles with trajectory sampling (PETS) that combines uncertainty-aware deep network dynamics models with sampling-based uncertainty propagation. Our comparison to state-of-the-art model-based and model-free deep RL algorithms shows that our approach matches the asymptotic performance of model-free algorithms on several challenging benchmark tasks, while requiring significantly fewer samples (e.g. 8 and 125 times fewer samples than Soft Actor Critic and Proximal Policy Optimization respectively on the half-cheetah task).

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned account of an environment's dynamics to support decision making. It can learn from relatively little experience, but its eventual performance often falls below that of strong model-free methods, particularly when deep networks represent the dynamics. This paper investigates whether explicitly handling uncertainty can narrow that gap.

The proposed algorithm, probabilistic ensembles with trajectory sampling, or PETS, combines uncertainty-aware deep dynamics models with sampling-based propagation of uncertainty. The approach carries uncertainty through predicted trajectories rather than relying only on a single forecast of what will happen. This connects the representation of uncertainty in the model to its use during decision making.

On several challenging benchmark tasks, the reported comparisons show PETS matching the eventual performance of model-free algorithms while using substantially fewer samples. On half-cheetah, the abstract reports eight times fewer samples than Soft Actor Critic and 125 times fewer than Proximal Policy Optimization. These results show that, on the evaluated tasks, strong final performance and efficient use of experience can coexist within a model-based approach.
summary.tldr: PETS combines uncertainty-aware dynamics models and trajectory sampling to match model-free performance on several benchmarks using far fewer samples.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning in a Handful of Trials using Probabilistic Dynamics Models

abstract: Machine Comprehension (MC) is one of the core problems in natural language processing, requiring both understanding of the natural language and knowledge about the world. Rapid progress has been made since the release of several benchmark datasets, and recently the state-of-the-art models even surpass human performance on the well-known SQuAD evaluation. In this paper, we transfer knowledge learned from machine comprehension to the sequence-to-sequence tasks to deepen the understanding of the text. We propose MacNet: a novel encoder-decoder supplementary architecture to the widely used attention-based sequence-to-sequence models. Experiments on neural machine translation (NMT) and abstractive text summarization show that our proposed framework can significantly improve the performance of the baseline models, and our method for the abstractive text summarization achieves the state-of-the-art results on the Gigaword dataset.

paragraphs: Machine comprehension requires a model to understand language and draw on knowledge about the world. This paper asks how knowledge learned for comprehension can help tasks that transform one text sequence into another. Its goal is to bring that learned understanding into sequence-to-sequence models used for translation and summarization.

The proposed MacNet architecture supplements attention-based sequence-to-sequence systems with an encoder-decoder component. This architecture provides the means for transferring knowledge from machine comprehension into the target model. The central idea is that learning to comprehend text can supply useful information for generating a translated or summarized version of an input.

Experiments on neural machine translation and abstractive summarization show significant improvements over the baseline models. For abstractive summarization, the authors report state-of-the-art results on Gigaword. These findings support the usefulness of transferring comprehension knowledge into the evaluated generation tasks. The contribution is both an architectural addition and empirical evidence that knowledge developed for understanding text can improve models whose output is another sequence of text.
summary.tldr: MacNet transfers machine-comprehension knowledge into attention-based sequence-to-sequence models, improving reported translation and summarization performance.

title: MacNet: Transferring Knowledge from Machine Comprehension to Sequence-to-Sequence Models

abstract: Scaling decision theoretic planning to large multiagent systems is challenging due to uncertainty and partial observability in the environment. We focus on a multiagent planning model subclass, relevant to urban settings, where agent interactions are dependent on their ``collective influence'' on each other, rather than their identities. Unlike previous work, we address a general setting where system reward is not decomposable among agents. We develop collective actor-critic RL approaches for this setting, and address the problem of multiagent credit assignment, and computing low variance policy gradient estimates that result in faster convergence to high quality solutions. We also develop difference rewards based credit assignment methods for the collective setting. Empirically our new approaches provide significantly better solutions than previous methods in the presence of global rewards on two real world problems modeling taxi fleet optimization and multiagent patrolling, and a synthetic grid navigation domain.

Unlike previous work, we address a general setting where system reward is not decomposable among agents. We develop collective actor-critic RL approaches for this setting, and address the problem of multiagent credit assignment, and computing low variance policy gradient estimates that result in faster convergence to high quality solutions. paragraphs: When many agents share a system-wide reward, it can be difficult to determine which decisions helped the group. This paper studies a class of multiagent problems where agents affect one another through their collective influence rather than their identities. The setting is relevant to urban systems and includes uncertainty and partial observability.

The authors allow the reward to be nondecomposable, meaning it cannot simply be split into separate rewards for individual agents. They develop collective actor-critic reinforcement learning methods that address credit assignment and produce low-variance policy-gradient estimates. They also develop credit-assignment methods based on difference rewards for this collective setting.

The goal of these estimates is faster convergence to high-quality solutions despite having only a global reward. Empirical evaluations cover taxi fleet optimization, multiagent patrolling, and a synthetic grid-navigation problem. The proposed approaches produce significantly better solutions than previous methods in those evaluations. The findings show how exploiting collective interaction structure can help learning systems use shared feedback even when individual contributions are not supplied directly.
summary.tldr: Collective actor-critic and difference-reward methods improve multiagent credit assignment when agents share a nondecomposable global reward.

title: Credit Assignment For Collective Multiagent RL With Global Rewards

abstract: Excessive reuse of test data has become commonplace in today's machine learning workflows. Popular benchmarks, competitions, industrial scale tuning, among other applications, all involve test data reuse beyond guidance by statistical confidence bounds. Nonetheless, recent replication studies give evidence that popular benchmarks continue to support progress despite years of extensive reuse. We proffer a new explanation for the apparent longevity of test data: Many proposed models are similar in their predictions and we prove that this similarity mitigates overfitting. Specifically, we show empirically that models proposed for the ImageNet ILSVRC benchmark agree in their predictions well beyond what we can conclude from their accuracy levels alone. Likewise, models created by large scale hyperparameter search enjoy high levels of similarity. Motivated by these empirical observations, we give a non-asymptotic generalization bound that takes similarity into account, leading to meaningful confidence bounds in practical settings.

paragraphs: Repeatedly evaluating models on the same test set raises concerns about overfitting to that benchmark. Yet replication studies suggest that some heavily reused benchmarks still track meaningful progress. This paper offers an explanation based on prediction similarity: many of the models being compared behave alike on individual examples.

The authors show empirically that models submitted to the ImageNet ILSVRC benchmark agree more than their accuracy levels alone would imply. They also observe substantial similarity among models produced by large-scale hyperparameter search. These findings make agreement between predictions relevant to understanding the consequences of repeated evaluation.

Motivated by those observations, the paper proves a non-asymptotic generalization bound that explicitly incorporates model similarity. The bound yields meaningful confidence statements in practical settings and establishes that similarity can mitigate overfitting from test-set reuse. The result supplies a qualified explanation for benchmark longevity: the effects of reuse depend in part on how similar the evaluated models are, rather than solely on how often evaluation occurs.
summary.tldr: Prediction similarity helps explain benchmark longevity and enables generalization bounds that account for repeated test-set use.

title: Model Similarity Mitigates Test Set Overuse

abstract: Throughout the past five years, the susceptibility of neural networks to minimal adversarial perturbations has moved from a peculiar phenomenon to a core issue in Deep Learning. Despite much attention, however, progress towards more robust models is significantly impaired by the difficulty of evaluating the robustness of neural network models. Today's methods are either fast but brittle (gradient-based attacks), or they are fairly reliable but slow (score- and decision-based attacks). We here develop a new set of gradient-based adversarial attacks which (a) are more reliable in the face of gradient-masking than other gradient-based attacks, (b) perform better and are more query efficient than current state-of-the-art gradient-based attacks, (c) can be flexibly adapted to a wide range of adversarial criteria and (d) require virtually no hyperparameter tuning. These findings are carefully validated across a diverse set of six different models and hold for L0, L1, L2 and Linf in both targeted as well as untargeted scenarios. Implementations will soon be available in all major toolboxes (Foolbox, CleverHans and ART). We hope that this class of attacks will make robustness evaluations easier and more reliable, thus contributing to more signal in the search for more robust machine learning models.
