paragraphs: Evaluating robustness requires finding small input changes that cause a neural network to fail. An attack that misses these changes can make a vulnerable model appear stronger than it is. The paper addresses a practical tradeoff: gradient-based attacks can be fast but unreliable, while attacks using scores or decisions can be more dependable but slower.

The authors introduce a family of gradient-based attacks designed to improve both reliability and efficiency. They report greater resistance to gradient masking, where gradient information obstructs attack methods, and better performance with fewer queries than existing leading gradient-based attacks. The attacks also accommodate different adversarial criteria and require almost no hyperparameter tuning.

The evaluation covers six models, four perturbation measures—L0, L1, L2, and Linf—and both targeted and untargeted attacks. The reported advantages hold across those tested settings. These results support using the attacks to make robustness assessments more informative and easier to conduct; the contribution concerns how accurately vulnerabilities are exposed, rather than a method for training stronger models.
summary.tldr: A family of gradient-based attacks improves the reliability and query efficiency of robustness evaluation across several tested models and attack settings.

title: Accurate, reliable and fast robustness evaluation

abstract: Label switching is a phenomenon arising in mixture model posterior inference that prevents one from meaningfully assessing posterior statistics using standard Monte Carlo procedures. This issue arises due to invariance of the posterior under actions of a group; for example, permuting the ordering of mixture components has no effect on the likelihood. We propose a resolution to label switching that leverages machinery from optimal transport. Our algorithm efficiently computes posterior statistics in the quotient space of the symmetry group. We give conditions under which there is a meaningful solution to label switching and demonstrate advantages over alternative approaches on simulated and real data.

This issue arises due to invariance of the posterior under actions of a group; for example, permuting the ordering of mixture components has no effect on the likelihood. We propose a resolution to label switching that leverages machinery from optimal transport. Our algorithm efficiently computes posterior statistics in the quotient space of the symmetry group. We give conditions under which there is a meaningful solution to label switching and demonstrate advantages over alternative approaches on simulated and real data.

paragraphs: Mixture models describe data using multiple components, but the names or ordering of those components need not have statistical meaning. Permuting their labels can leave the likelihood unchanged. During posterior inference, this symmetry creates label switching, which prevents standard Monte Carlo summaries from meaningfully tracking component-specific quantities.

The paper addresses the issue using optimal transport. Its algorithm computes posterior statistics in a quotient space of the symmetry group. In plain language, this means treating descriptions that differ only through the relevant symmetry as equivalent. The statistical summary is therefore organized around the underlying model rather than an arbitrary assignment of component labels.

The authors give conditions under which resolving label switching in this way has a meaningful solution. They also report advantages over alternative approaches on both simulated and real data. The approach matters because it incorporates the source of the ambiguity directly into posterior computation, while the stated conditions clarify that a meaningful resolution depends on the structure of the problem.
summary.tldr: An optimal-transport approach computes mixture-model posterior summaries while accounting for symmetries that cause label switching.

title: Alleviating Label Switching with Optimal Transport

abstract: We study the adversarial multi-armed bandit problem where the learner is supplied with partial observations modeled by a \emph{feedback graph} and where shifting to a new action incurs a fixed \emph{switching cost}. We give two new algorithms for this problem in the informed setting. Our best algorithm achieves a pseudo-regret of $\tilde O(\gamma(G)^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}})$, where $\gamma(G)$ is the domination number of the feedback graph. This significantly improves upon the previous best result for the same problem, which was based on the independence number of $G$. We also present matching lower bounds for our result that we describe in detail. Finally, we give a new algorithm with improved policy regret bounds when partial counterfactual feedback is available.
originalAbstract: We study the adversarial multi-armed bandit problem where the learner is supplied with partial observations modeled by a \emph{feedback graph} and where shifting to a new action incurs a fixed \emph{switching cost}. We give two new algorithms for this problem in the informed setting. Our best algorithm achieves a pseudo-regret of $\tilde O(\gamma(G)^{\frac{1}{3}}T^{\frac{2}{3}})$, where $\gamma(G)$ is the domination number of the feedback graph. This significantly improves upon the previous best result for the same problem, which was based on the independence number of $G$. We also present matching lower bounds for our result that we describe in detail. Finally, we give a new algorithm with improved policy regret bounds when partial counterfactual feedback is available.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decisions where actions have adversarially chosen losses, observations are incomplete, and changing actions carries a fixed cost. A feedback graph describes which observations become available after an action. The learner therefore has to balance gathering useful information, choosing low-loss actions, and avoiding expensive switching.

The authors introduce two algorithms for the informed setting. Their strongest pseudo-regret bound scales as the cube root of the graph's domination number times the number of rounds to the two-thirds power, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The domination number captures how small a collection of actions can provide coverage of the feedback graph. Using this quantity substantially improves the previous bound, which depended on the graph's independence number.

Matching lower bounds establish corresponding limits on achievable performance for the result studied. The paper also considers access to partial counterfactual feedback and gives an algorithm with improved policy regret bounds in that setting. Together, the results connect the structure of available information to learning performance when switching itself is costly.
summary.tldr: New bandit algorithms use feedback-graph structure to improve regret guarantees when changing actions incurs a cost.

title: Bandits with Feedback Graphs and Switching Costs

abstract: Providing feedback is an integral part of teaching. Most open online courses on programming make use of automated grading systems to support programming assignments and give real-time feedback. These systems usually rely on test results to quantify the programs' functional correctness. They return failing tests to the students as feedback. However, students may find it difficult to debug their programs if they receive no hints about where the bug is and how to fix it. In this work, we present NeuralBugLocator, a deep learning based technique, that can localize the bugs in a faulty program with respect to a failing test, without even running the program. At the heart of our technique is a novel tree convolutional neural network which is trained to predict whether a program passes or fails a given test. To localize the bugs, we analyze the trained network using a state-of-the-art neural prediction attribution technique and see which lines of the programs make it predict the test outcomes. Our experiments show that NeuralBugLocator is generally more accurate than two state-of-the-art program-spectrum based and one syntactic difference based bug-localization baselines.

paragraphs: Automated programming graders often tell students which tests failed, but that feedback may give little guidance about where to look in the code. NeuralBugLocator addresses this gap by identifying likely bug locations relative to a failing test. Its localization procedure does not require running the program.

The method first trains a tree convolutional neural network to predict whether a program passes or fails a particular test. It then applies neural prediction attribution to the trained model, examining which program lines contribute to the predicted outcome. This connects a model's correctness prediction to a location-based explanation that can help focus debugging.

Experiments show that NeuralBugLocator is generally more accurate than two program-spectrum baselines and one baseline based on syntactic differences. The finding concerns the accuracy of locating bugs, with the qualification that the advantage is general rather than universal. The practical contribution is to turn predicted test behavior into more targeted feedback than a failing-test report alone provides.
summary.tldr: NeuralBugLocator attributes predicted test outcomes to program lines to locate bugs without executing the program.

title: Neural Attribution for Semantic Bug-Localization in Student Programs

abstract: Deep neural networks have revolutionized many real world applications, due to their flexibility in data fitting and accurate predictions for unseen data. A line of research reveals that neural networks can approximate certain classes of functions with an arbitrary accuracy, while the size of the network scales exponentially with respect to the data dimension. Empirical results, however, suggest that networks of moderate size already yield appealing performance. To explain such a gap, a common belief is that many data sets exhibit low dimensional structures, and can be modeled as samples near a low dimensional manifold. In this paper, we prove that neural networks can efficiently approximate functions supported on low dimensional manifolds. The network size scales exponentially in the approximation error, with an exponent depending on the intrinsic dimension of the data and the smoothness of the function. Our result shows that exploiting low dimensional data structures can greatly enhance the efficiency in function approximation by neural networks. We also implement a sub-network that assigns input data to their corresponding local neighborhoods, which may be of independent interest.

Our result shows that exploiting low dimensional data structures can greatly enhance the efficiency in function approximation by neural networks. We also implement a sub-network that assigns input data to their corresponding local neighborhoods, which may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Neural network approximation theory can predict network sizes that grow sharply with data dimension, yet moderately sized networks often work well in practice. This paper investigates a proposed explanation: data may occupy a structure with far fewer dimensions than the surrounding input space. Its theoretical setting considers functions supported on low-dimensional manifolds.

The authors prove that neural networks can approximate such functions efficiently. The size requirement depends on the requested approximation accuracy, with an exponent determined by the data’s intrinsic dimension and the function’s smoothness. This identifies the dimension of the underlying structure as a key quantity in the approximation result and gives mathematical support to the value of exploiting that structure.

The work also implements a subnetwork that assigns inputs to their corresponding local neighborhoods. This supplies a concrete component for organizing computation around the manifold’s local structure. Together, the approximation result and neighborhood assignment construction help explain how low-dimensional organization can make function approximation more efficient, within the setting of functions supported on such manifolds.
summary.tldr: The paper proves efficient neural network approximation for functions on low-dimensional manifolds, with size requirements governed by intrinsic dimension and smoothness.

title: Efficient Approximation of Deep ReLU Networks for Functions on Low Dimensional Manifolds

abstract: It is believed that a model-based approach for reinforcement learning (RL) is the key to reduce sample complexity. However, the understanding of the sample optimality of model-based RL is still largely missing, even for the linear case. This work considers sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP) that admits a linear additive feature representation, given only access to a generative model. We solve this problem via a plug-in solver approach, which builds an empirical model and plans in this empirical model via an arbitrary plug-in solver. We prove that under the anchor-state assumption, which implies implicit non-negativity in the feature space, the minimax sample complexity of finding an $\epsilon$-optimal policy in a $\gamma$-discounted MDP is $O(K/(1-\gamma)^3\epsilon^2)$, which only depends on the dimensionality $K$ of the feature space and has no dependence on the state or action space. We further extend our results to a relaxed setting where anchor-states may not exist and show that a plug-in approach can be sample efficient as well, providing a flexible approach to design model-based algorithms for RL.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning first estimates an environment and then plans within that estimate. This paper asks whether this straightforward separation can use samples efficiently when a Markov decision process has a linear additive feature representation. The learner is assumed to have access to a generative model that supplies samples.

The proposed approach builds an empirical model and passes it to an arbitrary plug-in planning solver. Under an anchor-state assumption, which entails implicit non-negativity in feature space, the authors establish minimax sample complexity of order K divided by the product of (1 − gamma) cubed and epsilon squared. Here K is the feature dimension, gamma is the discount factor, and epsilon specifies the desired policy accuracy.

The bound depends on feature dimension rather than the number of states or actions. This gives theoretical support to estimating a model and then using a separate planner under the stated assumptions. The authors also study a relaxed setting without guaranteed anchor states and show that a plug-in approach can remain sample efficient. That extension broadens the approach's scope without asserting the same minimax result for every feature representation.
summary.tldr: Under an anchor-state assumption, estimating a feature-based environment model and planning in it achieves minimax sample efficiency.

title: Is Plug-in Solver Sample-Efficient for Feature-based Reinforcement Learning?

abstract: We provide a static data structure for distance estimation which supports {\it adaptive} queries. Concretely, given a dataset $X = \{x_i\}_{i = 1}^n$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and $0 < p \leq 2$, we construct a randomized data structure with low memory consumption and query time which, when later given any query point $q \in \mathbb{R}^d$, outputs a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation of $\|q - x_i\|_p$ with high probability for all $i\in[n]$. The main novelty is our data structure's correctness guarantee holds even when the sequence of queries can be chosen adaptively: an adversary is allowed to choose the $j$th query point $q_j$ in a way that depends on the answers reported by the data structure for $q_1,\ldots,q_{j-1}$. Previous randomized Monte Carlo methods do not provide error guarantees in the setting of adaptively chosen queries. Our memory consumption is $\tilde O(nd/\varepsilon^2)$, slightly more than the $O(nd)$ required to store $X$ in memory explicitly, but with the benefit that our time to answer queries is only $\tilde O(\varepsilon^{-2}(n + d))$, much faster than the naive $\Theta(nd)$ time obtained from a linear scan in the case of $n$ and $d$ very large. Here $\tilde O$ hides $\log(nd/\varepsilon)$ factors. We discuss applications to nearest neighbor search and nonparametric estimation. Our method is simple and likely to applicable to other domains: we describe a generic approach for transforming randomized Monte Carlo data structures which do not support adaptive queries to ones that do, and show that for the problem at hand it can be applied to standard nonadaptive solutions to $\ell_p$ norm estimation with negligible overhead in query time and a factor $d$ overhead in memory.

paragraphs: A distance-estimation data structure preprocesses a fixed dataset so it can quickly estimate distances from new query points. Randomized methods become harder to trust when later queries depend on earlier answers, because the queries can react to the structure's own randomness. This paper provides guarantees that survive such adaptive querying.

For n points in d dimensions and p between zero and two, the structure estimates every query-to-data-point distance with a multiplicative approximation controlled by epsilon, with high probability. Its guarantee allows even an adversary to choose each query after seeing previous responses. This addresses a dependency that prior nonadaptive Monte Carlo guarantees do not cover.

Ignoring logarithmic factors, memory scales as nd divided by epsilon squared, while query time scales as n plus d divided by epsilon squared. The latter improves on scanning every coordinate of every point when both dimensions are large. The authors also describe a general transformation for supporting adaptivity, apply it to standard distance-estimation methods, and discuss nearest-neighbor search and nonparametric estimation.
summary.tldr: A randomized distance-estimation structure retains high-probability accuracy even when queries adapt to its previous answers.

title: On Adaptive Distance Estimation

abstract: Many approaches have been proposed for time series forecasting, in light of its significance in wide applications including business demand prediction. However, the existing methods suffer from two key limitations. Firstly, most point prediction models only predict an exact value of each time step without flexibility, which can hardly capture the stochasticity of data. Even probabilistic prediction using the likelihood estimation suffers these problems in the same way. Besides, most of them use the auto-regressive generative mode, where ground-truth is provided during training and replaced by the network’s own one-step ahead output during inference, causing the error accumulation in inference. Thus they may fail to forecast time series for long time horizon due to the error accumulation. To solve these issues, in this paper, we propose a new time series forecasting model -- Adversarial Sparse Transformer (AST), based on Generated Adversarial Networks (GANs). Specifically, AST adopts a Sparse Transformer as the generator to learn a sparse attention map for time series forecasting, and uses a discriminator to improve the prediction performance from sequence level. Extensive experiments on several real-world datasets show the effectiveness and efficiency of our method.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting must account for variability in future observations and for errors that can compound over a long forecast. The paper highlights a training-to-inference mismatch in autoregressive prediction: training uses observed previous values, whereas inference feeds the model its own earlier predictions. Errors can therefore become inputs to subsequent predictions.

The proposed Adversarial Sparse Transformer, or AST, combines a Sparse Transformer generator with a discriminator. The generator learns a sparse attention map for forecasting, giving the model a learned pattern of connections within the sequence. The discriminator contributes a sequence-level training signal, so prediction quality is assessed across a sequence rather than only through individual forecast values.

This design brings sparse attention and adversarial learning together to address the forecasting problems identified by the authors. Experiments on several real-world datasets report that AST is effective and efficient. Those findings support the combined approach in the evaluated settings; the abstract does not establish that accumulated prediction errors disappear or that every future outcome is captured.
summary.tldr: AST combines learned sparse attention with sequence-level adversarial training to improve time series forecasting.

title: Adversarial Sparse Transformer for Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We consider the setting where players run the Hedge algorithm or its optimistic variant \cite{syrgkanis2015fast} to play an n-action game repeatedly for T rounds. 1) For two-player games, we show that the regret of optimistic Hedge decays at \tilde{O}( 1/T ^{5/6} ), improving the previous bound O(1/T^{3/4}) by \cite{syrgkanis2015fast}. 2) In contrast, we show that the convergence rate of vanilla Hedge is no better than \tilde{\Omega}(1/ \sqrt{T})}, addressing an open question posted in \cite{syrgkanis2015fast}. For general m-player games, we show that the swap regret of each player decays at rate \tilde{O}(m^{1/2} (n/T)^{3/4}) when they combine optimistic Hedge with the classical external-to-internal reduction of Blum and Mansour \cite{blum2007external}. The algorithm can also be modified to achieve the same rate against itself and a rate of \tilde{O}(\sqrt{n/T}) against adversaries. Via standard connections, our upper bounds also imply faster convergence to coarse correlated equilibria in two-player games and to correlated equilibria in multiplayer games.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated games in which players choose among n actions for T rounds using Hedge or its optimistic variant. Regret measures the advantage of alternative choices in hindsight. External regret compares against a fixed action, while swap regret considers replacing each chosen action according to a consistent mapping. Lower regret also connects learning behavior to game-theoretic equilibrium.

For two-player games, the authors improve the optimistic Hedge regret decay bound to roughly T^(-5/6), suppressing logarithmic factors, from the previous T^(-3/4) bound. They also show that ordinary Hedge cannot generally improve beyond a roughly T^(-1/2) rate. This establishes a theoretical separation between the two methods in this setting.

For m-player games, combining optimistic Hedge with a standard regret reduction yields swap regret decay of roughly m^(1/2)(n/T)^(3/4). A modification retains that rate in self-play and achieves roughly sqrt(n/T) against adversaries. Through standard connections between regret and equilibrium, the upper bounds imply faster convergence to coarse correlated equilibria for two players and correlated equilibria for multiple players.
summary.tldr: The paper proves faster regret decay for optimistic Hedge in repeated games and establishes a slower worst-case rate for ordinary Hedge.

title: Hedging in games: Faster convergence of external and swap regrets

abstract: In safety-critical but computationally resource-constrained applications, deep learning faces two key challenges: lack of robustness against adversarial attacks and large neural network size (often millions of parameters). While the research community has extensively explored the use of robust training and network pruning \emph{independently} to address one of these challenges, only a few recent works have studied them jointly. However, these works inherit a heuristic pruning strategy that was developed for benign training, which performs poorly when integrated with robust training techniques, including adversarial training and verifiable robust training. To overcome this challenge, we propose to make pruning techniques aware of the robust training objective and let the training objective guide the search for which connections to prune. We realize this insight by formulating the pruning objective as an empirical risk minimization problem which is solved efficiently using SGD. We demonstrate that our approach, titled HYDRA, achieves compressed networks with \textit{state-of-the-art} benign and robust accuracy, \textit{simultaneously}. We demonstrate the success of our approach across CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet dataset with four robust training techniques: iterative adversarial training, randomized smoothing, MixTrain, and CROWN-IBP. We also demonstrate the existence of highly robust sub-networks within non-robust networks.

paragraphs: Deploying neural networks under tight computational constraints can require both a smaller model and resistance to adversarial inputs. These objectives are often studied separately. This paper finds that pruning heuristics developed for ordinary training perform poorly when combined with robust training, motivating a pruning procedure that directly accounts for the robustness objective.

HYDRA lets the training objective guide which network connections should be removed. It expresses pruning as an empirical risk minimization problem and solves it efficiently using stochastic gradient descent. This makes the choice of retained connections responsive to the behavior the robust training process is trying to achieve.

The authors report compressed networks with state-of-the-art accuracy on both benign and adversarial inputs simultaneously. They evaluate CIFAR-10, SVHN, and ImageNet using iterative adversarial training, randomized smoothing, MixTrain, and CROWN-IBP. They also demonstrate highly robust subnetworks inside non-robust networks. These findings support coordinating compression with robust learning and show that the robustness of a whole network need not describe every subnetwork it contains.
summary.tldr: HYDRA uses the robust training objective to guide pruning, producing compressed networks with leading benign and robust accuracy in the reported experiments.

title: HYDRA: Pruning Adversarially Robust Neural Networks

abstract: This paper considers a canonical clustering problem where one receives unlabeled samples drawn from a balanced mixture of two elliptical distributions and aims for a classifier to estimate the labels. Many popular methods including PCA and k-means require individual components of the mixture to be somewhat spherical, and perform poorly when they are stretched. To overcome this issue, we propose a non-convex program seeking for an affine transform to turn the data into a one-dimensional point cloud concentrating around -1 and 1, after which clustering becomes easy. Our theoretical contributions are two-fold: (1) we show that the non-convex loss function exhibits desirable geometric properties when the sample size exceeds some constant multiple of the dimension, and (2) we leverage this to prove that an efficient first-order algorithm achieves near-optimal statistical precision without good initialization. We also propose a general methodology for clustering with flexible choices of feature transforms and loss objectives.

paragraphs: The paper studies clustering samples from a balanced mixture of two elliptical distributions. When these distributions are stretched, methods such as PCA and k-means can perform poorly because their success depends on components being sufficiently spherical. The objective is to estimate the hidden labels despite that elongated geometry.

The proposed method learns an affine transformation that maps the data into one dimension, with points concentrated near minus one and plus one. Once that transformation is found, the two groups become easy to distinguish. Finding it requires solving a nonconvex optimization problem, so the geometry of the objective is central to whether the approach is practical.

The authors show favorable properties of this objective when the sample size exceeds a constant multiple of the dimension. Using those properties, they prove that an efficient first-order algorithm achieves near-optimal statistical precision without needing a good initialization. They also propose a broader clustering methodology allowing flexible feature transformations and losses. The result links a useful transformed representation to guarantees for actually finding it.
summary.tldr: Learning an affine map to two one-dimensional clusters enables efficient, near-optimal clustering of balanced stretched mixtures under a sample-size condition.

title: Efficient Clustering for Stretched Mixtures: Landscape and Optimality

abstract: Recent studies show that advanced priors play a major role in deep generative models. Exemplar VAE, as a variant of VAE with an exemplar-based prior, has achieved impressive results. However, due to the nature of model design, an exemplar-based model usually requires vast amounts of data to participate in training, which leads to huge computational complexity. To address this issue, we propose Bayesian Pseudocoresets Exemplar VAE (ByPE-VAE), a new variant of VAE with a prior based on Bayesian pseudocoreset. The proposed prior is conditioned on a small-scale pseudocoreset rather than the whole dataset for reducing the computational cost and avoiding overfitting. Simultaneously, we obtain the optimal pseudocoreset via a stochastic optimization algorithm during VAE training aiming to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the prior based on the pseudocoreset and that based on the whole dataset. Experimental results show that ByPE-VAE can achieve competitive improvements over the state-of-the-art VAEs in the tasks of density estimation, representation learning, and generative data augmentation. Particularly, on a basic VAE architecture, ByPE-VAE is up to 3 times faster than Exemplar VAE while almost holding the performance. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Aiqz/ByPE-VAE}.

paragraphs: Exemplar variational autoencoders use a prior informed by examples from a dataset, but involving large amounts of data in that prior can make training expensive. ByPE-VAE replaces the full collection with a small Bayesian pseudocoreset. This compact collection supplies the information used to condition the prior, with the aim of reducing computation and avoiding overfitting.

The pseudocoreset is optimized during VAE training rather than simply selected once and left unchanged. A stochastic optimization procedure seeks to minimize the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the pseudocoreset-based prior and the prior based on the complete dataset. The design therefore gives the smaller prior an explicit target: approximate the distributional behavior of its full-data counterpart.

Experiments report competitive improvements in density estimation, representation learning, and generative data augmentation. On a basic VAE architecture, the method runs up to three times faster than Exemplar VAE while nearly retaining its performance. That result supports the practical value of learning a compact prior representation, with the stated speed comparison tied to that architecture.
summary.tldr: ByPE-VAE learns a small pseudocoreset-based prior to reduce exemplar VAE computation while largely preserving performance.

title: ByPE-VAE: Bayesian Pseudocoresets Exemplar VAE

abstract: Gaussian Process models are a rich distribution over functions with inductive biases controlled by a kernel function. Learning occurs through optimisation of the kernel hyperparameters using the marginal likelihood as the objective. This work proposes nested sampling as a means of marginalising kernel hyperparameters, because it is a technique that is well-suited to exploring complex, multi-modal distributions. We benchmark against Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on time-series and two-dimensional regression tasks, finding that a principled approach to quantifying hyperparameter uncertainty substantially improves the quality of prediction intervals.
originalAbstract: Gaussian Process models are a rich distribution over functions with inductive biases controlled by a kernel function. Learning occurs through optimisation of the kernel hyperparameters using the marginal likelihood as the objective. This work proposes nested sampling as a means of marginalising kernel hyperparameters, because it is a technique that is well-suited to exploring complex, multi-modal distributions. We benchmark against Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on time-series and two-dimensional regression tasks, finding that a principled approach to quantifying hyperparameter uncertainty substantially improves the quality of prediction intervals.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes describe a distribution over possible functions. Their kernel controls the kinds of patterns the model tends to expect, and kernel hyperparameters adjust those preferences. A common learning approach selects hyperparameters by optimizing marginal likelihood. This paper studies how to account for uncertainty about those settings in the predictions.

The authors propose using nested sampling to marginalize kernel hyperparameters: predictions incorporate a range of plausible settings instead of relying on one optimized choice. Nested sampling is motivated by its suitability for complex distributions with multiple modes. In this setting, multiple modes correspond to distinct plausible regions of hyperparameter values that uncertainty estimation needs to consider.

The study compares the approach with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo on time-series and two-dimensional regression problems. The reported finding is that principled treatment of hyperparameter uncertainty substantially improves prediction intervals. This places the emphasis on how well predictions express uncertainty, and shows why uncertainty about the kernel itself can matter to the final predictive distribution.
summary.tldr: Nested sampling integrates Gaussian process kernel uncertainty, with experiments finding substantial improvements in prediction intervals.

title: Marginalised Gaussian Processes with Nested Sampling

abstract: Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) [Ho et al. 2021] have shown impressive results on image and waveform generation in continuous state spaces. Here, we introduce Discrete Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (D3PMs), diffusion-like generative models for discrete data that generalize the multinomial diffusion model of Hoogeboom et al. [2021], by going beyond corruption processes with uniform transition probabilities. This includes corruption with transition matrices that mimic Gaussian kernels in continuous space, matrices based on nearest neighbors in embedding space, and matrices that introduce absorbing states. The third allows us to draw a connection between diffusion models and autoregressive and mask-based generative models. We show that the choice of transition matrix is an important design decision that leads to improved results in image and text domains. We also introduce a new loss function that combines the variational lower bound with an auxiliary cross entropy loss. For text, this model class achieves strong results on character-level text generation while scaling to large vocabularies on LM1B. On the image dataset CIFAR-10, our models approach the sample quality and exceed the log-likelihood of the continuous-space DDPM model.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a corruption process. This paper develops discrete denoising diffusion probabilistic models, or D3PMs, for data with discrete states. The main extension is to allow structured transition probabilities during corruption, expanding beyond a process that treats transitions uniformly.

The authors investigate transition matrices that resemble Gaussian kernels, matrices based on neighboring items in an embedding space, and matrices containing absorbing states. The absorbing-state construction connects diffusion with autoregressive and mask-based generation. They also introduce a training objective combining a variational lower bound with an auxiliary cross-entropy loss. These choices make the corruption structure and learning objective explicit parts of model design.

Experiments show that the transition matrix affects performance in both image and text generation. The models achieve strong character-level text results and scale to large vocabularies on LM1B. On CIFAR-10, they approach the sample quality of a continuous-space DDPM while exceeding its log-likelihood. Those are distinct findings: visual sample quality is reported as approaching the comparison model, whereas likelihood is reported as better.
summary.tldr: D3PMs use structured discrete corruption processes and a combined loss to improve diffusion-based image and text generation.

title: Structured Denoising Diffusion Models in Discrete State-Spaces

abstract: Motivated by packet routing in computer networks, online queuing systems are composed of queues receiving packets at different rates. Repeatedly, they send packets to servers, each of them treating only at most one packet at a time. In the centralized case, the number of accumulated packets remains bounded (i.e., the system is stable) as long as the ratio between service rates and arrival rates is larger than $1$. In the decentralized case, individual no-regret strategies ensures stability when this ratio is larger than $2$. Yet, myopically minimizing regret disregards the long term effects due to the carryover of packets to further rounds. On the other hand, minimizing long term costs leads to stable Nash equilibria as soon as the ratio exceeds $\frac{e}{e-1}$. Stability with decentralized learning strategies with a ratio below $2$ was a major remaining question. We first argue that for ratios up to $2$, cooperation is required for stability of learning strategies, as selfish minimization of policy regret, a patient notion of regret, might indeed still be unstable in this case. We therefore consider cooperative queues and propose the first learning decentralized algorithm guaranteeing stability of the system as long as the ratio of rates is larger than $1$, thus reaching performances comparable to centralized strategies.

paragraphs: The paper considers queues that continually receive packets and send them to servers, each able to process at most one packet at a time. The central concern is stability: keeping accumulated packets bounded. Centralized strategies can guarantee stability when the service-to-arrival rate ratio exceeds one, whereas individual no-regret strategies have a known guarantee above two.

A difficulty with decentralized learning is that today's decisions affect tomorrow's backlog. Minimizing immediate regret can overlook this carryover. The authors show that even the more patient objective of policy regret can permit instability for ratios up to two. Thus, simply making selfish learners more forward-looking does not resolve the coordination problem.

The proposed algorithm instead uses cooperative queues while keeping learning decentralized. It guarantees stability whenever the rate ratio exceeds one, matching the stated centralized threshold. The contribution closes the gap below two for cooperative decentralized learning and identifies cooperation as an essential part of obtaining the stronger guarantee in the setting studied.
summary.tldr: A cooperative decentralized learning algorithm stabilizes queues at the same stated service-to-arrival threshold as centralized strategies.

title: Decentralized Learning in Online Queuing Systems

abstract: Deep Learning methods are known to suffer from calibration issues: they typically produce over-confident estimates. These problems are exacerbated in the low data regime. Although the calibration of probabilistic models is well studied, calibrating extremely over-parametrized models in the low-data regime presents unique challenges. We show that deep-ensembles do not necessarily lead to improved calibration properties. In fact, we show that standard ensembling methods, when used in conjunction with modern techniques such as mixup regularization, can lead to less calibrated models. This text examines the interplay between three of the most simple and commonly used approaches to leverage deep learning when data is scarce: data-augmentation, ensembling, and post-processing calibration methods. We demonstrate that, although standard ensembling techniques certainly help to boost accuracy, the calibration of deep ensembles relies on subtle trade-offs. We also find that calibration methods such as temperature scaling need to be slightly tweaked when used with deep-ensembles and, crucially, need to be executed after the averaging process. Our simulations indicate that, in the low data regime, this simple strategy can halve the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) on a range of benchmark classification problems when compared to standard deep-ensembles.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict accurately while expressing too much confidence. This paper examines that calibration problem for heavily overparameterized models trained with little data, focusing on the interaction among data augmentation, model ensembles, and calibration after training.

The authors show that combining models does not necessarily improve calibration. Standard ensembling can even worsen it when paired with techniques such as mixup regularization. Consequently, the accuracy gains from an ensemble do not by themselves establish that its confidence estimates are more reliable.

The paper finds that calibration methods such as temperature scaling need adjustment for ensembles and should be applied after the predictions have been averaged. The order matters because the confidence estimates ultimately used are those of the combined predictor.

In low-data simulations across several classification benchmarks, this strategy can halve Expected Calibration Error relative to standard deep ensembles. The result supports treating calibration of the final ensemble as its own step, while preserving the distinction between empirical calibration improvements and the accuracy benefits of ensembling.
summary.tldr: Deep ensembles can worsen calibration, but calibrating after averaging can substantially improve confidence estimates in low-data settings.

title: Uncertainty Quantification and Deep Ensembles

abstract: The policy gradient theorem states that the policy should only be updated in states that are visited by the current policy, which leads to insufficient planning in the off-policy states, and thus to convergence to suboptimal policies. We tackle this planning issue by extending the policy gradient theory to policy updates with respect to any state density. Under these generalized policy updates, we show convergence to optimality under a necessary and sufficient condition on the updates’ state densities, and thereby solve the aforementioned planning issue. We also prove asymptotic convergence rates that significantly improve those in the policy gradient literature. To implement the principles prescribed by our theory, we propose an agent, Dr Jekyll & Mr Hyde (J&H), with a double personality: Dr Jekyll purely exploits while Mr Hyde purely explores. J&H’s independent policies allow to record two separate replay buffers: one on-policy (Dr Jekyll’s) and one off-policy (Mr Hyde’s), and therefore to update J&H’s models with a mixture of on-policy and off-policy updates. More than an algorithm, J&H defines principles for actor-critic algorithms to satisfy the requirements we identify in our analysis. We extensively test on finite MDPs where J&H demonstrates a superior ability to recover from converging to a suboptimal policy without impairing its speed of convergence. We also implement a deep version of the algorithm and test it on a simple problem where it shows promising results.

paragraphs: Policy updates focused on states visited by the current policy can leave other states insufficiently considered, contributing to convergence on a suboptimal policy. This paper extends policy gradient theory to updates defined using arbitrary state distributions. It establishes a necessary and sufficient condition on those distributions for convergence to optimality under the generalized updates.

The analysis also gives improved asymptotic convergence rates. To put its principles into practice, the authors introduce an agent with two independent policies: Dr Jekyll exploits current knowledge, while Mr Hyde explores. Their experience is stored in separate replay buffers, enabling a mixture of on-policy and off-policy updates.

Experiments on finite Markov decision processes show stronger recovery from convergence toward suboptimal policies without slowing convergence. A deep version produces promising results on a simple problem. The broader contribution is a set of principles for actor-critic methods: exploration and exploitation can generate distinct experience sources, and their use in updates should meet the state-distribution requirements identified by the theory.
summary.tldr: Generalized policy-update theory motivates separate exploring and exploiting policies that help an agent recover from suboptimal behavior.

title: Dr Jekyll & Mr Hyde: the strange case of off-policy policy updates

abstract: We study the problem of inferring heterogeneous treatment effects from time-to-event data. While both the related problems of (i) estimating treatment effects for binary or continuous outcomes and (ii) predicting survival outcomes have been well studied in the recent machine learning literature, their combination -- albeit of high practical relevance -- has received considerably less attention. With the ultimate goal of reliably estimating the effects of treatments on instantaneous risk and survival probabilities, we focus on the problem of learning (discrete-time) treatment-specific conditional hazard functions. We find that unique challenges arise in this context due to a variety of covariate shift issues that go beyond a mere combination of well-studied confounding and censoring biases. We theoretically analyse their effects by adapting recent generalization bounds from domain adaptation and treatment effect estimation to our setting and discuss implications for model design. We use the resulting insights to propose a novel deep learning method for treatment-specific hazard estimation based on balancing representations. We investigate performance across a range of experimental settings and empirically confirm that our method outperforms baselines by addressing covariate shifts from various sources.

paragraphs: SurvITE studies how treatment effects vary across individuals when the outcome is the time until an event. This combines treatment-effect estimation with survival analysis. The paper focuses on discrete-time, treatment-specific conditional hazard functions, which describe event risk at a given time conditional on survival so far and the relevant individual information.

The authors identify several covariate-shift challenges in this setting that go beyond simply combining familiar confounding and censoring biases. They analyze these shifts by adapting generalization bounds from domain adaptation and treatment-effect estimation. This theoretical analysis informs the design of a deep learning method that balances learned representations for treatment-specific hazard estimation.

Across a range of experimental settings, the resulting method outperforms baselines by addressing covariate shifts from multiple sources. The significance is that estimating treatment effects over time requires attention to how the populations relevant to learning and prediction differ. The framework targets hazard estimation as a route toward understanding treatment effects on instantaneous risk and survival probabilities, bringing those distributional differences into both the analysis and model design.
summary.tldr: SurvITE uses balanced representations to address multiple covariate shifts when estimating treatment-specific risks from time-to-event data.

title: SurvITE: Learning Heterogeneous Treatment Effects from Time-to-Event Data

abstract: We study the sample complexity of teaching, termed as "teaching dimension" (TD) in the literature, for the learning-with-equivalence-queries (LwEQ) paradigm. More concretely, we consider a learner who asks equivalence queries (i.e., "is the queried hypothesis the target hypothesis?"), and a teacher responds either "yes" or "no" along with a counterexample to the queried hypothesis. This learning paradigm has been extensively studied when the learner receives worst-case or random counterexamples; in this paper, we consider the optimal teacher who picks best-case counterexamples to teach the target hypothesis within a hypothesis class. For this optimal teacher, we introduce LwEQ-TD, a notion of TD capturing the teaching complexity (i.e., the number of queries made) in this paradigm. We show that a significant reduction in queries can be achieved with best-case counterexamples, in contrast to worst-case or random counterexamples, for different hypothesis classes. Furthermore, we establish new connections of LwEQ-TD to the well-studied notions of TD in the learning-from-samples paradigm.

paragraphs: The paper studies a teaching interaction in which a learner proposes a hypothesis and asks whether it is correct. A teacher either confirms it or provides a counterexample showing where it fails. Earlier work extensively considered random or worst-case counterexamples. Here, the teacher deliberately chooses the most helpful available counterexamples for teaching a target hypothesis.

The authors introduce LwEQ-TD, a teaching-dimension measure for this equivalence-query setting. It captures teaching complexity through the number of queries needed when counterexamples are selected by an optimal teacher. This makes the teacher's ability to choose informative corrections an explicit part of the mathematical problem, rather than treating every valid counterexample as equally useful.

For different hypothesis classes, the paper shows that best-case counterexamples can substantially reduce query requirements compared with random or worst-case responses. It also establishes connections with existing teaching-dimension notions for learning from samples. These results clarify how purposeful feedback can change learning complexity and relate an interactive teaching process to more familiar settings where the teacher supplies examples directly.
summary.tldr: An optimal teacher can substantially reduce equivalence queries by selecting helpful counterexamples, formalized through a new teaching-dimension measure.

title: Teaching via Best-Case Counterexamples in the Learning-with-Equivalence-Queries Paradigm

abstract: Multi-epoch, small-batch, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) has been the method of choice for learning with large over-parameterized models. A popular theory for explaining why SGD works well in practice is that the algorithm has an implicit regularization that biases its output towards a good solution. Perhaps the theoretically most well understood learning setting for SGD is that of Stochastic Convex Optimization (SCO), where it is well known that SGD learns at a rate of $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, where $n$ is the number of samples. In this paper, we consider the problem of SCO and explore the role of implicit regularization, batch size and multiple epochs for SGD. Our main contributions are threefold: * We show that for any regularizer, there is an SCO problem for which Regularized Empirical Risk Minimzation fails to learn. This automatically rules out any implicit regularization based explanation for the success of SGD.* We provide a separation between SGD and learning via Gradient Descent on empirical loss (GD) in terms of sample complexity. We show that there is an SCO problem such that GD with any step size and number of iterations can only learn at a suboptimal rate: at least $\widetilde{\Omega}(1/n^{5/12})$.* We present a multi-epoch variant of SGD commonly used in practice. We prove that this algorithm is at least as good as single pass SGD in the worst case. However, for certain SCO problems, taking multiple passes over the dataset can significantly outperform single pass SGD. We extend our results to the general learning setting by showing a problem which is learnable for any data distribution, and for this problem, SGD is strictly better than RERM for any regularization function. We conclude by discussing the implications of our results for deep learning, and show a separation between SGD and ERM for two layer diagonal neural networks.

paragraphs: Why does stochastic gradient descent learn well, and can its behavior be explained simply by an implicit regularizer? This paper examines that question in stochastic convex optimization. It shows that for every regularizer there is a problem where regularized empirical risk minimization fails to learn, ruling out that form of universal explanation for SGD’s success.

The authors also separate SGD from gradient descent on empirical loss. They construct a problem where gradient descent has a worse sample-complexity rate regardless of its step size or iteration count. This establishes that the distinction between these learning procedures can affect statistical efficiency, beyond how quickly they optimize training loss.

For a practical multi-epoch SGD variant, they prove worst-case performance at least as good as single-pass SGD, with substantial improvements on some problems. Further results extend the separation from regularized empirical risk minimization beyond the convex setting and separate SGD from empirical risk minimization for two-layer diagonal neural networks. These constructions clarify which explanations and comparisons hold across different learning settings.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes limits of regularization-based explanations for SGD and proves advantages over empirical gradient descent and, on some problems, single-pass training.

title: SGD: The Role of Implicit Regularization, Batch-size and Multiple-epochs

abstract: COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented negative impacts on our society, including further exposing inequity and disparity in public health. To study the impact of socioeconomic factors on COVID transmission, we first propose a spatial-temporal model to examine the socioeconomic heterogeneity and spatial correlation of COVID-19 transmission at the community level. Second, to assess the individual risk of severe COVID-19 outcomes after a positive diagnosis, we propose a dynamic, varying-coefficient model that integrates individual-level risk factors from electronic health records (EHRs) with community-level risk factors. The underlying neighborhood prevalence of infections (both symptomatic and pre-symptomatic) predicted from the previous spatial-temporal model is included in the individual risk assessment so as to better capture the background risk of virus exposure for each individual. We design a weighting scheme to mitigate multiple selection biases inherited in EHRs of COVID patients. We analyze COVID transmission data in New York City (NYC, the epicenter of the first surge in the United States) and EHRs from NYC hospitals, where time-varying effects of community risk factors and significant interactions between individual- and community-level risk factors are detected. By examining the socioeconomic disparity of infection risks and interaction among the risk factors, our methods can assist public health decision-making and facilitate better clinical management of COVID patients.

paragraphs: This paper connects community transmission patterns with individual risk of severe COVID outcomes after a positive diagnosis. It first builds a model of transmission across space and time, accounting for socioeconomic differences between communities and correlations between locations. This supplies a changing picture of the infection environment surrounding each patient.

A second model combines individual risk factors from electronic health records with community risk factors. Its coefficients can vary over time. Neighborhood infection prevalence predicted by the transmission model, including symptomatic and presymptomatic infections, enters the assessment as a measure of background exposure. A weighting scheme aims to mitigate multiple selection biases in the patient records.

The authors analyze New York City transmission data and records from its hospitals. They detect time-varying community effects and significant interactions between individual and community risk factors. These findings indicate that risk assessment can benefit from considering how personal characteristics and local conditions work together. The methods are intended to assist public health decisions and clinical management while examining socioeconomic disparities in infection risk.
summary.tldr: The paper combines community transmission estimates and patient records to model changing COVID risks and interactions between individual and neighborhood factors.

title: Dynamic COVID risk assessment accounting for community virus exposure from a spatial-temporal transmission model

abstract: The People’s Speech is a free-to-download 31,400-hour and growing supervised conversational English speech recognition dataset licensed for academic and commercial usage under CC-BY-SA. The data is collected via searching the Internet for appropriately licensed audio data with existing transcriptions. We describe our data collection methodology and release our data collection system under the Apache2.0 license. We show that a model trained on this dataset achieves a 32.17% word error rate on Librispeech’s test-clean test set. Finally, we discuss the legal and ethical issues surrounding the creation of a sizable machine learning corpora and plans for continued maintenance of the project under MLCommons’s sponsorship.

paragraphs: The People’s Speech provides a large supervised dataset for conversational English speech recognition. The paper describes a collection of 31,400 hours that is free to download and licensed under CC-BY-SA for academic and commercial use. Its contribution combines the scale of the audio collection with explicit terms for using the resource.

The authors gather appropriately licensed online audio that already has transcriptions. They describe this collection process and release the collection system under the Apache 2.0 license. Providing both the data and the software makes the resource useful at two levels: researchers can train with the assembled material and inspect the system used to collect it.

A model trained on the dataset achieves a 32.17% word error rate on LibriSpeech’s test-clean set, providing a concrete reported result for its use in speech recognition. The paper also discusses legal and ethical issues involved in assembling a large corpus and describes plans for continued maintenance with MLCommons sponsorship. These elements make dataset stewardship part of the contribution alongside collection and evaluation.
summary.tldr: The People’s Speech releases 31,400 hours of licensed English speech data and the software used to collect it.

title: The People’s Speech: A Large-Scale Diverse English Speech Recognition Dataset for Commercial Usage

abstract: A key goal of unsupervised learning is to go beyond density estimation and sample generation to reveal the structure inherent within observed data. Such structure can be expressed in the pattern of interactions between explanatory latent variables captured through a probabilistic graphical model. Although the learning of structured graphical models has a long history, much recent work in unsupervised modelling has instead emphasised flexible deep-network-based generation, either transforming independent latent generators to model complex data or assuming that distinct observed variables are derived from different latent nodes. Here, we extend amortised variational inference to incorporate structured factors over multiple variables, able to capture the observation-induced posterior dependence between latents that results from “explaining away” and thus allow complex observations to depend on multiple nodes of a structured graph. We show that appropriately parametrised factors can be combined efficiently with variational message passing in rich graphical structures. We instantiate the framework in nonlinear Gaussian Process Factor Analysis, evaluating the structured recognition framework using synthetic data from known generative processes. We fit the GPFA model to high-dimensional neural spike data from the hippocampus of freely moving rodents, where the model successfully identifies latent signals that correlate with behavioural covariates.

paragraphs: Unsupervised learning can aim to uncover interacting hidden causes, beyond fitting a data distribution or generating samples. When several hidden variables can explain the same observation, observing it can make those variables dependent. This phenomenon, called explaining away, creates a challenge for inference methods that do not represent those dependencies.

The paper extends amortized variational inference with structured factors involving multiple variables. These factors capture observation-induced dependencies and allow complex observations to depend on several nodes in a probabilistic graph. The authors show that appropriately parameterized factors can be combined efficiently with variational message passing across rich graphical structures.

They instantiate the framework in nonlinear Gaussian Process Factor Analysis and evaluate it on synthetic data with known generating processes. They also fit the model to high-dimensional hippocampal neural-spike recordings from freely moving rodents. The recovered latent signals correlate with behavioral covariates. This demonstrates the framework's ability to identify behavior-related hidden signals in that application, while the reported correlations do not by themselves establish causal relationships.
summary.tldr: Structured variational inference captures dependencies between hidden causes and recovers behavior-correlated latent signals from hippocampal recordings.

title: Structured Recognition for Generative Models with Explaining Away

abstract: The convergence of GD and SGD when training mildly parameterized neural networks starting from random initialization is studied. For a broad range of models and loss functions, including the widely used square loss and cross entropy loss, we prove an ''early stage convergence'' result. We show that the loss is decreased by a significant amount in the early stage of the training, and this decreasing is fast. Furthurmore, for exponential type loss functions, and under some assumptions on the training data, we show global convergence of GD. Instead of relying on extreme over-parameterization, our study is based on a microscopic analysis of the activation patterns for the neurons, which helps us derive gradient lower bounds. The results on activation patterns, which we call ``neuron partition'', help build intuitions for understanding the behavior of neural networks' training dynamics, and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: This paper studies why gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent can make progress when neural networks are only mildly parameterized and begin from random initialization. Its broadest result concerns early training: for a range of models and losses, including square loss and cross entropy, the loss decreases quickly by a significant amount.

The analysis examines individual neurons' activation patterns rather than relying on extreme overparameterization. By organizing these patterns into what the authors call a neuron partition, it derives lower bounds on gradients. These bounds provide a way to establish substantial optimization progress from the network's internal behavior.

The paper also proves global convergence of gradient descent for exponential-type losses under additional assumptions on the training data. That result has a narrower scope than the early-stage guarantee, which also covers stochastic gradient descent and a broader range of losses. Together, the results distinguish rapid initial improvement from convergence over the full training process, while offering activation-pattern tools that may help explain other aspects of neural-network training dynamics.
summary.tldr: Neuron activation analysis proves rapid early loss reduction in mildly parameterized networks and global gradient-descent convergence under additional conditions.

title: Early Stage Convergence and Global Convergence of Training Mildly Parameterized Neural Networks

abstract: We develop a new algorithm for non-convex stochastic optimization that finds an $\epsilon$-critical point in the optimal $O(\epsilon^{-3})$ stochastic gradient and Hessian-vector product computations. Our algorithm uses Hessian-vector products to "correct'' a bias term in the momentum of SGD with momentum. This leads to better gradient estimates in a manner analogous to variance reduction methods. In contrast to prior work, we do not require excessively large batch sizes and are able to provide an adaptive algorithm whose convergence rate automatically improves with decreasing variance in the gradient estimates. We validate our results on a variety of large-scale deep learning architectures and benchmarks tasks.

Our algorithm uses Hessian-vector products to "correct'' a bias term in the momentum of SGD with momentum. This leads to better gradient estimates in a manner analogous to variance reduction methods. In contrast to prior work, we do not require excessively large batch sizes and are able to provide an adaptive algorithm whose convergence rate automatically improves with decreasing variance in the gradient estimates. We validate our results on a variety of large-scale deep learning architectures and benchmarks tasks.

paragraphs: The paper improves stochastic optimization by changing how momentum combines gradient information. Momentum carries information from earlier updates into the current step, but this accumulated information can contain a bias. The proposed algorithm uses second-order information to correct that bias and produce better estimates of the gradient during optimization.

The correction uses Hessian-vector products, which supply information about how gradients change along a direction. The authors connect the resulting improvement to variance reduction: both approaches seek more reliable gradient estimates from stochastic information. Their method also avoids the excessively large batch sizes required by prior work and includes an adaptive version whose convergence rate improves as gradient-estimate variance decreases.

The theoretical result is an optimal O(ε⁻³) complexity in stochastic gradient and Hessian-vector product computations for finding an ε-critical point in nonconvex optimization. This is a guarantee about approaching a point with a small gradient, rather than finding a global optimum. The authors additionally validate their results across several large-scale deep learning architectures and benchmark tasks.
summary.tldr: Correcting momentum with Hessian-vector products gives stochastic optimization an optimal complexity guarantee and convergence that adapts to gradient noise.

title: Better SGD using Second-order Momentum

abstract: Conventional Federated Learning (FL) systems inherently assume a uniform processing capacity among clients for deployed models. However, diverse client hardware often leads to varying computation resources in practice. Such system heterogeneity results in an inevitable trade-off between model complexity and data accessibility as a bottleneck. To avoid such a dilemma and achieve resource-adaptive federated learning, we introduce a simple yet effective mechanism, termed All-In-One Neural Composition, to systematically support training complexity-adjustable models with flexible resource adaption. It is able to efficiently construct models at various complexities using one unified neural basis shared among clients, instead of pruning the global model into local ones. The proposed mechanism endows the system with unhindered access to the full range of knowledge scattered across clients and generalizes existing pruning-based solutions by allowing soft and learnable extraction of low footprint models. Extensive experiment results on popular FL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The resulting FL system empowered by our All-In-One Neural Composition, called FLANC, manifests consistent performance gains across diverse system/data heterogeneous setups while keeping high efficiency in computation and communication.

However, diverse client hardware often leads to varying computation resources in practice. Such system heterogeneity results in an inevitable trade-off between model complexity and data accessibility as a bottleneck. To avoid such a dilemma and achieve resource-adaptive federated learning, we introduce a simple yet effective mechanism, termed All-In-One Neural Composition, to systematically support training complexity-adjustable models with flexible resource adaption. It is able to efficiently construct models at various complexities using one unified neural basis shared among clients, instead of pruning the global model into local ones. The proposed mechanism endows the system with unhindered access to the full range of knowledge scattered across clients and generalizes existing pruning-based solutions by allowing soft and learnable extraction of low footprint models. Extensive experiment results on popular FL benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. The resulting FL system empowered by our All-In-One Neural Composition, called FLANC, manifests consistent performance gains across diverse system/data heterogeneous setups while keeping high efficiency in computation and communication.

paragraphs: Federated learning systems often deploy models as though participating devices had similar computing resources. When hardware differs, choosing a complex model can restrict access to data held by less capable clients. This paper introduces All-In-One Neural Composition to support models whose computational complexity can adapt to each client's available resources.

The mechanism constructs models of different complexities from a unified neural basis shared across clients. Its soft, learnable extraction of smaller models generalizes pruning-based approaches, which derive local models by removing parts of a global model. The shared basis provides a common foundation for learning while allowing participating devices to work with different model sizes.

The resulting system, FLANC, is evaluated on federated learning benchmarks with varied hardware and data heterogeneity. The authors report consistent performance gains while maintaining high computation and communication efficiency. These findings support adapting the model construction process to client resources as a way to use knowledge distributed across devices without imposing a uniform model complexity on all participants.
summary.tldr: FLANC composes resource-adapted client models from a shared neural basis, improving performance across heterogeneous federated learning settings.

title: Resource-Adaptive Federated Learning with All-In-One Neural Composition

abstract: In this work, we initiate the study of \emph{Dynamic Tensor Product Regression}. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}}~\|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is extremely expensive so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.

paragraphs: The paper studies regression whose design matrix is a tensor product of several smaller matrices. The resulting matrix combines the factors into a much larger structured object. The goal is to fit a label vector, but the factors change over time: at each step, one receives a sparse update.

Recomputing the regression solution after every change is expensive because the full product can be large even when its constituent matrices are manageable. The authors instead maintain a sketch, a compact representation of the tensor product that supports updating the solution. Their central contribution is a dynamic tree data structure that propagates a change to one factor quickly through the tree.

This organization makes the evolving product structure useful for computation rather than requiring a fresh solution at every step. The authors show that the same data structure supports dynamic tensor product regression, tensor product spline regression, and maintenance of low-rank approximations. Its significance is therefore a shared update mechanism for several computations involving changing tensor products.
summary.tldr: A dynamic tree maintains tensor-product sketches so regression solutions and related approximations can be updated efficiently after sparse changes.

title: Dynamic Tensor Product Regression

abstract: We describe a customizable benchmark for hierarchical and ontological multi-label classification, a task where labels are equipped with a graph structure and data items can be assigned multiple labels. We find that current benchmarks do not adequately represent the problem space, casting doubt on the generalizability of current results. We consider three dimensions of the problem space: context (availability of rich features on the data and labels), distribution of labels over data, and graph structure. For context, the lack of complex features on the labels (and in some cases, the data) artificially prevent the use of modern representation learning techniques as an appropriate baseline. For distribution, we find the long tail of labels over data constitute a few-shot learning problem that artificially confounds the results: for most common benchmarks, over 40% of the labels have fewer than 5 data points in the training set. For structure, we find that the correlation between performance and the height of the tree can explain some of the variation in performance, informing practical utility. In this paper, we demonstrate how the lack of diversity in benchmarks can confound performance analysis, then present a declarative query system called Ontologue for generating custom benchmarks with specific properties, then use this system to design 4 new benchmarks extracted from DBPedia that better represent the problem space. We evaluate state-of-the-art algorithms on both existing and new benchmarks and show that the performance conclusions can vary significantly depending on the dimensions we consider. We intend the system and derived benchmarks to improve the analysis of generalizability for these problems.

paragraphs: Hierarchical and ontological multi-label classification assigns multiple labels to an item while accounting for relationships among labels in a graph. This paper argues that existing benchmarks cover too little of that problem space to support broad conclusions. It examines three dimensions: available features, the distribution of labels across examples, and graph structure.

The analysis identifies several sources of confounding. Missing rich features can prevent modern representation learning from serving as an appropriate baseline. In most common benchmarks, over 40% of labels have fewer than five training examples, mixing classification performance with few-shot learning difficulty. Correlations between performance and tree height also help explain variation in results.

Ontologue is a declarative query system for creating benchmarks with specified properties. The authors use it to construct four new benchmarks from DBPedia and evaluate leading algorithms on both existing and new datasets. Performance conclusions vary substantially across the examined dimensions. The system therefore provides a way to investigate which problem characteristics support a result and how broadly that result may generalize.
summary.tldr: Ontologue generates customizable graph-structured classification benchmarks to reveal how dataset properties change performance conclusions.

title: Ontologue: Declarative Benchmark Construction for Ontological Multi-Label Classification

abstract: Provably efficient Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) based on optimism or posterior sampling (PSRL) is ensured to attain the global optimality asymptotically by introducing the complexity measure of the model. However, the complexity might grow exponentially for the simplest nonlinear models, where global convergence is impossible within finite iterations. When the model suffers a large generalization error, which is quantitatively measured by the model complexity, the uncertainty can be large. The sampled model that current policy is greedily optimized upon will thus be unsettled, resulting in aggressive policy updates and over-exploration. In this work, we propose Conservative Dual Policy Optimization (CDPO) that involves a Referential Update and a Conservative Update. The policy is first optimized under a reference model, which imitates the mechanism of PSRL while offering more stability. A conservative range of randomness is guaranteed by maximizing the expectation of model value. Without harmful sampling procedures, CDPO can still achieve the same regret as PSRL. More importantly, CDPO enjoys monotonic policy improvement and global optimality simultaneously. Empirical results also validate the exploration efficiency of CDPO.
