paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning chooses actions using a model of the environment. When that model generalizes poorly, uncertainty can make a sampled model unstable as a target for policy optimization. The paper connects this instability to aggressive policy changes and excessive exploration, especially when model-complexity measures become large even for simple nonlinear models.

Conservative Dual Policy Optimization addresses the problem through a Referential Update and a Conservative Update. It first optimizes a policy under a reference model, preserving an aspect of posterior sampling while providing greater stability. Maximizing expected model value then maintains a conservative range of randomness, aiming to control exploration without the harmful sampling behavior identified by the authors.

The theoretical results give CDPO the same regret as posterior-sampling reinforcement learning, together with monotonic policy improvement and global optimality. These claims concern the method's analyzed setting and do not establish a general finite-iteration solution for arbitrary nonlinear models. Empirical results also support its exploration efficiency. The contribution links more stable policy updates with both exploration guarantees and observed performance.
summary.tldr: CDPO combines reference-model and conservative policy updates to stabilize exploration while retaining theoretical regret and policy-improvement guarantees.

title: Conservative Dual Policy Optimization for Efficient Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The ability of likelihood-based probabilistic models to generalize to unseen data is central to many machine learning applications such as lossless compression. In this work, we study the generalization of a popular class of probabilistic model - the Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We discuss the two generalization gaps that affect VAEs and show that overfitting is usually dominated by amortized inference. Based on this observation, we propose a new training objective that improves the generalization of amortized inference. We demonstrate how our method can improve performance in the context of image modeling and lossless compression.

paragraphs: A probabilistic model must work on data it did not see during training. This is particularly relevant when the model supports lossless compression, where its probability estimates affect performance. The paper studies this issue in variational autoencoders, focusing on how their inference component contributes to the difference between training performance and performance on unseen examples.

The authors distinguish two generalization gaps affecting VAEs and find that amortized inference usually dominates overfitting. Amortized inference uses a shared learned procedure to perform inference across examples. The result points to the generalization of that shared procedure as a major source of the model's overall training-to-test gap in the studied setting.

Based on this diagnosis, the paper introduces a training objective intended to improve how amortized inference generalizes. The authors demonstrate performance improvements in image modeling and lossless compression. The contribution therefore links an explanation of where overfitting tends to arise with a targeted training change, rather than treating the VAE's generalization behavior as a single undifferentiated problem.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies amortized inference as a usual dominant source of VAE overfitting and proposes a training objective that improves generalization.

title: Generalization Gap in Amortized Inference

abstract: Deep neural networks have seen great success in recent years; however, training a deep model is often challenging as its performance heavily depends on the hyper-parameters used. In addition, finding the optimal hyper-parameter configuration, even with state-of-the-art (SOTA) hyper-parameter optimization (HPO) algorithms, can be time-consuming, requiring multiple training runs over the entire datasetfor different possible sets of hyper-parameters. Our central insight is that using an informative subset of the dataset for model training runs involved in hyper-parameter optimization, allows us to find the optimal hyper-parameter configuration significantly faster. In this work, we propose AUTOMATA, a gradient-based subset selection framework for hyper-parameter tuning. We empirically evaluate the effectiveness of AUTOMATA in hyper-parameter tuning through several experiments on real-world datasets in the text, vision, and tabular domains. Our experiments show that using gradient-based data subsets for hyper-parameter tuning achieves significantly faster turnaround times and speedups of 3×-30× while achieving comparable performance to the hyper-parameters found using the entire dataset.

paragraphs: A neural network’s performance can depend strongly on its hyperparameters, so finding a good configuration often requires repeated training runs. Even sophisticated search methods can be expensive when each candidate is trained using the entire dataset. AUTOMATA addresses the cost of these individual trials by reducing the data used during tuning.

The method selects informative subsets using gradient information. Its central idea is that a carefully chosen portion of the training data can provide enough guidance to identify useful hyperparameter settings more quickly. The selected subset therefore serves the tuning process: the question is whether configurations found with less training data deliver performance comparable to configurations found using all the data.

Experiments cover real-world datasets in text, vision, and tabular domains. The authors report tuning speedups ranging from 3× to 30×, with comparable performance from the resulting hyperparameters. These empirical findings suggest that dataset selection can substantially reduce tuning turnaround time while preserving the practical value of the search in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: AUTOMATA uses gradient-selected data subsets to speed up hyperparameter tuning while retaining comparable resulting performance.

title: AUTOMATA: Gradient Based Data Subset Selection for Compute-Efficient Hyper-parameter Tuning

abstract: Despite a surge of recent advances in promoting machine Learning (ML) fairness, the existing mainstream approaches mostly require training or finetuning the entire weights of the neural network to meet the fairness criteria. However, this is often infeasible in practice for those large-scale trained models due to large computational and storage costs, low data efficiency, and model privacy issues. In this paper, we propose a new generic fairness learning paradigm, called FairReprogram, which incorporates the model reprogramming technique. Specifically, FairReprogram considers the case where models can not be changed and appends to the input a set of perturbations, called the fairness trigger, which is tuned towards the fairness criteria under a min-max formulation. We further introduce an information-theoretic framework that explains why and under what conditions fairness goals can be achieved using the fairness trigger. We show both theoretically and empirically that the fairness trigger can effectively obscure demographic biases in the output prediction of fixed ML models by providing false demographic information that hinders the model from utilizing the correct demographic information to make the prediction. Extensive experiments on both NLP and CV datasets demonstrate that our method can achieve better fairness improvements than retraining-based methods with far less data dependency under two widely-used fairness criteria. Codes are available at https://github.com/UCSB-NLP-Chang/Fairness-Reprogramming.git.

paragraphs: FairReprogram addresses fairness when a trained model's parameters cannot be changed. Updating an entire large network can impose substantial computation, storage, and data costs, while model privacy can further restrict access. The paper instead learns a small addition to the input, called a fairness trigger, to influence the fixed model's predictions.

The trigger is optimized toward fairness criteria through a min-max formulation. Its proposed mechanism is to supply misleading demographic information that interferes with the model's use of the correct demographic information. An information-theoretic analysis explains why this can obscure demographic bias and identifies conditions under which the fairness goals can be achieved.

Experiments on language and vision datasets report better fairness improvements than retraining-based methods under two widely used fairness criteria, with substantially less dependence on data. These results support input reprogramming as a practical route to improving the measured fairness of fixed models. The theoretical conditions remain part of the claim: the paper does not present every possible trigger as sufficient for every fairness goal.
summary.tldr: FairReprogram improves measured fairness in fixed models by learning input triggers that interfere with demographic information used in predictions.

title: Fairness Reprogramming

abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have recently achieved comparable or superior performance to Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in computer vision. This empirical breakthrough is even more remarkable since ViTs discards spatial information by mixing patch embeddings and positional encodings and do not embed any visual inductive bias (e.g.\ spatial locality). Yet, recent work showed that while minimizing their training loss, ViTs specifically learn spatially delocalized patterns. This raises a central question: how do ViTs learn this pattern by solely minimizing their training loss using gradient-based methods from \emph{random initialization}? We propose a structured classification dataset and a simplified ViT model to provide preliminary theoretical justification of this phenomenon. Our model relies on a simplified attention mechanism --the positional attention mechanism-- where the attention matrix solely depends on the positional encodings. While the problem admits multiple solutions that generalize, we show that our model implicitly learns the spatial structure of the dataset while generalizing. We finally prove that learning the structure helps to sample-efficiently transfer to downstream datasets that share the same structure as the pre-training one but with different features. We empirically verify that ViTs using only the positional attention mechanism perform similarly to the original one on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Vision transformers can perform well without explicitly building spatial locality into their architecture. This paper asks how gradient-based training from random initialization can nevertheless recover spatial patterns. To investigate, the authors construct a structured classification dataset and analyze a simplified transformer rather than attempting a theory of every component in a full vision transformer.

Their positional attention mechanism makes the attention matrix depend only on positional encodings. Although the classification problem has multiple generalizing solutions, the analyzed model implicitly learns the dataset’s spatial structure while generalizing. The authors also prove that this learned structure supports sample-efficient transfer when downstream datasets share the structure but use different features.

Experiments show that transformers using positional attention alone perform similarly to original vision transformers on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet. These results complement the theoretical analysis by examining the simplified mechanism on established image tasks. The paper offers preliminary theoretical justification for spatial structure learning, with its formal transfer result specifically requiring shared structure between pretraining and downstream data.
summary.tldr: A simplified vision transformer provably learns spatial structure that improves transfer to datasets sharing that structure.

title: Vision Transformers provably learn spatial structure

abstract: The Partial Area Under the ROC Curve (PAUC), typically including One-way Partial AUC (OPAUC) and Two-way Partial AUC (TPAUC), measures the average performance of a binary classifier within a specific false positive rate and/or true positive rate interval, which is a widely adopted measure when decision constraints must be considered. Consequently, PAUC optimization has naturally attracted increasing attention in the machine learning community within the last few years. Nonetheless, most of the existing methods could only optimize PAUC approximately, leading to inevitable biases that are not controllable. Fortunately, a recent work presents an unbiased formulation of the PAUC optimization problem via distributional robust optimization. However, it is based on the pair-wise formulation of AUC, which suffers from the limited scalability w.r.t. sample size and a slow convergence rate, especially for TPAUC. To address this issue, we present a simpler reformulation of the problem in an asymptotically unbiased and instance-wise manner. For both OPAUC and TPAUC, we come to a nonconvex strongly concave min-max regularized problem of instance-wise functions. On top of this, we employ an efficient solver that enjoys a linear per-iteration computational complexity w.r.t. the sample size and a time-complexity of $O(\epsilon^{-1/3})$ to reach a $\epsilon$ stationary point. Furthermore, we find that the min-max reformulation also facilitates the theoretical analysis of generalization error as a byproduct. Compared with the existing results, we present new error bounds that are much easier to prove and could deal with hypotheses with real-valued outputs. Finally, extensive experiments on several benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: Partial AUC evaluates a binary classifier within selected false-positive or true-positive rate ranges. This makes it useful when performance must satisfy particular decision constraints. The paper addresses a difficulty in optimizing this measure: existing approximations can introduce uncontrolled bias, while an unbiased formulation based on pairs of examples has scalability and convergence drawbacks.

The authors reformulate both one-way and two-way partial AUC using functions of individual examples. Their formulation is asymptotically unbiased and produces a regularized min-max problem that is nonconvex in one part and strongly concave in the other. Working with individual examples gives the proposed solver computational cost per iteration that grows linearly with sample size.

The paper also supplies a time-complexity guarantee for reaching an approximate stationary point. The same reformulation makes generalization analysis easier and yields error bounds that accommodate real-valued model outputs. Experiments on several benchmark datasets support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines a more scalable optimization formulation with theoretical control over optimization and generalization, while retaining the qualification that unbiasedness is asymptotic.
summary.tldr: An asymptotically unbiased, instance-wise partial-AUC formulation improves optimization scalability and simplifies generalization analysis.

title: Asymptotically Unbiased Instance-wise Regularized Partial AUC Optimization: Theory and Algorithm

abstract: In partial multi-label learning (PML), each training example is associated with a set of candidate labels, among which only some labels are valid. As a common strategy to tackle PML problem, disambiguation aims to recover the ground-truth labeling information from such inaccurate annotations. However, existing approaches mainly rely on heuristics or ad-hoc rules to disambiguate candidate labels, which may not be universal enough in complicated real-world scenarios. To provide a principled way for disambiguation, we make a first attempt to explore the probabilistic graphical model for PML problem, where a directed graph is tailored to infer latent ground-truth labeling information from the generative process of partial multi-label data. Under the framework of stochastic gradient variational Bayes, a unified variational lower bound is derived for this graphical model, which is further relaxed probabilistically so that the desired prediction model can be induced with simultaneously identified ground-truth labeling information. Comprehensive experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world data sets show that our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art counterparts.

paragraphs: In partial multi-label learning, each example arrives with several candidate labels, but only some are correct. Learning therefore requires both identifying valid labels and building a predictor. This paper addresses that ambiguity with a probabilistic graphical model, aiming to replace heuristic disambiguation rules with a principled account of how the observed candidate-label data arise.

The authors construct a directed graph in which the true labels are hidden quantities to be inferred. Within stochastic gradient variational Bayes, they derive a shared lower-bound objective for the model. They then relax that objective probabilistically so that training can induce the prediction model while simultaneously identifying the underlying labeling information. Label disambiguation and prediction are handled within one learning framework.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in the reported comparisons. The significance is that inaccurate candidate sets can be treated through an explicit generative account and joint inference. This provides a structured alternative to relying mainly on handcrafted rules for deciding which candidate labels to trust.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic graphical model jointly identifies valid labels within ambiguous candidate sets and learns a multi-label predictor.

title: Partial Multi-Label Learning with Probabilistic Graphical Disambiguation

abstract: In many information processing systems, it may be desirable to ensure that any change of the input, whether by shifting or scaling, results in a corresponding change in the system response. While deep neural networks are gradually replacing all traditional automatic processing methods, they surprisingly do not guarantee such normalization-equivariance (scale + shift) property, which can be detrimental in many applications. To address this issue, we propose a methodology for adapting existing neural networks so that normalization-equivariance holds by design. Our main claim is that not only ordinary convolutional layers, but also all activation functions, including the ReLU (rectified linear unit), which are applied element-wise to the pre-activated neurons, should be completely removed from neural networks and replaced by better conditioned alternatives. To this end, we introduce affine-constrained convolutions and channel-wise sort pooling layers as surrogates and show that these two architectural modifications do preserve normalization-equivariance without loss of performance. Experimental results in image denoising show that normalization-equivariant neural networks, in addition to their better conditioning, also provide much better generalization across noise levels.
originalAbstract: In many information processing systems, it may be desirable to ensure that any change of the input, whether by shifting or scaling, results in a corresponding change in the system response. While deep neural networks are gradually replacing all traditional automatic processing methods, they surprisingly do not guarantee such normalization-equivariance (scale + shift) property, which can be detrimental in many applications. To address this issue, we propose a methodology for adapting existing neural networks so that normalization-equivariance holds by design. Our main claim is that not only ordinary convolutional layers, but also all activation functions, including the ReLU (rectified linear unit), which are applied element-wise to the pre-activated neurons, should be completely removed from neural networks and replaced by better conditioned alternatives. To this end, we introduce affine-constrained convolutions and channel-wise sort pooling layers as surrogates and show that these two architectural modifications do preserve normalization-equivariance without loss of performance. Experimental results in image denoising show that normalization-equivariant neural networks, in addition to their better conditioning, also provide much better generalization across noise levels.

paragraphs: Normalization equivariance means that shifting or scaling an input produces a corresponding change in the output. Standard neural networks do not guarantee this behavior, even when it is desirable for a processing task. This paper develops architectural changes that make the property hold by construction rather than depend on what training happens to learn.

The proposed design replaces ordinary convolutions with affine-constrained convolutions and replaces element-wise activation functions, including ReLU, with channel-wise sort pooling. The authors argue that both kinds of replacement are needed in their methodology. Together, these operations preserve the desired response to shifts and scaling while providing better-conditioned alternatives.

Image-denoising experiments show that the modified networks retain performance and generalize much better across noise levels. This matters because the architectural property governs how the network responds when input normalization changes, while the experiments test a practical benefit in denoising. The evidence supports the proposed design for that application without requiring the property to emerge indirectly from training examples.
summary.tldr: The paper redesigns convolutions and activations to guarantee shift-and-scale equivariance and improve denoising generalization across noise levels.

title: Normalization-Equivariant Neural Networks with Application to Image Denoising

abstract: We present \emph{DreamHuman}, a method to generate realistic animatable 3D human avatar models entirely from textual descriptions. Recent text-to-3D methods have made considerable strides in generation, but are still lacking in important aspects. Control and often spatial resolution remain limited, existing methods produce fixed rather than 3D human models that can be placed in different poses (i.e. re-posable or animatable), and anthropometric consistency for complex structures like people remains a challenge. \emph{DreamHuman} connects large text-to-image synthesis models, neural radiance fields, and statistical human body models in a novel optimization framework. This makes it possible to generate dynamic 3D human avatars with high-quality textures and learnt per-instance rigid and non rigid geometric deformations. We demonstrate that our method is capable to generate a wide variety of animatable, realistic 3D human models from text. These have diverse appearance, clothing, skin tones and body shapes, and outperform both generic text-to-3D approaches and previous text-based 3D avatar generators in visual fidelity.

paragraphs: DreamHuman generates realistic three-dimensional human avatars from written descriptions. Its goal includes making those avatars usable in different poses. This addresses several problems identified in earlier text-to-3D approaches: limited control and resolution, fixed generated poses, and difficulty maintaining plausible human proportions in complex human figures.

The method combines large text-to-image synthesis models, neural radiance fields, and statistical human body models within one optimization framework. These components bring together text-guided appearance generation and a representation of human shape. The resulting avatars include detailed textures and geometric deformations learned separately for each instance, covering both rigid changes and changes that alter shape.

The authors demonstrate avatars with varied clothing, appearance, skin tones, and body shapes that can be animated or posed differently. They report higher visual fidelity than both general text-to-3D methods and earlier text-based avatar generators. The contribution therefore joins visual quality with pose flexibility: the generated human is a dynamic 3D model rather than merely an appealing result in one fixed configuration.
summary.tldr: DreamHuman combines text-to-image models, neural radiance fields, and body models to generate realistic, animatable human avatars from text.

title: DreamHuman: Animatable 3D Avatars from Text

abstract: We establish generic uniform convergence guarantees for Gaussian data in terms of the Radamacher complexity of the hypothesis class and the Lipschitz constant of the square root of the scalar loss function. We show how these guarantees substantially generalize previous results based on smoothness (Lipschitz constant of the derivative), and allow us to handle the broader class of square-root-Lipschtz losses, which includes also non-smooth loss functions appropriate for studying phase retrieval and ReLU regression, as well as rederive and better understand “optimistic rate” and interpolation learning guarantees.

We show how these guarantees substantially generalize previous results based on smoothness (Lipschitz constant of the derivative), and allow us to handle the broader class of square-root-Lipschtz losses, which includes also non-smooth loss functions appropriate for studying phase retrieval and ReLU regression, as well as rederive and better understand “optimistic rate” and interpolation learning guarantees.

paragraphs: Uniform convergence guarantees connect measured training performance with population performance across an entire hypothesis class. This paper establishes such guarantees for Gaussian data using the complexity of the hypothesis class and the regularity of the square root of the loss. Its focus is the mathematical condition needed to obtain these guarantees.

The bounds depend on Rademacher complexity and a Lipschitz constant for the square-root loss. The latter controls how quickly the square root of the loss can change. This differs from requiring a Lipschitz derivative, the smoothness condition used in earlier results, and allows the analysis to cover a broader family of losses.

That broader family includes nonsmooth losses relevant to phase retrieval and ReLU regression. The framework also recovers and helps explain optimistic-rate and interpolation learning guarantees. The contribution is therefore both an extension of applicable loss functions and a common perspective on existing learning results. Gaussian data remain an explicit condition of the stated guarantees; expanding the loss family does not remove that distributional setting.
summary.tldr: Square-root Lipschitz conditions extend uniform convergence guarantees for Gaussian data to a broader class of losses, including nonsmooth ones.

title: Uniform Convergence with Square-Root Lipschitz Loss

abstract: We develop a general framework for finding approximately-optimal preconditioners for solving linear systems. Leveraging this framework we obtain improved runtimes for fundamental preconditioning and linear system solving problems including:Diagonal preconditioning. We give an algorithm which, given positive definite $\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ with $\mathrm{nnz}(\mathbf{K})$ nonzero entries, computes an $\epsilon$-optimal diagonal preconditioner in time $\widetilde{O}(\mathrm{nnz}(\mathbf{K}) \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\kappa^\star,\epsilon^{-1}))$, where $\kappa^\star$ is the optimal condition number of the rescaled matrix.Structured linear systems. We give an algorithm which, given $\mathbf{M} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ that is either the pseudoinverse of a graph Laplacian matrix or a constant spectral approximation of one, solves linear systems in $\mathbf{M}$ in $\widetilde{O}(d^2)$ time. Our diagonal preconditioning results improve state-of-the-art runtimes of $\Omega(d^{3.5})$ attained by general-purpose semidefinite programming, and our solvers improve state-of-the-art runtimes of $\Omega(d^{\omega})$ where $\omega > 2.3$ is the current matrix multiplication constant. We attain our results via new algorithms for a class of semidefinite programs (SDPs) we call matrix-dictionary approximation SDPs, which we leverage to solve an associated problem we call matrix-dictionary recovery.

paragraphs: Preconditioning transforms a linear system into a form that is easier to solve. This paper develops a framework for finding approximately optimal preconditioners by exploiting matrix structure. Its technical foundation is a new class of semidefinite optimization problems, called matrix-dictionary approximation SDPs, together with an associated matrix-dictionary recovery problem.

For a positive definite matrix, the framework computes an epsilon-optimal diagonal preconditioner. Its runtime depends on the number of nonzero matrix entries and polynomial factors in the best achievable condition number and inverse accuracy, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This replaces the cited general-purpose semidefinite-programming runtime of at least order d^3.5 with a structure-sensitive bound.

The paper also gives a nearly quadratic-time solver for matrices that are graph Laplacian pseudoinverses or constant spectral approximations of them. This improves on the cited matrix-multiplication-based runtime for that structured setting. Together, the results show how specialized semidefinite optimization can improve both preconditioner construction and linear-system solving. The guarantees retain explicit conditions on matrix structure and, for diagonal preconditioning, conditioning and requested accuracy.
summary.tldr: Specialized semidefinite programs yield faster approximate diagonal preconditioning and nearly quadratic solvers for particular Laplacian-related systems.

title: Structured Semidefinite Programming for Recovering Structured Preconditioners

abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs), such as CLIP, have demonstrated impressive zero-shot transfer capabilities in image-level visual perception. However, these models have shown limited performance in instance-level tasks that demand precise localization and recognition. Previous works have suggested that incorporating visual prompts, such as colorful boxes or circles, can improve the ability of models to recognize objects of interest. Nonetheless, compared to language prompting, visual prompting designs are rarely explored. Existing approaches, which employ coarse visual cues such as colorful boxes or circles, often result in sub-optimal performance due to the inclusion of irrelevant and noisy pixels. In this paper, we carefully study the visual prompting designs by exploring more fine-grained markings, such as segmentation masks and their variations. In addition, we introduce a new zero-shot framework that leverages pixel-level annotations acquired from a generalist segmentation model for fine-grained visual prompting. Consequently, our investigation reveals that a straightforward application of blur outside the target mask, referred to as the Blur Reverse Mask, exhibits exceptional effectiveness. This proposed prompting strategy leverages the precise mask annotations to reduce focus on weakly related regions while retaining spatial coherence between the target and the surrounding background. Our **F**ine-**G**rained **V**isual **P**rompting (**FGVP**) demonstrates superior performance in zero-shot comprehension of referring expressions on the RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg benchmarks. It outperforms prior methods by an average margin of 3.0\% to 4.6\%, with a maximum improvement of 12.5\% on the RefCOCO+ testA subset. The part detection experiments conducted on the PACO dataset further validate the preponderance of FGVP over existing visual prompting techniques. Code is available at https://github.com/ylingfeng/FGVP.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to direct a vision-language model toward a particular object in an image. Models such as CLIP can perform well at image-level recognition yet struggle with tasks requiring precise localization. Coarse prompts such as colored boxes or circles can include irrelevant pixels, weakening their ability to isolate the intended object.

The authors investigate finer prompts based on segmentation masks and introduce a zero-shot framework that obtains pixel-level annotations from a generalist segmentation model. Their particularly effective strategy, Blur Reverse Mask, blurs the area outside the target mask. This reduces emphasis on loosely related regions while retaining the target's spatial relationship with its surroundings.

Fine-Grained Visual Prompting improves zero-shot referring-expression comprehension on RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, and RefCOCOg. The abstract reports average improvements of 3.0% to 4.6% over prior methods and a maximum of 12.5% on RefCOCO+ testA. Part-detection experiments on PACO provide additional support. The findings show how precise visual emphasis can improve the use of existing vision-language capabilities.
summary.tldr: Blurring outside a precise object mask improves zero-shot visual prompting while preserving surrounding spatial context.

title: Fine-Grained Visual Prompting

abstract: Large language models have emerged as a promising approach towards achieving general-purpose AI agents. The thriving open-source LLM community has greatly accelerated the development of agents that support human-machine dialogue interaction through natural language processing. However, human interaction with the world extends beyond only text as a modality, and other modalities such as vision are also crucial. Recent works on multi-modal large language models, such as GPT-4V and Bard, have demonstrated their effectiveness in handling visual modalities. However, the transparency of these works is limited and insufficient to support academic research. To the best of our knowledge, we present one of the very first open-source endeavors in the field, LAMM, encompassing a Language-Assisted Multi-Modal instruction tuning dataset, framework, and benchmark. Our aim is to establish LAMM as a growing ecosystem for training and evaluating MLLMs, with a specific focus on facilitating AI agents capable of bridging the gap between ideas and execution, thereby enabling seamless human-AI interaction. Our main contribution is three-fold: 1) We present a comprehensive dataset and benchmark, which cover a wide range of vision tasks for 2D and 3D vision. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of our dataset and benchmark. 2) We outline the detailed methodology of constructing multi-modal instruction tuning datasets and benchmarks for MLLMs, enabling rapid scaling and extension of MLLM research to diverse domains, tasks, and modalities. 3) We provide a primary but potential MLLM training framework optimized for modality extension. We also provide baseline models, comprehensive experimental observations, and analysis to accelerate future research. Our baseline model is trained within 24 A100 GPU hours, framework supports training with V100 and RTX3090 is available thanks to the open-source society. Codes and data are now available at https://openlamm.github.io.

paragraphs: LAMM provides an open research ecosystem for language models that work with visual information as well as text. The authors motivate it through the limited transparency of existing multimodal systems, which makes academic investigation harder. Their contribution combines instruction-tuning data, evaluation benchmarks, and a training framework instead of supplying only a model.

The dataset and benchmark cover a broad range of tasks in both 2D and 3D vision. The paper also explains how to construct multimodal instruction datasets and benchmarks, supporting extension to additional domains, tasks, and modalities. Its initial training framework is specifically designed to accommodate modality expansion, while baseline models and experimental analyses provide starting points for further research.

Experiments support the usefulness of the dataset and benchmark. The reported baseline training uses 24 A100 GPU hours, and the framework also supports training on V100 and RTX3090 hardware. Together, these resources make multimodal instruction-tuning methods more accessible to study and extend, while the broader goal remains enabling richer interaction between people and AI agents.
summary.tldr: LAMM supplies open multimodal instruction data, benchmarks, and an extensible training framework spanning 2D and 3D vision tasks.

title: LAMM: Language-Assisted Multi-Modal Instruction-Tuning Dataset, Framework, and Benchmark

abstract: Recovering the latent factors of variation of high dimensional data has so far focused on simple synthetic settings. Mostly building on unsupervised and weakly-supervised objectives, prior work missed out on the positive implications for representation learning on real world data. In this work, we propose to leverage knowledge extracted from a diversified set of supervised tasks to learn a common disentangled representation. Assuming each supervised task only depends on an unknown subset of the factors of variation, we disentangle the feature space of a supervised multi-task model, with features activating sparsely across different tasks and information being shared as appropriate. Importantly, we never directly observe the factors of variations but establish that access to multiple tasks is sufficient for identifiability under sufficiency and minimality assumptions.We validate our approach on six real world distribution shift benchmarks, and different data modalities (images, text), demonstrating how disentangled representations can be transferred to real settings.

paragraphs: Disentangled representation learning aims to separate the underlying factors that make observations vary. Much previous work studied this goal in simple synthetic settings. This paper instead draws information from a diverse collection of supervised tasks, seeking a common representation that can work with real-world data even when the underlying factors are never directly observed.

The approach assumes that each task depends on an unknown subset of those factors. It encourages features to activate sparsely across tasks while sharing information where appropriate. Different tasks therefore provide complementary evidence about the representation. The theoretical result establishes that access to multiple tasks is sufficient for identifiability under sufficiency and minimality assumptions, making those assumptions central to the claim.

The authors validate the approach on six real-world distribution-shift benchmarks involving images and text. These experiments demonstrate how disentangled representations can transfer to practical settings. The contribution connects a conditional theoretical account of factor recovery with a supervised multitask method that uses selective feature activation and sharing to organize learned information.
summary.tldr: Sparse feature use across supervised tasks supports disentangled representations, with identifiability under stated assumptions and validation on real-world benchmarks.

title: Leveraging sparse and shared feature activations for disentangled representation learning

abstract: In this work, we demonstrate a method for implementing policy iteration using a large language model. While the application of foundation models to RL has received considerable attention, most approaches rely on either (1) the curation of expert demonstrations (either through manual design or task-specific pretraining) or (2) adaptation to the task of interest using gradient methods (either fine-tuning or training of adapter layers). Both of these techniques have drawbacks. Collecting demonstrations is labor-intensive, and algorithms that rely on them do not outperform the experts from which the demonstrations were derived. All gradient techniques are inherently slow, sacrificing the “few-shot” quality that makes in-context learning attractive to begin with. Our method demonstrates that a large language model can be used to implement policy iteration using the machinery of in-context learning, enabling it to learn to perform RL tasks without expert demonstrations or gradients. Our approach iteratively updates the contents of the prompt from which it derives its policy through trial-and-error interaction with an RL environment. In order to eliminate the role of in-weights learning (on which approaches like Decision Transformer rely heavily), we demonstrate our method using Codex (M. Chen et al. 2021b), a language model with no prior knowledge of the domains on which we evaluate it.

paragraphs: This paper demonstrates reinforcement learning through changes to a language model's prompt. Its goal is to implement policy iteration, repeatedly updating how the system chooses actions as it gains experience. The motivation is to avoid collecting expert demonstrations or adapting the model with gradient-based training, both of which introduce substantial work before or during task adaptation.

The method interacts with a reinforcement-learning environment through trial and error. It uses that experience to iteratively revise the prompt from which its policy is derived. Learning therefore occurs through the changing context supplied to the model, allowing the approach to use in-context learning without updating model parameters for the task.

The authors demonstrate the method with Codex, which they describe as having no prior knowledge of the evaluated domains. This choice is intended to separate the demonstrated learning from domain knowledge already stored in the model's weights. The result establishes a way for a language model to implement policy iteration without expert demonstrations or gradients, showing that the prompt itself can carry task adaptation.
summary.tldr: A language model can implement policy iteration by updating its prompt through trial-and-error interaction, without expert demonstrations or gradient updates.

title: Large Language Models can Implement Policy Iteration

abstract: In real-world reinforcement learning (RL) systems, various forms of {\it impaired observability} can complicate matters. These situations arise when an agent is unable to observe the most recent state of the system due to latency or lossy channels, yet the agent must still make real-time decisions. This paper introduces a theoretical investigation into efficient RL in control systems where agents must act with delayed and missing state observations. We establish near-optimal regret bounds, of the form $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{{\rm poly}(H) SAK})$, for RL in both the delayed and missing observation settings. Despite impaired observability posing significant challenges to the policy class and planning, our results demonstrate that learning remains efficient, with the regret bound optimally depending on the state-action size of the original system. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the performance of the optimal policy under impaired observability, comparing it to the optimal value obtained with full observability.

paragraphs: An agent may have to act even when its latest state observation is delayed or missing. This paper studies the learning difficulty created by those conditions in reinforcement learning. The issue concerns access to the current state itself: the agent must make decisions with an incomplete or outdated view of the system.

The authors establish near-optimal regret bounds for both delayed and missing observations. Regret measures the performance shortfall accumulated while learning. Their bounds have square-root dependence on the product of the original system's state count, action count, and number of episodes, together with a polynomial dependence on the horizon and suppressed logarithmic factors. The state-action dependence is optimal despite the more difficult policy and planning problems.

The paper also characterizes the best policy achievable under impaired observability relative to the optimal value with full observations. This separates two questions: how efficiently an agent can learn with its available information, and how much that information restriction affects achievable performance. The results support efficient learning in the studied settings without claiming that delayed or missing observations leave optimal performance unchanged.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes near-optimal learning guarantees for reinforcement learning with delayed or missing state observations.

title: Efficient RL with Impaired Observability: Learning to Act with Delayed and Missing State Observations

abstract: Optimal auction design is a fundamental problem in algorithmic game theory. This problem is notoriously difficult already in very simple settings. Recent work in differentiable economics showed that neural networks can efficiently learn known optimal auction mechanisms and discover interesting new ones. In an attempt to theoretically justify their empirical success, we focus on one of the first such networks, RochetNet, and a generalized version for affine maximizer auctions. We prove that they satisfy mode connectivity, i.e., locally optimal solutions are connected by a simple, piecewise linear path such that every solution on the path is almost as good as one of the two local optima. Mode connectivity has been recently investigated as an intriguing empirical and theoretically justifiable property of neural networks used for prediction problems. Our results give the first such analysis in the context of differentiable economics, where neural networks are used directly for solving non-convex optimization problems.

paragraphs: Finding optimal auction rules is difficult even in relatively simple settings. Neural networks have nevertheless shown an ability to recover known optimal mechanisms and discover new ones. This paper seeks theoretical insight into that empirical success by examining the shape of the optimization problem for networks used to design auctions.

The authors study RochetNet and a generalized network for affine maximizer auctions. They prove a property called mode connectivity: locally optimal solutions can be joined by a simple piecewise linear path, and every solution along that path is almost as good as one of the two endpoint optima. The statement concerns the quality of connecting paths; it does not identify every local optimum as globally optimal.

Mode connectivity had already attracted attention in networks used for prediction. This work brings that analysis into differentiable economics, where networks directly solve non-convex optimization problems. The result provides a structural explanation relevant to auction-learning success: good solutions in these studied models are connected through paths that preserve the stated level of solution quality.
summary.tldr: The authors prove that local optima in two neural auction-design models are connected by piecewise linear paths with controlled solution quality.

title: Mode Connectivity in Auction Design

abstract: Recently, commonsense reasoning in text generation has attracted much attention. Generative commonsense reasoning is the task that requires machines, given a group of keywords, to compose a single coherent sentence with commonsense plausibility. While existing datasets targeting generative commonsense reasoning focus on everyday scenarios, it is unclear how well machines reason under specific geographical and temporal contexts. We formalize this challenging task as SituatedGen, where machines with commonsense should generate a pair of contrastive sentences given a group of keywords including geographical or temporal entities. We introduce a corresponding English dataset consisting of 8,268 contrastive sentence pairs, which are built upon several existing commonsense reasoning benchmarks with minimal manual labor. Experiments show that state-of-the-art generative language models struggle to generate sentences with commonsense plausibility and still lag far behind human performance. Our dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/yunx-z/situated_gen.

Our dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/yunx-z/situated_gen.

paragraphs: Generative commonsense tasks ask a model to turn a collection of keywords into a coherent, plausible sentence. Plausibility can depend on where or when a situation occurs, yet everyday-scenario benchmarks leave this ability unclear. SituatedGen makes geographical and temporal context an explicit part of what a model must reason about.

The task provides keywords that include geographical or temporal entities and asks for a pair of contrasting sentences. The accompanying English dataset contains 8,268 sentence pairs, assembled from existing commonsense benchmarks with minimal manual labor. The contrastive format brings context into the generation requirement rather than evaluating only an isolated sentence about a general situation.

Experiments show that the evaluated leading generative language models struggle to produce commonsensically plausible sentences and remain far behind human performance. The findings identify a weakness in generating text whose content fits a specified place or time. The publicly released dataset supplies a focused evaluation resource for this capability, extending commonsense generation beyond the everyday settings emphasized by earlier datasets.
summary.tldr: SituatedGen tests context-dependent commonsense generation and finds that evaluated language models lag far behind humans.

title: SituatedGen: Incorporating Geographical and Temporal Contexts into Generative Commonsense Reasoning

abstract: Albeit revealing impressive predictive performance for several computer vision tasks, deep neural networks (DNNs) are prone to making overconfident predictions. This limits the adoption and wider utilization of DNNs in many safety-critical applications. There have been recent efforts toward calibrating DNNs, however, almost all of them focus on the classification task. Surprisingly, very little attention has been devoted to calibrating modern DNN-based object detectors, especially detection transformers, which have recently demonstrated promising detection performance and are influential in many decision-making systems. In this work, we address the problem by proposing a mechanism for calibrated detection transformers (Cal-DETR), particularly for Deformable-DETR, UP-DETR, and DINO. We pursue the train-time calibration route and make the following contributions. First, we propose a simple yet effective approach for quantifying uncertainty in transformer-based object detectors. Second, we develop an uncertainty-guided logit modulation mechanism that leverages the uncertainty to modulate the class logits. Third, we develop a logit mixing approach that acts as a regularizer with detection-specific losses and is also complementary to the uncertainty-guided logit modulation technique to further improve the calibration performance. Lastly, we conduct extensive experiments across three in-domain and four out-domain scenarios. Results corroborate the effectiveness of Cal-DETR against the competing train-time methods in calibrating both in-domain and out-domain detections while maintaining or even improving the detection performance. Our codebase and pre-trained models can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/akhtarvision/cal-detr}.

Together, these mechanisms aim to improve confidence estimates while preserving the detector's ability to recognize and locate objects.

Against competing methods that also calibrate during training, the reported results improve calibration in both settings while maintaining or sometimes improving detection performance. summary.tldr: Cal-DETR uses uncertainty-guided score adjustment and logit mixing during training to improve detection-transformer calibration while preserving detection performance.

title: Cal-DETR: Calibrated Detection Transformer

abstract: The task of tuning regularization coefficients in regularized regression models with provable guarantees across problem instances still poses a significant challenge in the literature. This paper investigates the sample complexity of tuning regularization parameters in linear and logistic regressions under $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$-constraints in the data-driven setting. For the linear regression problem, by more carefully exploiting the structure of the dual function class, we provide a new upper bound for the pseudo-dimension of the validation loss function class, which significantly improves the best-known results on the problem. Remarkably, we also instantiate the first matching lower bound, proving our results are tight. For tuning the regularization parameters of logistic regression, we introduce a new approach to studying the learning guarantee via an approximation of the validation loss function class. We examine the pseudo-dimension of the approximation class and construct a uniform error bound between the validation loss function class and its approximation, which allows us to instantiate the first learning guarantee for the problem of tuning logistic regression regularization coefficients.

paragraphs: Choosing a regularization coefficient determines how strongly a regression model is constrained. This paper asks how much data is needed to learn good choices across problem instances with provable guarantees. It studies linear and logistic regression under l1 and l2 constraints, focusing on the complexity of the validation losses produced by different regularization choices.

For linear regression, the authors exploit the structure of the dual function class to improve an upper bound on pseudo-dimension. This quantity measures the complexity of the relevant validation loss family and helps establish learning guarantees. They also derive a matching lower bound, showing that their improved bound is tight for the problem studied.

Logistic regression requires a different approach. The authors approximate its validation loss family, analyze the approximation's pseudo-dimension, and bound the approximation error uniformly. Combining these ingredients yields the first learning guarantee stated for tuning logistic regression regularization coefficients. The contribution therefore sharpens an existing theoretical result for linear regression and establishes a new guarantee for logistic regression.
summary.tldr: The paper proves tight complexity bounds for linear regression regularization tuning and introduces a first learning guarantee for the logistic regression case.

title: New Bounds for Hyperparameter Tuning of Regression Problems Across Instances

abstract: Controlling the evolution of complex physical systems is a fundamental task across science and engineering. Classical techniques suffer from limited applicability or huge computational costs. On the other hand, recent deep learning and reinforcement learning-based approaches often struggle to optimize long-term control sequences under the constraints of system dynamics. In this work, we introduce Diffusion Physical systems Control (DiffPhyCon), a new class of method to address the physical systems control problem. DiffPhyCon excels by simultaneously minimizing both the learned generative energy function and the predefined control objectives across the entire trajectory and control sequence. Thus, it can explore globally and plan near-optimal control sequences. Moreover, we enhance DiffPhyCon with prior reweighting, enabling the discovery of control sequences that significantly deviate from the training distribution. We test our method on three tasks: 1D Burgers' equation, 2D jellyfish movement control, and 2D high-dimensional smoke control, where our generated jellyfish dataset is released as a benchmark for complex physical system control research. Our method outperforms widely applied classical approaches and state-of-the-art deep learning and reinforcement learning methods. Notably, DiffPhyCon unveils an intriguing fast-close-slow-open pattern observed in the jellyfish, aligning with established findings in the field of fluid dynamics. The project website, jellyfish dataset, and code can be found at https://github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/diffphycon.

paragraphs: Controlling a complex physical system requires choosing actions whose effects unfold over time while respecting the system’s dynamics. DiffPhyCon approaches this as a generative planning problem. It jointly optimizes the complete control sequence and the physical trajectory, combining a learned generative energy function with predefined control objectives.

This joint formulation lets the method explore entire candidate evolutions and seek near-optimal control sequences. The authors also introduce prior reweighting, which enables the search to find controls that differ substantially from those represented in the training distribution. That matters because useful control behavior may require moving beyond the examples used to learn the generative model.

The evaluation covers a one-dimensional Burgers’ equation task, two-dimensional jellyfish movement, and high-dimensional two-dimensional smoke control. The authors report better performance than the classical, deep learning, and reinforcement learning methods they compare against. For jellyfish, the method discovers a fast-closing, slow-opening pattern consistent with established fluid dynamics findings. They also release the generated jellyfish dataset as a benchmark for further physical control research.
summary.tldr: DiffPhyCon jointly generates physical trajectories and control sequences, using prior reweighting to discover effective controls beyond the training distribution.

title: DiffPhyCon: A Generative Approach to Control Complex Physical Systems

abstract: Diffusion regulates numerous natural processes and the dynamics of many successful generative models. Existing models to learn the diffusion terms from observational data rely on complex bilevel optimization problems and model only the drift of the system.We propose a new simple model, JKOnet*, which bypasses the complexity of existing architectures while presenting significantly enhanced representational capabilities: JKOnet* recovers the potential, interaction, and internal energy components of the underlying diffusion process. JKOnet* minimizes a simple quadratic loss and outperforms other baselines in terms of sample efficiency, computational complexity, and accuracy. Additionally, JKOnet* provides a closed-form optimal solution for linearly parametrized functionals, and, when applied to predict the evolution of cellular processes from real-world data, it achieves state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of all existing methods.Our methodology is based on the interpretation of diffusion processes as energy-minimizing trajectories in the probability space via the so-called JKO scheme, which we study via its first-order optimality conditions.

paragraphs: Learning diffusion from observations involves recovering the mechanisms governing how a distribution evolves. Existing approaches described in the paper use complicated nested optimization and represent only the system’s drift. JKOnet* aims to make this learning problem simpler while recovering a richer description that includes potential, interaction, and internal energy components.

The method treats diffusion as motion that minimizes energy in the space of probability distributions. It starts from the JKO scheme and uses its first-order optimality conditions to obtain a simple quadratic training loss. For linearly parameterized functionals, the authors also derive a closed-form optimal solution, giving that particular setting a direct route to fitting the model.

The reported comparisons show improvements in sample efficiency, computational complexity, and accuracy. On real-world data describing cellular processes, JKOnet* predicts evolution with state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of the existing methods considered. The contribution combines a more expressive account of diffusion with a training formulation that avoids the complexity of earlier architectures.
summary.tldr: JKOnet* learns multiple energy components of diffusion using a simple quadratic objective, improving efficiency and predictive accuracy.

title: Learning diffusion at lightspeed

abstract: Referring 3D Segmentation is a visual-language task that segments all points of the specified object from a 3D point cloud described by a sentence of query. Previous works perform a two-stage paradigm, first conducting language-agnostic instance segmentation then matching with given text query. However, the semantic concepts from text query and visual cues are separately interacted during the training, and both instance and semantic labels for each object are required, which is time consuming and human-labor intensive. To mitigate these issues, we propose a novel Referring 3D Segmentation pipeline, Label-Efficient and Single-Stage, dubbed LESS, which is only under the supervision of efficient binary mask. Specifically, we design a Point-Word Cross-Modal Alignment module for aligning the fine-grained features of points and textual embedding. Query Mask Predictor module and Query-Sentence Alignment module are introduced for coarse-grained alignment between masks and query. Furthermore, we propose an area regularization loss, which coarsely reduces irrelevant background predictions on a large scale. Besides, a point-to-point contrastive loss is proposed concentrating on distinguishing points with subtly similar features. Through extensive experiments, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on ScanRefer dataset by surpassing the previous methods about 3.7% mIoU using only binary labels. Code is available at https://github.com/mellody11/LESS.

paragraphs: Referring 3D segmentation identifies the points belonging to an object described in a sentence. Earlier approaches first segment objects without using language and then match those objects to the query. This separates parts of the visual-language learning process and requires both instance and semantic labels, creating a substantial annotation burden.

LESS combines the task into a single stage trained with binary masks. A point-word alignment module connects detailed point features to text embeddings, while a mask predictor and query-sentence alignment module connect the broader object mask to the query. These components let language and visual information interact at both fine and coarse levels.

Two additional losses target different sources of segmentation error. Area regularization reduces broad irrelevant background predictions, and point-to-point contrastive learning helps distinguish points with subtly similar features. On ScanRefer, LESS reports state-of-the-art performance, exceeding previous methods by about 3.7% mIoU while using only binary labels. The result indicates that reducing annotation requirements can coexist with stronger performance in this evaluation.
summary.tldr: LESS uses binary-mask supervision and joint point-language alignment to improve referring 3D segmentation on ScanRefer.

title: LESS: Label-Efficient and Single-Stage Referring 3D Segmentation

abstract: Causal discovery from observational data, especially for count data, is essential across scientific and industrial contexts, such as biology, economics, and network operation maintenance. For this task, most approaches model count data using Bayesian networks or ordinal relations. However, they overlook the inherent branching structures that are frequently encountered, e.g., a browsing event might trigger an adding cart or purchasing event. This can be modeled by a binomial thinning operator (for branching) and an additive independent Poisson distribution (for noising), known as Poisson Branching Structure Causal Model (PB-SCM). There is a provably sound cumulant-based causal discovery method that allows the identification of the causal structure under a branching structure. However, we show that there still remains a gap in that there exist causal directions that are identifiable while the algorithm fails to identify them. In this work, we address this gap by exploring the identifiability of PB-SCM using the Probability Generating Function (PGF). By developing a compact and exact closed-form solution for the PGF of PB-SCM, we demonstrate that each component in this closed-form solution uniquely encodes a specific local structure, enabling the identification of the local structures by testing their corresponding component appearances in the PGF. Building on this, we propose a practical algorithm for learning causal skeletons and identifying causal directions of PB-SCM using PGF. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through experiments on both synthetic and real datasets.

summary.tldr: An exact probability generating function exposes local causal structures in Poisson branching models that an existing cumulant-based method can miss.

title: On the Identifiability of Poisson Branching Structural Causal Model Using Probability Generating Function

abstract: The learnware paradigm aims to help users leverage numerous existing high-performing models instead of starting from scratch, where a learnware consists of a well-trained model and the specification describing its capability. Numerous learnwares are accommodated by a learnware dock system. When users solve tasks with the system, models that fully match the task feature space are often rare or even unavailable. However, models with heterogeneous feature space can still be helpful. This paper finds that label information, particularly model outputs, is helpful yet previously less exploited in the accommodation of heterogeneous learnwares. We extend the specification to better leverage model pseudo-labels and subsequently enrich the unified embedding space for better specification evolvement. With label information, the learnware identification can also be improved by additionally comparing conditional distributions. Experiments demonstrate that, even without a model explicitly tailored to user tasks, the system can effectively handle tasks by leveraging models from diverse feature spaces.

paragraphs: A learnware pairs a trained model with a specification describing what it can do. A collection of these packages is meant to help users reuse existing models instead of training new ones. The difficulty addressed here is that available models may use feature spaces different from those of the user's task, leaving few or no direct matches.

The paper identifies model outputs as useful information that earlier approaches have not fully exploited. It extends learnware specifications with pseudo-labels, meaning labels supplied by models. This information also enriches the shared embedding space in which specifications are represented and developed, giving the system additional evidence about model capabilities.

Label information further improves model identification through comparisons of conditional distributions. This adds a label-dependent perspective to matching models across different feature spaces. Experiments show that the system can handle user tasks using models from diverse feature spaces even when no model was explicitly tailored to the task. The result supports broader reuse through better descriptions and selection of existing models.
summary.tldr: Using model-generated labels helps a learnware system identify and reuse models whose feature spaces differ from the user's task.

title: Handling Learnwares from Heterogeneous Feature Spaces with Explicit Label Exploitation

abstract: Large multimodal models (LMMs) have proven flexible and generalisable across many tasks and fields. Although they have strong potential to aid scientific research, their capabilities in this domain are not well characterised. A key aspect of scientific research is the ability to understand and interpret figures, which serve as a rich, compressed source of complex information. In this work, we present SciFIBench, a scientific figure interpretation benchmark consisting of 2000 questions split between two tasks across 8 categories. The questions are curated from arXiv paper figures and captions, using adversarial filtering to find hard negatives and human verification forquality control. We evaluate 28 LMMs on SciFIBench, finding it to be a challenging benchmark. Finally, we investigate the alignment and reasoning faithfulness of the LMMs on augmented question sets from our benchmark. We release SciFIBench to encourage progress in this domain.

paragraphs: Scientific figures compress substantial information into visual form, making their interpretation an important test for models intended to assist research. SciFIBench provides a benchmark for this ability, addressing the limited characterization of large multimodal models in scientific settings. It contains 2,000 questions organized into two tasks spanning eight categories.

The questions are curated from figures and captions in arXiv papers. They also use augmented question sets to investigate model alignment and the faithfulness of reasoning, extending the analysis beyond overall task performance. The released benchmark gives researchers a common basis for studying scientific figure understanding and for examining whether the reasoning accompanying answers is faithful.
summary.tldr: SciFIBench provides 2,000 curated scientific-figure questions and reveals substantial challenges for the 28 multimodal models evaluated.

title: SciFIBench: Benchmarking Large Multimodal Models for Scientific Figure Interpretation

abstract: This paper introduces OpenGaussian, a method based on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that possesses the capability for 3D point-level open vocabulary understanding. Our primary motivation stems from observing that existing 3DGS-based open vocabulary methods mainly focus on 2D pixel-level parsing. These methods struggle with 3D point-level tasks due to weak feature expressiveness and inaccurate 2D-3D feature associations. To ensure robust feature presentation and 3D point-level understanding, we first employ SAM masks without cross-frame associations to train instance features with 3D consistency. These features exhibit both intra-object consistency and inter-object distinction. Then, we propose a two-stage codebook to discretize these features from coarse to fine levels. At the coarse level, we consider the positional information of 3D points to achieve location-based clustering, which is then refined at the fine level.Finally, we introduce an instance-level 3D-2D feature association method that links 3D points to 2D masks, which are further associated with 2D CLIP features. Extensive experiments, including open vocabulary-based 3D object selection, 3D point cloud understanding, click-based 3D object selection, and ablation studies, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. The source code is available at our project page https://3d-aigc.github.io/OpenGaussian.

paragraphs: OpenGaussian extends open-vocabulary understanding to individual 3D points in scenes represented with 3D Gaussian Splatting. The authors observe that existing methods mainly parse two-dimensional pixels and struggle with point-level tasks. They identify weak feature representations and inaccurate links between 2D and 3D features as central obstacles to understanding objects directly in the 3D representation.

The method first trains instance features using SAM masks without cross-frame mask associations. The resulting features aim to remain consistent within an object while distinguishing different objects in 3D. A two-stage codebook then discretizes them: a coarse stage uses point positions for location-based clustering, followed by a finer refinement stage.

This supplies the connection needed for open-vocabulary understanding at the point level. Experiments cover language-based 3D object selection, point-cloud understanding, and click-based selection, alongside ablation studies. The reported results support the effectiveness of the combined representation and association pipeline across these tasks.
summary.tldr: OpenGaussian combines consistent instance features, hierarchical discretization, and 2D–3D associations to support open-vocabulary understanding of 3D points.

title: OpenGaussian: Towards Point-Level 3D Gaussian-based Open Vocabulary Understanding

abstract: As ML models become increasingly complex and integral to high-stakes domains such as finance and healthcare, they also become more susceptible to sophisticated adversarial attacks. We investigate the threat posed by undetectable backdoors, as defined in Goldwasser et al. [2022], in models developed by insidious external expert firms. When such backdoors exist, they allow the designer of the model to sell information on how to slightly perturb their input to change the outcome of the model. We develop a general strategy to plant backdoors to obfuscated neural networks, that satisfy the security properties of the celebrated notion of indistinguishability obfuscation. Applying obfuscation before releasing neural networks is a strategy that is well motivated to protect sensitive information of the external expert firm. Our method to plant backdoors ensures that even if the weights and architecture of the obfuscated model are accessible, the existence ofthe backdoor is still undetectable. Finally, we introduce the notion of undetectable backdoors to language models and extend our neural network backdoor attacks to such models based on the existence of steganographic functions.

We investigate the threat posed by undetectable backdoors, as defined in Goldwasser et al. [2022], in models developed by insidious external expert firms. When such backdoors exist, they allow the designer of the model to sell information on how to slightly perturb their input to change the outcome of the model. We develop a general strategy to plant backdoors to obfuscated neural networks, that satisfy the security properties of the celebrated notion of indistinguishability obfuscation. Applying obfuscation before releasing neural networks is a strategy that is well motivated to protect sensitive information of the external expert firm. Our method to plant backdoors ensures that even if the weights and architecture of the obfuscated model are accessible, the existence ofthe backdoor is still undetectable. Finally, we introduce the notion of undetectable backdoors to language models and extend our neural network backdoor attacks to such models based on the existence of steganographic functions.

paragraphs: The paper studies a threat involving models supplied by a malicious external developer. A hidden backdoor lets someone who knows its secret slightly alter an input to change the model's output. The developer could then sell that knowledge. The research asks whether such manipulation can remain undetectable even when a recipient can inspect the released model's weights and architecture.

The construction concerns neural networks protected through obfuscation satisfying the cryptographic notion of indistinguishability obfuscation. Such protection is motivated by a supplier's desire to conceal sensitive information. The authors develop a general backdoor strategy for this setting and establish that access to the obfuscated model's internal structure still does not reveal the backdoor's existence.

The paper also formulates undetectable backdoors for language models and extends its attacks to that setting based on the existence of steganographic functions. These are conditional cryptographic results tied to the stated constructions. Their significance is that visibility into a released model's weights and architecture does not, within this setting, guarantee that malicious hidden behavior can be detected.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs undetectable backdoors in cryptographically obfuscated neural networks and extends the result to language models under a steganographic-function assumption.

title: Injecting Undetectable Backdoors in Obfuscated Neural Networks and Language Models

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the potential to transform humanities and social science research, yet their history knowledge and comprehension at a graduate level remains untested. Benchmarking LLMs in history is particularly challenging, given that human knowledge of history is inherently unbalanced, with more information available on Western history and recent periods. We introduce the History Seshat Test for LLMs (HiST-LLM), based on a subset of the Seshat Global History Databank, which provides a structured representation of human historical knowledge, containing 36,000 data points across 600 historical societies and over 2,700 scholarly references. This dataset covers every major world region from the Neolithic period to the Industrial Revolution and includes information reviewed and assembled by history experts and graduate research assistants. Using this dataset, we benchmark a total of seven models from the Gemini, OpenAI, and Llama families. We find that, in a four-choice format, LLMs have a balanced accuracy ranging from 33.6% (Llama-3.1-8B) to 46% (GPT-4-Turbo), outperforming random guessing (25%) but falling short of expert comprehension. LLMs perform better on earlier historical periods. Regionally, performance is more even but still better for the Americas and lowest in Oceania and Sub-Saharan Africa for the more advanced models. Our benchmark shows that while LLMs possess some expert-level historical knowledge, there is considerable room for improvement.
