paragraphs: Combining image frames with event streams can improve object tracking, but processing both can introduce substantial computational overhead. Event streams are sparse and asynchronous, and conventional fusion methods do not fully exploit their suitability for energy-efficient spiking computation. SpikeFET addresses this with a fully spiking framework for joint frame-event tracking.

The network combines convolutional extraction of local features with Transformer-based global modeling inside the spiking architecture. Its Random Patchwork Module addresses positional bias from convolutional padding through randomized spatial reorganization and learnable type encoding while preserving residual structures. This targets a weakness in maintaining consistent responses when objects shift position.

A second component, Spatial-Temporal Regularization, enforces consistency among temporal template features in latent space to address degraded similarity measurements caused by asymmetric features. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report higher tracking accuracy than existing methods together with significantly lower power consumption. The stated results support integrating both fusion and feature-consistency mechanisms into the spiking framework.
summary.tldr: SpikeFET combines image frames and event streams in a fully spiking tracker, reporting improved accuracy with reduced power consumption.

title: Fully Spiking Neural Networks for Unified Frame-Event Object Tracking

abstract: Text-to-Visualization (Text2VIS) enables users to create visualizations from natural language queries, making data insights more accessible. However, Text2VIS faces challenges in interpreting ambiguous queries, as users often express their visualization needs in imprecise language. To address this challenge, we introduce nBench 2.0, a new benchmark designed to evaluate Text2VIS systems in scenarios involving ambiguous queries. nvBench 2.0 includes 7,878 natural language queries and 24,076 corresponding visualizations, derived from 780 tables across 153 domains. It is built using a controlled ambiguity-injection pipeline that generates ambiguous queries through a reverse-generation workflow. By starting with unambiguous seed visualizations and selectively injecting ambiguities, the pipeline yields multiple valid interpretations for each query, with each ambiguous query traceable to its corresponding visualization through step-wise reasoning paths.We evaluate various Large Language Models (LLMs) on their ability to perform ambiguous Text2VIS tasks using nBench 2.0. We also propose Step-Text2Vis, an LLM-based model trained on nvBench 2.0, which enhances performance in ambiguous scenarios through step-wise preference optimization. Our results show that Step-Text2Vis outperforms all baselines, setting a new state-of-the-art for ambiguous Text2VIS tasks. Our source code and data are available at https://nvbench2.github.io/

paragraphs: nvBench 2.0 studies a common difficulty in generating charts from language: a user's request may reasonably correspond to more than one visualization. The benchmark is designed around this ambiguity, giving systems a setting in which interpreting an imprecise request is part of the task. It includes 7,878 queries and 24,076 visualizations from 780 tables spanning 153 domains.

The dataset starts with unambiguous seed visualizations and works backward to create queries with selected ambiguities. This controlled process produces multiple valid interpretations while preserving stepwise reasoning paths that connect queries to their corresponding visualizations. Those paths make the alternative interpretations traceable within the benchmark's construction.

The authors evaluate language models on these tasks and introduce Step-Text2Vis, a model trained on the benchmark using stepwise preference optimization. It outperforms all evaluated baselines for ambiguous text-to-visualization tasks. The combined contribution is an evaluation resource that explicitly represents multiple valid readings and a training approach that improves how a model reasons through those readings.
summary.tldr: nvBench 2.0 evaluates ambiguous chart requests, and Step-Text2Vis improves results through stepwise preference optimization.

title: nvBench 2.0: Resolving Ambiguity in Text-to-Visualization through Stepwise Reasoning

abstract: Privacy and security concerns are becoming increasingly critical for recommender systems, as model extraction attack provides an effective way to probe system robustness by replicating the model’s recommendation logic — potentially exposing sensitive user preferences and proprietary algorithmic knowledge. Despite the promising performance of existing model extraction methods, they still face two key challenges: unrealistic assumptions on the requirement of accessible member or surrogate data and generalization problem where surrogate model architecture constraints lead to overfitting on generated data. To tackle these challenges, in this paper, we first thoroughly analyze how the architecture of surrogate models influences extraction attack performance, highlighting the superior effectiveness of the graph convolution architecture. Based on this, we propose a novel Data-free Black-box Graph convolution-based Recommender Model Extraction method, dubbed DBGRME. Specifically, DBGRME contains: (1) an interaction generator to alleviate the need for member data requirements in a data-free scenario; and (2) a generalization-aware graph convolution-based surrogate model to capture diverse and complex recommender interaction patterns for mitigating the overfitting issue. Experimental results on various datasets and victim models demonstrate the superiority of our attack in data-free scenarios (e.g., surpassing PTQ data-require methods with 17.4% improvement on LightGCN). Code is available: \url{https://github.com/Vencent-Won/DBGRME.git}.

paragraphs: This paper studies copying the recommendation logic of a system whose internal model is unavailable. Such extraction can reveal weaknesses in protection of user preferences and proprietary knowledge. The authors focus on two obstacles in existing approaches: needing accessible member or surrogate data, and training a replacement model that overfits generated interactions.

Their method, DBGRME, combines an interaction generator with a graph convolution-based surrogate. The generator addresses the absence of the data that extraction methods commonly assume is available. The surrogate is designed to capture varied and complex interaction patterns while improving generalization. This choice follows an analysis showing that the architecture of the replacement model substantially affects extraction performance.

Across several datasets and target models, the authors report stronger extraction in data-free settings. One stated example is a 17.4% improvement over the data-requiring PTQ method on LightGCN. The findings show that access to existing interaction data is not required for the reported attack performance, and that surrogate architecture is an important part of assessing extraction risk.
summary.tldr: DBGRME combines generated interactions and a graph convolution surrogate to extract black-box recommender behavior without accessible interaction data.

title: Data-Free Model Extraction for Black-box Recommender Systems via Graph Convolutions

abstract: Classifier guidance is a widely adopted technique in diffusion language models, used to steer generation toward desired attributes. However, such guidance often introduces instability during the generation process, where token-level updates fluctuate across timesteps. We identify and formally characterize this phenomenon as update-forgetting. This instability disrupts the refinement process by overwriting semantic edits, ultimately degrading fluency and coherence, which is particularly problematic in tasks like controllable text generation. To address this, we propose TTA-Diffusion, a novel inference-time approach that dynamically allocates timesteps per token based on refinement needs. Unlike conventional diffusion models that apply uniform updates, TTA-Diffusion employs structured timestep allocation, preserving stable tokens while allowing uncertain tokens to undergo progressive adjustment. Experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that TTA-Diffusion significantly outperforms both diffusion-based and auto-regressive baselines in fluency and control accuracy while improving computational efficiency by reducing the number of required timesteps. On the sentiment control task, TTA-Diffusion achieves over 20\% higher accuracy and nearly half the perplexity of prior diffusion models, using less than one-fifth the denoising steps. This work highlights the importance of mitigating fluctuations in token updates and promoting a balanced refinement process, thereby enhancing stability and controllability in controllable language modeling.

paragraphs: Classifier guidance helps diffusion language models generate text with desired attributes, but repeated refinement can overwrite useful changes. The paper identifies and formally characterizes this instability as update-forgetting. Token updates fluctuate across generation steps, so an edit that improves control at one point may later disappear, harming the fluency and coherence of the resulting text.

TTA-Diffusion addresses this problem during inference by assigning refinement timesteps separately to individual tokens. Tokens that have become stable are preserved, while uncertain tokens receive further adjustment. This replaces a uniform update schedule with one that reflects differing refinement needs, aiming to retain successful semantic edits while continuing to improve unsettled parts of the text.

Across diverse tasks, the authors report better fluency and control accuracy than diffusion and autoregressive baselines, alongside fewer required timesteps. For sentiment control, they report over 20% higher accuracy and nearly half the perplexity of prior diffusion models using less than one-fifth as many denoising steps. These results connect more selective refinement with both stronger controllability and greater computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: TTA-Diffusion preserves useful text edits by allocating refinement steps per token, improving control and fluency while reducing denoising work.

title: Don’t Let It Fade: Preserving Edits in Diffusion Language Models via Token Timestep Allocation

abstract: Selecting artificial intelligence (AI) models, such as large language models (LLMs), from multiple candidates requires accurate performance estimation. This is ideally achieved through empirical evaluations involving abundant real-world data. However, such evaluations are costly and impractical at scale. To address this challenge, autoevaluation methods leverage synthetic data produced by automated evaluators, such as LLMs-as-judges, reducing variance but potentially introducing bias. Recent approaches have employed semi-supervised prediction-powered inference ($\texttt{PPI}$) to correct for the bias of autoevaluators. However, the use of autoevaluators may lead in practice to a degradation in sample efficiency compared to conventional methods using only real-world data. In this paper, we propose $\texttt{R-AutoEval+}$, a novel framework that provides finite-sample reliability guarantees on the model evaluation, while also ensuring an enhanced (or at least no worse) sample efficiency compared to conventional methods. The key innovation of $\texttt{R-AutoEval+}$ is an adaptive construction of the model evaluation variable, which dynamically tunes its reliance on synthetic data, reverting to conventional methods when the autoevaluator is insufficiently accurate. Experiments on the use of LLMs-as-judges for the optimization of quantization settings for the weights of an LLM, for prompt design in LLMs, and for test-time reasoning budget allocation in LLMs confirm the reliability and efficiency of $\texttt{R-AutoEval+}$.

paragraphs: Automated evaluators can make comparing AI models cheaper by supplying synthetic evaluations alongside real-world observations. Their judgments may reduce statistical variability, but they can also introduce bias. Prediction-powered inference corrects that bias using real observations, yet an inaccurate evaluator can still make estimation less sample-efficient than using real data alone.

R-AutoEval+ addresses this problem by adaptively controlling how much the performance estimate depends on synthetic data. Its evaluation variable changes according to the usefulness of the automated evaluator. When that evaluator is insufficiently accurate, the framework falls back to conventional evaluation, rather than continuing to rely on an unhelpful source of information.

The paper provides finite-sample reliability guarantees together with sample efficiency that is improved or at least no worse than conventional methods. Experiments examine LLM judges in quantization-setting selection, prompt design, and reasoning-budget allocation. The stated contribution is therefore both statistical and practical: synthetic judgments become an adjustable resource whose value is assessed within the evaluation procedure.
summary.tldr: R-AutoEval+ adaptively uses automated judgments to estimate model performance with reliability guarantees and sample efficiency no worse than conventional evaluation.

title: Adaptive Prediction-Powered AutoEval with Reliability and Efficiency Guarantees

abstract: Visuomotor policies trained via behavior cloning are vulnerable to covariate shift, where small deviations from expert trajectories can compound into failure. Common strategies to mitigate this issue involve expanding the training distribution through human-in-the-loop corrections or synthetic data augmentation. However, these approaches are often labor-intensive, rely on strong task assumptions, or compromise the quality of imitation. We introduce Latent Policy Barrier, a framework for robust visuomotor policy learning. Inspired by Control Barrier Functions, LPB treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as an implicit barrier separating safe, in-distribution states from unsafe, out-of-distribution (OOD) ones. Our approach decouples the role of precise expert imitation and OOD recovery into two separate modules: a base diffusion policy solely on expert data, and a dynamics model trained on both expert and suboptimal policy rollout data. At inference time, the dynamics model predicts future latent states and optimizes them to stay within the expert distribution. Both simulated and real-world experiments show that LPB improves both policy robustness and data efficiency, enabling reliable manipulation from limited expert data and without additional human correction or annotation. More details are on our anonymous project website https://latentpolicybarrier.github.io.

paragraphs: A robot trained to imitate expert demonstrations can struggle after a small mistake puts it in an unfamiliar situation. Further mistakes can then compound. Latent Policy Barrier addresses this distribution shift by using the internal representations of expert demonstrations as an implicit boundary around familiar states, drawing inspiration from control barrier functions.

The framework separates imitation from recovery. A base diffusion policy learns only from expert demonstrations, preserving its focus on expert behavior. A dynamics model learns from both expert data and suboptimal policy rollouts. During execution, this dynamics model predicts future latent states and optimizes them to remain within the expert distribution. The additional rollout data therefore supports recovery without becoming imitation targets for the base policy.

Experiments in simulation and the real world report improved robustness and data efficiency, including reliable manipulation with limited expert data and no additional human correction or annotation. The results support using a learned model of future states to counter departures from demonstrated behavior. The implicit barrier is the framework's mechanism for encouraging familiar behavior during execution.
summary.tldr: Latent Policy Barrier improves imitation-based robot control by predicting future states and steering them toward the expert distribution.

title: Latent Policy Barrier: Learning Robust Visuomotor Policies by Staying In-Distribution

abstract: Many real world datasets occur or can be arranged into multi-modal structures. With such datasets, the tasks to be learnt can be referenced by multiple indices. Current multitask learning frameworks are not designed to account for the preservation of this information. We propose the use of multilinear algebra as a natural way to model such a set of related tasks. We present two learning methods; one is an adapted convex relaxation method used in the context of tensor completion. The second method is based on the Tucker decomposition and on alternating minimization. Experiments on synthetic and real data indicate that the multilinear approaches provide a significant improvement over other multitask learning methods. Overall our second approach yields the best performance in all datasets.

paragraphs: Related learning tasks can have several organizing dimensions, so identifying a task requires multiple indices. The paper argues that existing multitask frameworks do not preserve this information adequately. It proposes multilinear algebra as a way to represent the tasks while retaining the multidimensional organization of the dataset.

The authors develop two methods within this approach. The first adapts a convex relaxation technique used for tensor completion. The second uses Tucker decomposition and alternating minimization. Both methods organize learning around the multiple task dimensions, allowing the model to use structure that would be lost if tasks were treated as an unstructured collection.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show significant improvements over the multitask methods used for comparison. The Tucker-based method gives the best overall performance on every dataset evaluated. These findings support preserving the multiple indices that define related tasks. They also identify the second method as the stronger of the two proposed approaches within the reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Tensor-based multitask methods preserve multiple task dimensions and improve performance in the reported synthetic and real-data experiments.

title: Multilinear Multitask Learning

abstract: We present a machine learning framework for modeling protein dynamics. Our approach uses L1-regularized, reversible hidden Markov models to understand large protein datasets generated via molecular dynamics simulations. Our model is motivated by three design principles: (1) the requirement of massive scalability; (2) the need to adhere to relevant physical law; and (3) the necessity of providing accessible interpretations, critical for rational protein engineering and drug design. We present an EM algorithm for learning and introduce a model selection criteria based on the physical notion of relaxation timescales. We contrast our model with standard methods in biophysics and demonstrate improved robustness. We implement our algorithm on GPUs and apply the method to two large protein simulation datasets generated respectively on the NCSA Bluewaters supercomputer and the Folding@Home distributed computing network. Our analysis identifies the conformational dynamics of the ubiquitin protein responsible for signaling, and elucidates the stepwise activation mechanism of the c-Src kinase protein.

paragraphs: The paper develops a framework for understanding protein motion from large molecular dynamics simulation datasets. Its design follows three requirements: handling massive amounts of data, respecting relevant physical law, and producing interpretations accessible enough to support protein engineering and drug design. The model uses L1-regularized, reversible hidden Markov models.

The authors present an expectation-maximization algorithm for learning and a model selection criterion based on physical relaxation timescales. This connects the choice of model to the timescales of the protein dynamics being represented. They also implement the algorithm on GPUs and report improved robustness compared with standard biophysics methods.

The framework is applied to two large simulation datasets generated on the NCSA Bluewaters supercomputer and the Folding@Home network. title: Understanding Protein Dynamics with L1-Regularized Reversible Hidden Markov Models

abstract: We study the following generalized matrix rank estimation problem: given an n-by-n matrix and a constant c > 0, estimate the number of eigenvalues that are greater than c. In the distributed setting, the matrix of interest is the sum of m matrices held by separate machines. We show that any deterministic algorithm solving this problem must communicate Ω(n^2) bits, which is order-equivalent to transmitting the whole matrix. In contrast, we propose a randomized algorithm that communicates only O(n) bits. The upper bound is matched by an Ω(n) lower bound on the randomized communication complexity. We demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the proposed algorithm with some numerical experiments.

In the distributed setting, the matrix of interest is the sum of m matrices held by separate machines. We show that any deterministic algorithm solving this problem must communicate Ω(n^2) bits, which is order-equivalent to transmitting the whole matrix. In contrast, we propose a randomized algorithm that communicates only O(n) bits. The upper bound is matched by an Ω(n) lower bound on the randomized communication complexity. paragraphs: The paper studies a thresholded version of matrix rank: count how many eigenvalues exceed a fixed positive value. The matrix is distributed indirectly, as a sum of matrices stored on separate machines. The central question is how much information those machines must exchange to estimate the count.

The authors establish a sharp separation between deterministic and randomized methods. Any deterministic algorithm for the studied problem requires communication proportional to the square of the matrix dimension, comparable in order to sending the entire matrix. Their randomized algorithm reduces the communication requirement to a quantity proportional to the dimension.

A matching lower bound shows that randomized methods also need at least linear communication in this setting. Thus the proposed communication scaling matches the best possible order established by the analysis. Numerical experiments demonstrate practical effectiveness as well. The result matters because it identifies randomness as a way to change the fundamental communication burden, rather than merely speeding up local calculations on each machine.
summary.tldr: Randomization reduces distributed generalized-rank estimation from quadratic to linear communication, matching a randomized lower bound.

title: Distributed Estimation of Generalized Matrix Rank: Efficient Algorithms and Lower Bounds

abstract: We develop a novel preconditioning method for ridge regression, based on recent linear sketching methods. By equipping Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient (SVRG) with this preconditioning process, we obtain a significant speed-up relative to fast stochastic methods such as SVRG, SDCA and SAG.
originalAbstract: We develop a novel preconditioning method for ridge regression, based on recent linear sketching methods. By equipping Stochastic Variance Reduced Gradient (SVRG) with this preconditioning process, we obtain a significant speed-up relative to fast stochastic methods such as SVRG, SDCA and SAG.

paragraphs: The paper focuses on solving ridge regression more quickly. Its contribution is a preconditioning method based on linear sketching, combined with stochastic variance reduced gradient, or SVRG. The target remains the ridge regression problem; the new method changes how the solver is equipped to approach that problem.

Preconditioning serves as a preparation step for optimization, and linear sketching supplies the basis for constructing that preparation. The proposed combination therefore has two distinct components: a sketch-based preconditioner and the SVRG optimization procedure that uses it. This arrangement matters because the contribution is not simply another use of SVRG; it modifies the conditions under which SVRG performs its work.

The abstract reports a significant speed-up relative to fast stochastic methods, specifically SVRG, SDCA, and SAG. Including SVRG itself among the comparisons makes the benefit of adding the preconditioning process especially relevant to the stated result. The paper’s central finding is thus computational: combining sketch-based preparation with an established stochastic solver can substantially accelerate ridge regression.
summary.tldr: A linear-sketching-based preconditioner significantly accelerates SVRG for ridge regression relative to several fast stochastic solvers.

title: Solving Ridge Regression using Sketched Preconditioned SVRG

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are distributions over sets of items that model diversity using kernels. Their applications in machine learning include summary extraction and recommendation systems. Yet, the cost of sampling from a DPP is prohibitive in large-scale applications, which has triggered an effort towards efficient approximate samplers. We build a novel MCMC sampler that combines ideas from combinatorial geometry, linear programming, and Monte Carlo methods to sample from DPPs with a fixed sample cardinality, also called projection DPPs. Our sampler leverages the ability of the hit-and-run MCMC kernel to efficiently move across convex bodies. Previous theoretical results yield a fast mixing time of our chain when targeting a distribution that is close to a projection DPP, but not a DPP in general. Our empirical results demonstrate that this extends to sampling projection DPPs, i.e., our sampler is more sample-efficient than previous approaches which in turn translates to faster convergence when dealing with costly-to-evaluate functions, such as summary extraction in our experiments.

The authors demonstrate this connection in summary extraction. The contribution therefore joins a geometric sampling construction with empirical evidence of practical gains for the intended distributions.
summary.tldr: A geometric hit-and-run sampler improves empirical projection-DPP sampling efficiency, with fast-mixing theory applying to a nearby target distribution.

title: Zonotope Hit-and-run for Efficient Sampling from Projection DPPs

abstract: Many sequential processing tasks require complex nonlinear transition functions from one step to the next. However, recurrent neural networks with “deep” transition functions remain difficult to train, even when using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. We introduce a novel theoretical analysis of recurrent networks based on Gersgorin’s circle theorem that illuminates several modeling and optimization issues and improves our understanding of the LSTM cell. Based on this analysis we propose Recurrent Highway Networks, which extend the LSTM architecture to allow step-to-step transition depths larger than one. Several language modeling experiments demonstrate that the proposed architecture results in powerful and efficient models. On the Penn Treebank corpus, solely increasing the transition depth from 1 to 10 improves word-level perplexity from 90.6 to 65.4 using the same number of parameters. On the larger Wikipedia datasets for character prediction (text8 and enwik8), RHNs outperform all previous results and achieve an entropy of 1.27 bits per character.

Some tasks require a complicated transformation between consecutive steps, but making that transformation deeper can make training difficult. The paper addresses this problem even in the setting of Long Short-Term Memory networks, which already provide a specialized recurrent architecture.

The authors first analyze recurrent networks using Gersgorin’s circle theorem. This mathematical perspective clarifies issues in modeling and optimization and gives additional insight into the LSTM cell. Motivated by that analysis, they introduce Recurrent Highway Networks, extending the LSTM architecture so that each step-to-step transition can contain more than one layer of computation.

On Penn Treebank, increasing depth from one to ten reduces word-level perplexity from 90.6 to 65.4 without increasing the parameter count. On text8 and enwik8 character prediction, the models surpass previous reported results and reach 1.27 bits per character. The results show that deeper transitions can improve predictive performance without simply enlarging the parameter budget.
summary.tldr: Recurrent Highway Networks deepen the computation between sequence steps, improving language modeling without requiring more parameters.

title: Recurrent Highway Networks

abstract: The problem of rank aggregation from pairwise and multiway comparisons has a wide range of implications, ranging from recommendation systems to sports rankings to social choice. Some of the most popular algorithms for this problem come from the class of spectral ranking algorithms; these include the rank centrality (RC) algorithm for pairwise comparisons, which returns consistent estimates under the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model for pairwise comparisons (Negahban et al., 2017), and its generalization, the Luce spectral ranking (LSR) algorithm, which returns consistent estimates under the more general multinomial logit (MNL) model for multiway comparisons (Maystre & Grossglauser, 2015). In this paper, we design a provably faster spectral ranking algorithm, which we call accelerated spectral ranking (ASR), that is also consistent under the MNL/BTL models. Our accelerated algorithm is achieved by designing a random walk that has a faster mixing time than the random walks associated with previous algorithms. In addition to a faster algorithm, our results yield improved sample complexity bounds for recovery of the MNL/BTL parameters: to the best of our knowledge, we give the first general sample complexity bounds for recovering the parameters of the MNL model from multiway comparisons under any (connected) comparison graph (and improve significantly over previous bounds for the BTL model for pairwise comparisons). We also give a message-passing interpretation of our algorithm, which suggests a decentralized distributed implementation. Our experiments on several real-world and synthetic datasets confirm that our new ASR algorithm is indeed orders of magnitude faster than existing algorithms.

summary.tldr: ASR accelerates spectral ranking through faster-mixing random walks while improving parameter-recovery bounds under standard comparison models.

title: Accelerated Spectral Ranking

abstract: The local model for differential privacy is emerging as the reference model for practical applications of collecting and sharing sensitive information while satisfying strong privacy guarantees. In the local model, there is no trusted entity which is allowed to have each individual’s raw data as is assumed in the traditional curator model. Individuals’ data are usually perturbed before sharing them. We explore the design of private hypothesis tests in the local model, where each data entry is perturbed to ensure the privacy of each participant. Specifically, we analyze locally private chi-square tests for goodness of fit and independence testing.

paragraphs: Statistical testing on sensitive data must account for how information is collected as well as how it is analyzed. This paper studies hypothesis testing under local differential privacy, where participants' data are perturbed before sharing. The setup does not rely on a trusted collector being allowed to inspect every person's original record.

The authors focus on locally private chi-square tests for goodness of fit and independence. Goodness-of-fit testing asks whether data agree with a proposed distribution, while independence testing asks whether variables are statistically independent. Both questions must be addressed using entries that have already been altered to protect the participants who supplied them.

The contribution is an analysis of these testing problems within the local privacy model. This connects familiar statistical questions with a collection process that builds privacy into each participant's shared data. The distinction matters because the information available to the test is the perturbed data, making the privacy mechanism part of the statistical problem from the outset.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes chi-square goodness-of-fit and independence tests when each participant's data are perturbed for local differential privacy.

title: Local Private Hypothesis Testing: Chi-Square Tests

abstract: Distributed learning aims at computing high-quality models by training over scattered data. This covers a diversity of scenarios, including computer clusters or mobile agents. One of the main challenges is then to deal with heterogeneous machines and unreliable communications. In this setting, we propose and analyze a flexible asynchronous optimization algorithm for solving nonsmooth learning problems. Unlike most existing methods, our algorithm is adjustable to various levels of communication costs, machines computational powers, and data distribution evenness. We prove that the algorithm converges linearly with a fixed learning rate that does not depend on communication delays nor on the number of machines. Although long delays in communication may slow down performance, no delay can break convergence.

paragraphs: Distributed learning must combine work from machines that can differ in computing power, communication reliability, and the amount of data they hold. These differences make coordination part of the optimization problem. This paper develops an asynchronous algorithm for nonsmooth learning problems, allowing distributed computation to proceed despite uneven communication and computation.

The method is designed to be adjustable across several practical conditions: expensive communication, unequal machine speeds, and uneven data distribution. That flexibility matters because a single coordination pattern may suit one distributed setting poorly even if it works well in another. The paper both proposes the algorithm and analyzes its convergence behavior.

The central guarantee is linear convergence with a fixed learning rate that does not depend on communication delays or the number of machines. Within the analyzed setting, delays can slow progress but cannot destroy convergence. This separates speed from eventual reliability: delayed information may make learning take longer, while the algorithm still retains its convergence guarantee without choosing a delay-dependent learning rate.
summary.tldr: An asynchronous optimization algorithm tolerates communication delays while retaining linear convergence with a fixed, delay-independent learning rate.

title: A Delay-tolerant Proximal-Gradient Algorithm for Distributed Learning

abstract: Gradient coding is a technique for straggler mitigation in distributed learning. In this paper we design novel gradient codes using tools from classical coding theory, namely, cyclic MDS codes, which compare favourably with existing solutions, both in the applicable range of parameters and in the complexity of the involved algorithms. Second, we introduce an approximate variant of the gradient coding problem, in which we settle for approximate gradient computation instead of the exact one. This approach enables graceful degradation, i.e., the $\ell_2$ error of the approximate gradient is a decreasing function of the number of stragglers. Our main result is that the normalized adjacency matrix of an expander graph can yield excellent approximate gradient codes, and that this approach allows us to perform significantly less computation compared to exact gradient coding. We experimentally test our approach on Amazon EC2, and show that the generalization error of approximate gradient coding is very close to the full gradient while requiring significantly less computation from the workers.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can be slowed by workers that finish their computations late. Gradient coding addresses these stragglers by organizing computations so learning can proceed despite missing worker results. This paper develops new exact gradient codes using cyclic MDS codes, reporting favorable parameter coverage and algorithmic complexity compared with existing solutions.

The authors also introduce an approximate version of gradient coding, allowing the computed gradient to differ from the exact one. Their main construction uses the normalized adjacency matrix of an expander graph. This approach can substantially reduce worker computation compared with exact gradient coding, making approximation an explicit option in the design.

Experiments on Amazon EC2 find that approximate gradient coding produces generalization error very close to that obtained with the full gradient while requiring significantly less worker computation. The result connects an approximation in distributed computation to the quality of the learned model. It supports the practical value of approximate codes in the tested setting alongside the new exact constructions.
summary.tldr: New exact and approximate gradient codes mitigate distributed-learning stragglers, with approximate codes reducing computation while preserving similar reported generalization error.

title: Gradient Coding from Cyclic MDS Codes and Expander Graphs

abstract: Physical construction—the ability to compose objects, subject to physical dynamics, to serve some function—is fundamental to human intelligence. We introduce a suite of challenging physical construction tasks inspired by how children play with blocks, such as matching a target configuration, stacking blocks to connect objects together, and creating shelter-like structures over target objects. We examine how a range of deep reinforcement learning agents fare on these challenges, and introduce several new approaches which provide superior performance. Our results show that agents which use structured representations (e.g., objects and scene graphs) and structured policies (e.g., object-centric actions) outperform those which use less structured representations, and generalize better beyond their training when asked to reason about larger scenes. Model-based agents which use Monte-Carlo Tree Search also outperform strictly model-free agents in our most challenging construction problems. We conclude that approaches which combine structured representations and reasoning with powerful learning are a key path toward agents that possess rich intuitive physics, scene understanding, and planning.

The paper introduces tasks inspired by children’s block play, including matching a target arrangement, connecting objects with stacked blocks, and building shelter-like structures over targets. These tasks provide a setting for examining how learning agents handle construction, scene understanding, and planning.

The authors compare deep reinforcement learning agents and introduce approaches that perform better on these challenges. Agents using structured representations, such as objects and scene graphs, and structured policies, such as object-centered actions, outperform less structured alternatives. They also generalize better when tested on scenes larger than those encountered during training.

On the most challenging construction problems, model-based agents using Monte Carlo Tree Search outperform strictly model-free agents. The findings support combining explicit structure and reasoning with learned behavior. This conclusion is grounded in the construction tasks studied: both how an agent represents a scene and how it plans actions affect its ability to build successfully.
summary.tldr: Object-based representations, structured actions, and model-based planning improve agents’ performance on physical construction tasks and generalization to larger scenes.

title: Structured agents for physical construction

abstract: We propose a new point of view for regularizing deep neural networks by using the norm of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). Even though this norm cannot be computed, it admits upper and lower approximations leading to various practical strategies. Specifically, this perspective (i) provides a common umbrella for many existing regularization principles, including spectral norm and gradient penalties, or adversarial training, (ii) leads to new effective regularization penalties, and (iii) suggests hybrid strategies combining lower and upper bounds to get better approximations of the RKHS norm. We experimentally show this approach to be effective when learning on small datasets, or to obtain adversarially robust models.

Specifically, this perspective (i) provides a common umbrella for many existing regularization principles, including spectral norm and gradient penalties, or adversarial training, (ii) leads to new effective regularization penalties, and (iii) suggests hybrid strategies combining lower and upper bounds to get better approximations of the RKHS norm. We experimentally show this approach to be effective when learning on small datasets, or to obtain adversarially robust models.

paragraphs: Regularization guides a neural network toward solutions with desirable behavior beyond fitting its training examples. This paper proposes understanding several regularization methods through a common mathematical quantity: the norm associated with a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. That perspective gives different training penalties a shared reference point for describing and controlling the learned function.

The central practical obstacle is that this norm cannot be computed directly. The authors instead use upper and lower approximations that lead to usable training strategies. Through these approximations, they connect spectral norm penalties, gradient penalties, and adversarial training. They also derive new penalties and suggest combining upper and lower bounds to approximate the underlying norm more closely.

Experiments support the approach for learning from small datasets and for producing models resistant to adversarial perturbations. Its contribution therefore combines an organizing explanation of existing methods with additional regularization choices. The reported effectiveness concerns those experimental settings; the shared mathematical perspective does not make every approximation equally effective in every application.
summary.tldr: Approximations to an RKHS norm unify existing neural-network regularizers and motivate new penalties effective in small-data and adversarial-robustness experiments.

title: A Kernel Perspective for Regularizing Deep Neural Networks

abstract: There has recently been a steady increase in the number iterative approaches to density estimation. However, an accompanying burst of formal convergence guarantees has not followed; all results pay the price of heavy assumptions which are often unrealistic or hard to check. The Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) literature — seemingly orthogonal to the aforementioned pursuit — has had the side effect of a renewed interest in variational divergence minimisation (notably $f$-GAN). We show how to combine this latter approach and the classical boosting theory in supervised learning to get the first density estimation algorithm that provably achieves geometric convergence under very weak assumptions. We do so by a trick allowing to combine classifiers as the sufficient statistics of an exponential family. Our analysis includes an improved variational characterisation of $f$-GAN.

paragraphs: Density estimation aims to learn a probability distribution from data. Iterative methods repeatedly refine that estimate, but the paper identifies a gap between the availability of such methods and convincing convergence guarantees. Earlier guarantees, as characterized by the authors, depend on assumptions that can be demanding or difficult to verify.

The proposed approach combines variational divergence minimization, associated with f-GAN, and classical supervised boosting theory. Its key construction uses classifiers as sufficient statistics of an exponential family. This gives the classifiers a direct role in specifying the density model, providing a mathematical connection between combining supervised predictors and improving a distribution estimate.

The authors prove geometric convergence under assumptions they describe as very weak, presenting this as the first density estimation algorithm with that combination of guarantees. Geometric convergence means the relevant error bound decreases by a multiplicative factor across iterations. The analysis also improves the variational characterization of f-GAN, so the contribution includes both an estimation algorithm and a refinement of its theoretical foundation.
summary.tldr: Combining boosting with variational divergence minimization yields a density estimator with provable geometric convergence under very weak assumptions.

title: Boosted Density Estimation Remastered

abstract: We provide the first importance sampling variants of variance reduced algorithms for empirical risk minimization with non-convex loss functions. In particular, we analyze non-convex versions of \texttt{SVRG}, \texttt{SAGA} and \texttt{SARAH}. Our methods have the capacity to speed up the training process by an order of magnitude compared to the state of the art on real datasets. Moreover, we also improve upon current mini-batch analysis of these methods by proposing importance sampling for minibatches in this setting. Surprisingly, our approach can in some regimes lead to superlinear speedup with respect to the minibatch size, which is not usually present in stochastic optimization. All the above results follow from a general analysis of the methods which works with arbitrary sampling , i.e., fully general randomized strategy for the selection of subsets of examples to be sampled in each iteration. Finally, we also perform a novel importance sampling analysis of \texttt{SARAH} in the convex setting.

paragraphs: Training methods that use sampled examples must decide which examples to select at each iteration. This paper studies that choice for variance-reduced optimization with nonconvex losses. It develops importance-sampling variants of SVRG, SAGA, and SARAH, bringing unequal sampling choices into methods designed to reduce noise in optimization updates.

The common foundation is an analysis that permits arbitrary randomized selection of subsets of examples. This includes mini-batches and supports improved mini-batch guarantees through importance sampling. In some regimes, the analysis yields superlinear speedup with respect to batch size: increasing the batch can deliver a more-than-proportional improvement in the relevant convergence behavior.

On real datasets, the methods have the capacity to accelerate training by an order of magnitude relative to the stated prior state of the art. The paper also supplies a new importance-sampling analysis of SARAH for convex objectives. Its main contribution is a general analytical framework that connects sampling design to optimization performance, with unusually strong gains possible in particular regimes.
summary.tldr: A general sampling analysis enables importance-sampled variance-reduced methods for nonconvex learning, with substantial acceleration possible in certain settings.

title: Nonconvex Variance Reduced Optimization with Arbitrary Sampling

abstract: Recent advances in deep learning theory have evoked the study of generalizability across different local minima of deep neural networks (DNNs). While current work focused on either discovering properties of good local minima or developing regularization techniques to induce good local minima, no approach exists that can tackle both problems. We achieve these two goals successfully in a unified manner. Specifically, based on the observed Fisher information we propose a metric both strongly indicative of generalizability of local minima and effectively applied as a practical regularizer. We provide theoretical analysis including a generalization bound and empirically demonstrate the success of our approach in both capturing and improving the generalizability of DNNs. Experiments are performed on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet for various network architectures.

paragraphs: Different local minima of a neural network’s training objective can differ in how well they generalize. The paper brings together two questions that are often treated separately: how to recognize solutions that generalize well, and how to steer training toward such solutions. It proposes a single information-theoretic quantity for both purposes.

That quantity is based on observed Fisher information. The authors present it as a metric strongly indicative of a local minimum’s generalization behavior and also turn it into a practical regularizer. This links assessment and intervention: the same underlying measure helps characterize a trained solution and influences the process used to obtain one.

The theoretical analysis includes a generalization bound, while experiments evaluate both the metric’s descriptive role and its use in improving generalization. The evaluations cover CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet with multiple network architectures. The reported findings support this unified approach across those experiments, without making the metric an infallible predictor of generalization for every network or minimum.
summary.tldr: An observed-Fisher-information metric both characterizes generalization at local minima and serves as a regularizer that improves it empirically.

title: Information-Theoretic Local Minima Characterization and Regularization

abstract: The latent spaces of GAN models often have semantically meaningful directions. Moving in these directions corresponds to human-interpretable image transformations, such as zooming or recoloring, enabling a more controllable generation process. However, the discovery of such directions is currently performed in a supervised manner, requiring human labels, pretrained models, or some form of self-supervision. These requirements severely restrict a range of directions existing approaches can discover. In this paper, we introduce an unsupervised method to identify interpretable directions in the latent space of a pretrained GAN model. By a simple model-agnostic procedure, we find directions corresponding to sensible semantic manipulations without any form of (self-)supervision. Furthermore, we reveal several non-trivial findings, which would be difficult to obtain by existing methods, e.g., a direction corresponding to background removal. As an immediate practical benefit of our work, we show how to exploit this finding to achieve competitive performance for weakly-supervised saliency detection. The implementation of our method is available online.

paragraphs: A GAN's latent space can contain directions that correspond to understandable image changes, such as zooming or recoloring. Finding these directions gives users more control over generated images. The paper argues that discovery methods relying on labels, pretrained models, or self-supervision restrict the range of transformations they can uncover.

summary.tldr: An unsupervised procedure discovers meaningful controls in pretrained GANs, including a background-removal direction useful for saliency detection.

title: Unsupervised Discovery of Interpretable Directions in the GAN Latent Space

abstract: We introduce and analyze a best arm identification problem in the rested bandit setting, wherein arms are themselves learning algorithms whose expected losses decrease with the number of times the arm has been played. The shape of the expected loss functions is similar across arms, and is assumed to be available up to unknown parameters that have to be learned on the fly. We define a novel notion of regret for this problem, where we compare to the policy that always plays the arm having the smallest expected loss at the end of the game. We analyze an arm elimination algorithm whose regret vanishes as the time horizon increases. The actual rate of convergence depends in a detailed way on the postulated functional form of the expected losses. We complement our analysis with lower bounds, indicating strengths and limitations of the proposed solution.
originalAbstract: We introduce and analyze a best arm identification problem in the rested bandit setting, wherein arms are themselves learning algorithms whose expected losses decrease with the number of times the arm has been played. The shape of the expected loss functions is similar across arms, and is assumed to be available up to unknown parameters that have to be learned on the fly. We define a novel notion of regret for this problem, where we compare to the policy that always plays the arm having the smallest expected loss at the end of the game. We analyze an arm elimination algorithm whose regret vanishes as the time horizon increases. The actual rate of convergence depends in a detailed way on the postulated functional form of the expected losses. We complement our analysis with lower bounds, indicating strengths and limitations of the proposed solution.

paragraphs: Choosing among learning algorithms differs from choosing among fixed alternatives because an algorithm improves when more computation is assigned to it. This paper models that process as a rested bandit: each arm is a learning algorithm whose expected loss decreases with the number of times it is selected.

The expected loss curves share a known functional form, while their parameters must be learned during allocation. The authors define regret relative to a policy that always trains the arm with the smallest expected loss at the end of the horizon. They then analyze an elimination algorithm that removes arms as evidence accumulates about their likely performance.

The algorithm’s regret vanishes as the horizon grows, with the convergence rate depending on the assumed shapes of the learning curves. Lower bounds clarify where the proposed solution is strong and where limitations remain. The analysis therefore provides a principled model-selection framework when curve structure is available, rather than a guarantee for arbitrary and unpredictable learning dynamics.
summary.tldr: A rested-bandit model analyzes how to allocate training among algorithms whose losses improve with additional effort.

title: Best Model Identification: A Rested Bandit Formulation

abstract: Episodic memory-based methods can rapidly latch onto past successful strategies by a non-parametric memory and improve sample efficiency of traditional reinforcement learning. However, little effort is put into the continuous domain, where a state is never visited twice, and previous episodic methods fail to efficiently aggregate experience across trajectories. To address this problem, we propose Generalizable Episodic Memory (GEM), which effectively organizes the state-action values of episodic memory in a generalizable manner and supports implicit planning on memorized trajectories. GEM utilizes a double estimator to reduce the overestimation bias induced by value propagation in the planning process. Empirical evaluation shows that our method significantly outperforms existing trajectory-based methods on various MuJoCo continuous control tasks. To further show the general applicability, we evaluate our method on Atari games with discrete action space, which also shows a significant improvement over baseline algorithms.

The paper focuses on the difficulty of doing this in continuous domains, where exact states do not recur. Earlier episodic approaches also struggle to combine useful experience across different trajectories, limiting how effectively stored successes inform new decisions.

Generalizable Episodic Memory, or GEM, organizes remembered state-action values so they can generalize and support implicit planning over stored trajectories. Its memory therefore serves as more than a collection of isolated past outcomes. GEM also uses two estimators to reduce overestimation bias introduced when values propagate through the planning process.

On several MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, GEM significantly outperforms existing trajectory-based methods. Additional Atari experiments show significant improvements over baseline algorithms in a discrete-action setting. These results support both the continuous-domain motivation and broader applicability: organizing memory for generalization and controlling planning-related overestimation can make remembered experience more useful in the evaluated reinforcement-learning tasks.
summary.tldr: GEM makes episodic value memory generalizable and supports implicit planning, improving results on continuous-control tasks and Atari.

title: Generalizable Episodic Memory for Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we propose scalable methods for maximizing a regularized submodular function $f \triangleq g-\ell$ expressed as the difference between a monotone submodular function $g$ and a modular function $\ell$. Submodularity is inherently related to the notions of diversity, coverage, and representativeness. In particular, finding the mode (i.e., the most likely configuration) of many popular probabilistic models of diversity, such as determinantal point processes and strongly log-concave distributions, involves maximization of (regularized) submodular functions. Since a regularized function $f$ can potentially take on negative values, the classic theory of submodular maximization, which heavily relies on the non-negativity assumption of submodular functions, is not applicable. To circumvent this challenge, we develop the first one-pass streaming algorithm for maximizing a regularized submodular function subject to a $k$-cardinality constraint. Furthermore, we develop the first distributed algorithm that returns a solution $S$ in $O(1/ \epsilon)$ rounds of MapReduce computation. We highlight that our result, even for the unregularized case where the modular term $\ell$ is zero, improves the memory and communication complexity of the state-of-the-art by a factor of $O(1/ \epsilon)$ while arguably provides a simpler distributed algorithm and a unifying analysis. We empirically study the performance of our scalable methods on a set of real-life applications, including finding the mode of negatively correlated distributions, vertex cover of social networks, and several data summarization tasks.

That breaks assumptions used by much of classical submodular-maximization theory. This paper develops scalable algorithms for maximizing a monotone submodular benefit minus such a cost under a cardinality constraint.

Even when the cost term is zero, the distributed result improves the stated memory and communication complexity of prior methods by a factor of O(1/ε).

Experiments cover finding likely configurations of negatively correlated distributions, social-network vertex cover, and data summarization. These applications show why diversity rewards and explicit costs need to be handled together at scale. The contribution is an algorithmic and analytical framework for that objective class; the abstract does not claim exact optimization of every instance or specify all approximation constants.
summary.tldr: Streaming and distributed algorithms scale submodular maximization with modular costs, including objectives that can be negative.

title: Regularized Submodular Maximization at Scale

abstract: Linear residualization is a common practice for confounding adjustment in machine learning applications. Recently, causality-aware predictive modeling has been proposed as an alternative causality-inspired approach for adjusting for confounders. In this paper, we compare the linear residualization approach against the causality-aware confounding adjustment in anticausal prediction tasks. Our comparisons include both the settings where the training and test sets come from the same distributions, as well as, when the training and test sets are shifted due to selection biases. In the absence of dataset shifts, we show that the causality-aware approach tends to (asymptotically) outperform the residualization adjustment in terms of predictive performance in linear learners. Importantly, our results still holds even when the true model generating the data is not linear. We illustrate our results in both regression and classification tasks. Furthermore, in the presence of dataset shifts in the joint distribution of the confounders and outcome variables, we show that the causality-aware approach is more stable than linear residualization.

paragraphs: Adjusting for confounders can change how well a predictive model works. This paper compares the common practice of linear residualization with a causality-aware adjustment approach. Its focus is anticausal prediction using linear learners, and it considers both matched training and test distributions and distribution shifts caused by selection bias.

When there is no dataset shift, the authors show that the causality-aware approach tends to outperform residualization asymptotically. This describes a tendency in the large-data setting, rather than a claim that every finite dataset must favor it. The result also holds when the underlying process generating the data is nonlinear, despite the use of linear prediction models.

The authors illustrate their results in regression and classification. They also examine changes in the joint distribution of confounders and outcomes, finding that causality-aware adjustment is more stable than residualization. Together, the findings connect the choice of confounding adjustment to both predictive performance and robustness under the particular distribution shifts studied.
summary.tldr: For the studied anticausal prediction tasks, causality-aware adjustment tends to improve large-sample linear prediction and is more stable under specified distribution shifts.

title: Causality-aware counterfactual confounding adjustment as an alternative to linear residualization in anticausal prediction tasks based on linear learners

abstract: We combine two advanced ideas widely used in optimization for machine learning: \textit{shuffling} strategy and \textit{momentum} technique to develop a novel shuffling gradient-based method with momentum, coined \textbf{S}huffling \textbf{M}omentum \textbf{G}radient (SMG), for non-convex finite-sum optimization problems. While our method is inspired by momentum techniques, its update is fundamentally different from existing momentum-based methods. We establish state-of-the-art convergence rates of SMG for any shuffling strategy using either constant or diminishing learning rate under standard assumptions (i.e. \textit{$L$-smoothness} and \textit{bounded variance}). When the shuffling strategy is fixed, we develop another new algorithm that is similar to existing momentum methods, and prove the same convergence rates for this algorithm under the $L$-smoothness and bounded gradient assumptions. We demonstrate our algorithms via numerical simulations on standard datasets and compare them with existing shuffling methods. Our tests have shown encouraging performance of the new algorithms.

paragraphs: Machine learning optimization often combines repeated passes through training examples with momentum, which incorporates information from earlier updates. This paper develops Shuffling Momentum Gradient for non-convex objectives expressed as finite sums. Although inspired by momentum, SMG uses an update that differs fundamentally from existing momentum methods.

The authors establish state-of-the-art convergence rates for any shuffling strategy with either constant or diminishing learning rates, assuming L-smoothness and bounded variance. The result therefore covers multiple ways of ordering the terms rather than depending on a single shuffling rule. The assumptions specify the regularity and variability conditions under which the rates hold.

For a fixed shuffling strategy, the paper introduces another algorithm closer to conventional momentum methods. It achieves the same convergence rates under L-smoothness and bounded gradients, a different set of assumptions. Numerical simulations on standard datasets compare both algorithms with existing shuffling methods and show encouraging performance, complementing the theoretical analysis without asserting universal empirical superiority.
summary.tldr: SMG combines shuffling and a distinctive momentum update with convergence guarantees for non-convex finite-sum optimization under stated assumptions.

title: SMG: A Shuffling Gradient-Based Method with Momentum

abstract: Many existing neural architecture search (NAS) solutions rely on downstream training for architecture evaluation, which takes enormous computations. Considering that these computations bring a large carbon footprint, this paper aims to explore a green (namely environmental-friendly) NAS solution that evaluates architectures without training. Intuitively, gradients, induced by the architecture itself, directly decide the convergence and generalization results. It motivates us to propose the gradient kernel hypothesis: Gradients can be used as a coarse-grained proxy of downstream training to evaluate random-initialized networks. To support the hypothesis, we conduct a theoretical analysis and find a practical gradient kernel that has good correlations with training loss and validation performance. According to this hypothesis, we propose a new kernel based architecture search approach KNAS. Experiments show that KNAS achieves competitive results with orders of magnitude faster than “train-then-test” paradigms on image classification tasks. Furthermore, the extremely low search cost enables its wide applications. The searched network also outperforms strong baseline RoBERTA-large on two text classification tasks.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search can require substantial computation because candidate networks are trained before being evaluated. This paper seeks to reduce that search cost and its associated environmental burden by assessing architectures without training them. The central question is whether information available at random initialization can provide a useful indication of later performance.

The authors propose the gradient kernel hypothesis: gradients induced by an architecture can act as a coarse proxy for downstream training. They provide theoretical analysis and identify a practical gradient kernel that correlates well with training loss and validation performance. KNAS uses this kernel to guide architecture search, treating the gradient signal as an approximate evaluation tool.

On image-classification tasks, experiments show competitive results with search running orders of magnitude faster than train-then-test approaches. A searched network also outperforms RoBERTa-large on two text-classification tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the proxy in the evaluated settings. The environmental motivation is addressed through reduced search computation; the reported evidence concerns search speed and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: KNAS uses gradient kernels at random initialization to search architectures without candidate training, greatly reducing search time in experiments.

title: KNAS: Green Neural Architecture Search

abstract: Real-world networks often come with side information that can help to improve the performance of network analysis tasks such as clustering. Despite a large number of empirical and theoretical studies conducted on network clustering methods during the past decade, the added value of side information and the methods used to incorporate it optimally in clustering algorithms are relatively less understood. We propose a new iterative algorithm to cluster networks with side information for nodes (in the form of covariates) and show that our algorithm is optimal under the Contextual Symmetric Stochastic Block Model. Our algorithm can be applied to general Contextual Stochastic Block Models and avoids hyperparameter tuning in contrast to previously proposed methods. We confirm our theoretical results on synthetic data experiments where our algorithm significantly outperforms other methods, and show that it can also be applied to signed graphs. Finally we demonstrate the practical interest of our method on real data.

paragraphs: Clustering a network can draw on two sources of information: which nodes connect and what is known about each node. This paper investigates how to combine connections with node covariates. Its motivation is that the benefits of this additional information, and how to incorporate it optimally, are less well understood than network clustering alone.

The authors introduce an iterative clustering algorithm and establish its optimality under the Contextual Symmetric Stochastic Block Model. This model provides the setting in which the guarantee holds. The algorithm can also be applied to more general Contextual Stochastic Block Models, and it avoids the hyperparameter tuning required by previously proposed methods.

Synthetic experiments support the theoretical results and show substantial improvements over other methods. The authors also demonstrate applicability to signed graphs and examine real data. These findings establish both a model-specific optimality result and broader practical applicability; the abstract does not extend the optimality guarantee to every network on which the algorithm can run.
summary.tldr: An iterative algorithm combines network connections and node information, achieving optimality under a symmetric contextual block model without hyperparameter tuning.

title: An iterative clustering algorithm for the Contextual Stochastic Block Model with optimality guarantees

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are known to be highly vulnerable to adversarial examples (AEs) that include malicious perturbations. Assumptions about the statistical differences between natural and adversarial inputs are commonplace in many detection techniques. As a best practice, AE detectors are evaluated against ’adaptive’ attackers who actively perturb their inputs to avoid detection. Due to the difficulties in designing adaptive attacks, however, recent work suggests that most detectors have incomplete evaluation. We aim to fill this gap by designing a generic adaptive attack against detectors: the ’statistical indistinguishability attack’ (SIA). SIA optimizes a novel objective to craft adversarial examples (AEs) that follow the same distribution as the natural inputs with respect to DNN representations. Our objective targets all DNN layers simultaneously as we show that AEs being indistinguishable at one layer might fail to be so at other layers. SIA is formulated around evading distributional detectors that inspect a set of AEs as a whole and is also effective against four individual AE detectors, two dataset shift detectors, and an out-of-distribution sample detector, curated from published works. This suggests that SIA can be a reliable tool for evaluating the security of a range of detectors.

paragraphs: Many adversarial-example detectors rely on statistical differences between natural inputs and deliberately perturbed inputs. Evaluating those defenses requires attackers that actively try to evade detection. This paper addresses the difficulty of constructing such adaptive attacks, which can otherwise leave detector evaluations incomplete.

The proposed statistical indistinguishability attack, SIA, optimizes an objective intended to make adversarial examples match natural inputs in the distributions of their neural-network representations. It targets every network layer simultaneously. The authors show why that matters: examples that appear indistinguishable at one layer may still look different at another, leaving a detector with a usable signal.

SIA is formulated for detectors that inspect a collection of adversarial examples together. The authors also find it effective against four detectors of individual adversarial examples, two dataset-shift detectors, and one out-of-distribution detector from published work. These results suggest that distribution matching can provide a useful adaptive test across several detector types, strengthening security evaluation beyond attacks that ignore the detector.
summary.tldr: SIA crafts adversarial inputs whose representations resemble natural data across network layers, providing an adaptive test for statistical detectors.

title: Generating Distributional Adversarial Examples to Evade Statistical Detectors

abstract: Important problems in causal inference, economics, and, more generally, robust machine learning can be expressed as conditional moment restrictions, but estimation becomes challenging as it requires solving a continuum of unconditional moment restrictions. Previous works addressed this problem by extending the generalized method of moments (GMM) to continuum moment restrictions. In contrast, generalized empirical likelihood (GEL) provides a more general framework and has been shown to enjoy favorable small-sample properties compared to GMM-based estimators. To benefit from recent developments in machine learning, we provide a functional reformulation of GEL in which arbitrary models can be leveraged. Motivated by a dual formulation of the resulting infinite dimensional optimization problem, we devise a practical method and explore its asymptotic properties. Finally, we provide kernel- and neural network-based implementations of the estimator, which achieve state-of-the-art empirical performance on two conditional moment restriction problems.

paragraphs: Many estimation problems in causal inference, economics, and robust machine learning can be expressed through conditional moment restrictions. These require certain average relationships to hold conditional on other information. Estimation is challenging because such requirements correspond to a continuum of unconditional restrictions, rather than a finite list that can be handled directly.

Previous approaches extend the generalized method of moments to this setting. The paper instead develops a functional version of generalized empirical likelihood, a broader framework with previously established favorable small-sample properties relative to GMM estimators. Its reformulation allows arbitrary models to be incorporated, creating a route for using modern machine learning within this estimation framework.

A dual formulation of the infinite-dimensional optimization problem motivates a practical estimation method. The authors investigate its asymptotic properties and implement it using both kernels and neural networks. These implementations achieve state-of-the-art empirical performance on two conditional moment restriction problems. The work thus connects a flexible statistical formulation to usable estimators and evidence of strong performance in the evaluated problems.
summary.tldr: A functional reformulation of generalized empirical likelihood enables kernel and neural estimators for conditional moment restrictions.

title: Functional Generalized Empirical Likelihood Estimation for Conditional Moment Restrictions

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have known a tremendous success for many continuous generation tasks, especially in the field of image generation. However, for discrete outputs such as language, optimizing GANs remains an open problem with many instabilities, as no gradient can be properly back-propagated from the discriminator output to the generator parameters. An alternative is to learn the generator network via reinforcement learning, using the discriminator signal as a reward, but such a technique suffers from moving rewards and vanishing gradient problems. Finally, it often falls short compared to direct maximum-likelihood approaches. In this paper, we introduce Generative Cooperative Networks, in which the discriminator architecture is cooperatively used along with the generation policy to output samples of realistic texts for the task at hand. We give theoretical guarantees of convergence for our approach, and study various efficient decoding schemes to empirically achieve state-of-the-art results in two main NLG tasks.

paragraphs: Adversarial generation is difficult for text because discrete outputs interrupt the usual gradient path from a discriminator back to a generator. Training the generator through reinforcement learning provides an alternative, but the discriminator’s changing rewards and vanishing gradients create further difficulties. Such methods can also underperform direct maximum-likelihood training.

The paper introduces Generative Cooperative Networks, which use the discriminator architecture cooperatively with the generation policy to produce realistic text for a task. This changes the role of the discriminator within generation. Its contribution is brought together with the policy in the sampling process, providing a different way to use the information the discriminator supplies.

The authors give theoretical convergence guarantees for their approach and investigate efficient decoding schemes. Their empirical study reports state-of-the-art performance on two natural-language-generation tasks. The work therefore combines a cooperative formulation with both theoretical analysis and practical decoding choices. The reported findings support this formulation as a productive approach to the optimization difficulties associated with discrete language generation.
summary.tldr: Generative Cooperative Networks combine discriminator information with a generation policy, with convergence guarantees and strong reported text-generation results.

title: Generative Cooperative Networks for Natural Language Generation

abstract: Attention mechanisms are dominating the explainability of deep models. They produce probability distributions over the input, which are widely deemed as feature-importance indicators. However, in this paper, we find one critical limitation in attention explanations: weakness in identifying the polarity of feature impact. This would be somehow misleading – features with higher attention weights may not faithfully contribute to model predictions; instead, they can impose suppression effects. With this finding, we reflect on the explainability of current attention-based techniques, such as Attention $\bigodot$ Gradient and LRP-based attention explanations. We first propose an actionable diagnostic methodology (henceforth faithfulness violation test) to measure the consistency between explanation weights and the impact polarity. Through the extensive experiments, we then show that most tested explanation methods are unexpectedly hindered by the faithfulness violation issue, especially the raw attention. Empirical analyses on the factors affecting violation issues further provide useful observations for adopting explanation methods in attention models.
