paragraphs: Attention weights are often read as indicators of which input features support a model's prediction. This paper identifies a problem with that interpretation: a feature receiving high attention can suppress a prediction instead of supporting it. The size of an attention weight therefore may fail to communicate the direction, or polarity, of the feature's influence.

The authors propose a faithfulness violation test that measures consistency between explanation weights and impact polarity. This turns the concern into an actionable diagnostic rather than relying only on visual inspection of attention patterns. They apply the perspective to raw attention and other attention-based explanation techniques, including Attention multiplied by Gradient and methods based on layer-wise relevance propagation.

Across the reported experiments, most tested explanation methods exhibit faithfulness violations, with raw attention especially affected. Further empirical analysis examines factors associated with these violations and offers observations for choosing explanation methods. The findings challenge a specific interpretation of attention: prominence in an explanation need not faithfully indicate that a feature pushes the prediction in the implied direction.
summary.tldr: A faithfulness violation test reveals that attention explanations often misrepresent whether features support or suppress a prediction.

title: Rethinking Attention-Model Explainability through Faithfulness Violation Test

abstract: Conservatism has led to significant progress in offline reinforcement learning (RL) where an agent learns from pre-collected datasets. However, as many real-world scenarios involve interaction among multiple agents, it is important to resolve offline RL in the multi-agent setting. Given the recent success of transferring online RL algorithms to the multi-agent setting, one may expect that offline RL algorithms will also transfer to multi-agent settings directly. Surprisingly, we empirically observe that conservative offline RL algorithms do not work well in the multi-agent setting—the performance degrades significantly with an increasing number of agents. Towards mitigating the degradation, we identify a key issue that non-concavity of the value function makes the policy gradient improvements prone to local optima. Multiple agents exacerbate the problem severely, since the suboptimal policy by any agent can lead to uncoordinated global failure. Following this intuition, we propose a simple yet effective method, Offline Multi-Agent RL with Actor Rectification (OMAR), which combines the first-order policy gradients and zeroth-order optimization methods to better optimize the conservative value functions over the actor parameters. Despite the simplicity, OMAR achieves state-of-the-art results in a variety of multi-agent control tasks.

Given the recent success of transferring online RL algorithms to the multi-agent setting, one may expect that offline RL algorithms will also transfer to multi-agent settings directly. Surprisingly, we empirically observe that conservative offline RL algorithms do not work well in the multi-agent setting—the performance degrades significantly with an increasing number of agents. Towards mitigating the degradation, we identify a key issue that non-concavity of the value function makes the policy gradient improvements prone to local optima. Multiple agents exacerbate the problem severely, since the suboptimal policy by any agent can lead to uncoordinated global failure. Following this intuition, we propose a simple yet effective method, Offline Multi-Agent RL with Actor Rectification (OMAR), which combines the first-order policy gradients and zeroth-order optimization methods to better optimize the conservative value functions over the actor parameters. Despite the simplicity, OMAR achieves state-of-the-art results in a variety of multi-agent control tasks.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains policies from previously collected data. Conservative methods have been successful in this setting, but this paper finds that transferring them directly to multiple interacting agents can work poorly. In the reported experiments, performance deteriorates substantially as the number of agents increases.

The authors identify a difficulty in optimizing the value function: its non-concave shape makes policy-gradient updates vulnerable to local optima. Multiple agents amplify this problem because one agent’s poor policy can disrupt coordination across the group. Improving individual policies is therefore closely tied to achieving useful collective behavior.

OMAR, or Offline Multi-Agent RL with Actor Rectification, combines first-order policy gradients with zeroth-order optimization, which does not rely on gradients. The combination aims to optimize actors more effectively against conservative value functions. OMAR achieves state-of-the-art results across a variety of multi-agent control tasks in the paper. The findings support actor optimization as a practical intervention for the observed degradation of conservative offline learning in multi-agent settings.
summary.tldr: OMAR combines gradient-based and gradient-free actor optimization to improve conservative offline reinforcement learning with multiple agents.

title: Plan Better Amid Conservatism: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Actor Rectification

abstract: We propose the Bayes-UCBVI algorithm for reinforcement learning in tabular, stage-dependent, episodic Markov decision process: a natural extension of the Bayes-UCB algorithm by Kaufmann et al. 2012 for multi-armed bandits. Our method uses the quantile of a Q-value function posterior as upper confidence bound on the optimal Q-value function. For Bayes-UCBVI, we prove a regret bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$ where $H$ is the length of one episode, $S$ is the number of states, $A$ the number of actions, $T$ the number of episodes, that matches the lower-bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{H^3SAT})$ up to poly-$\log$ terms in $H,S,A,T$ for a large enough $T$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm that obtains an optimal dependence on the horizon $H$ (and $S$) without the need of an involved Bernstein-like bonus or noise. Crucial to our analysis is a new fine-grained anti-concentration bound for a weighted Dirichlet sum that can be of independent interest. We then explain how Bayes-UCBVI can be easily extended beyond the tabular setting, exhibiting a strong link between our algorithm and Bayesian bootstrap (Rubin,1981).

Bayes-UCBVI implements this idea using an upper quantile of a posterior distribution over Q-values, which describe the value of taking an action in a state. This quantile serves as an upper confidence bound without requiring an elaborate explicit exploration bonus.

The authors prove regret of order the square root of H cubed times S, A, and T, up to logarithmic factors. Here H is episode length, S and A count states and actions, and T counts episodes. For sufficiently large T, this matches the stated lower bound up to those logarithmic factors.

A new anti-concentration bound for weighted Dirichlet sums is central to the proof. It supports the analysis of posterior-based optimism. The paper also explains an extension beyond tables through a connection to the Bayesian bootstrap. This broader connection is separate from the regret guarantee established for the tabular setting.
summary.tldr: Bayes-UCBVI uses posterior quantiles for optimistic exploration and achieves near-optimal tabular regret without elaborate exploration bonuses.

title: From Dirichlet to Rubin: Optimistic Exploration in RL without Bonuses

abstract: The policy gradient theorem (Sutton et al., 2000) prescribes the usage of a cumulative discounted state distribution under the target policy to approximate the gradient. Most algorithms based on this theorem, in practice, break this assumption, introducing a distribution shift that can cause the convergence to poor solutions. In this paper, we propose a new approach of reconstructing the policy gradient from the start state without requiring a particular sampling strategy. The policy gradient calculation in this form can be simplified in terms of a gradient critic, which can be recursively estimated due to a new Bellman equation of gradients. By using temporal-difference updates of the gradient critic from an off-policy data stream, we develop the first estimator that side-steps the distribution shift issue in a model-free way. We prove that, under certain realizability conditions, our estimator is unbiased regardless of the sampling strategy. We empirically show that our technique achieves a superior bias-variance trade-off and performance in presence of off-policy samples.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods estimate how changing an agent’s policy would change its expected return. The standard theorem requires states to be weighted according to a particular discounted distribution under the target policy. Many practical algorithms use samples that do not follow this distribution, creating a mismatch that can lead learning toward poor solutions.

This paper reconstructs the policy gradient from the start state without prescribing a particular sampling strategy. Its central object is a gradient critic, which represents information needed to calculate that gradient. A new Bellman equation expresses this information recursively, allowing the critic to be learned through temporal-difference updates from a stream of off-policy data.

The authors prove that the resulting estimator is unbiased under specified realizability conditions, regardless of the sampling strategy. Those conditions qualify the guarantee; sampling flexibility alone does not establish unbiasedness. Experiments show a better bias-variance trade-off and improved performance with off-policy samples. The approach makes the gradient itself something that can be learned recursively while addressing the distribution mismatch.
summary.tldr: A recursively learned gradient critic enables model-free policy gradient estimation from off-policy data, with unbiasedness under realizability conditions.

title: A Temporal-Difference Approach to Policy Gradient Estimation

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution inputs is critical for the safe deployment of machine learning models in the real world. However, neural networks are known to suffer from the overconfidence issue, where they produce abnormally high confidence for both in- and out-of-distribution inputs. In this work, we show that this issue can be mitigated through Logit Normalization (LogitNorm)—a simple fix to the cross-entropy loss—by enforcing a constant vector norm on the logits in training. Our method is motivated by the analysis that the norm of the logit keeps increasing during training, leading to overconfident output. Our key idea behind LogitNorm is thus to decouple the influence of output’s norm during network optimization. Trained with LogitNorm, neural networks produce highly distinguishable confidence scores between in- and out-of-distribution data. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of LogitNorm, reducing the average FPR95 by up to 42.30% on common benchmarks.

paragraphs: A neural network can assign high confidence to unfamiliar inputs as well as familiar ones. This makes confidence less useful for detecting data outside the training distribution. The paper connects this overconfidence to the growing norm of the logits, the vector of scores used to produce the model's classification output.

Logit Normalization, or LogitNorm, modifies cross-entropy training by enforcing a constant norm on that score vector. The motivation is to separate the effect of the vector's overall magnitude from the optimization of its classification information. By controlling a quantity that otherwise increases during training, the method targets a specific mechanism associated with excessive confidence rather than adding a separate detection model.

The authors report that networks trained with LogitNorm produce much more distinguishable confidence scores for in-distribution and out-of-distribution inputs. Across common benchmarks, the reported reduction in average FPR95 reaches up to 42.30%. This is an empirical maximum improvement, not a universal guarantee. The findings suggest that a small change to the training loss can substantially improve confidence-based detection of unfamiliar inputs.
summary.tldr: LogitNorm constrains logit magnitude during training to reduce overconfidence and improve out-of-distribution detection.

title: Mitigating Neural Network Overconfidence with Logit Normalization

abstract: Natural language understanding and generation models follow one of the two dominant architectural paradigms: language models (LMs) that process concatenated sequences in a single stack of layers, and encoder-decoder models (EncDec) that utilize separate layer stacks for input and output processing. In machine translation, EncDec has long been the favoured approach, but with few studies investigating the performance of LMs. In this work, we thoroughly examine the role of several architectural design choices on the performance of LMs on bilingual, (massively) multilingual and zero-shot translation tasks, under systematic variations of data conditions and model sizes. Our results show that: (i) Different LMs have different scaling properties, where architectural differences often have a significant impact on model performance at small scales, but the performance gap narrows as the number of parameters increases, (ii) Several design choices, including causal masking and language-modeling objectives for the source sequence, have detrimental effects on translation quality, and (iii) When paired with full-visible masking for source sequences, LMs could perform on par with EncDec on supervised bilingual and multilingual translation tasks, and improve greatly on zero-shot directions by facilitating the reduction of off-target translations.

paragraphs: Machine translation commonly uses separate encoder and decoder stacks for processing source and target text. This paper examines the alternative of a language model that processes concatenated sequences within one stack. It systematically varies architecture, model size, and data conditions across bilingual, multilingual, and zero-shot translation tasks.

The results show that language-model architectures scale differently. Design choices often strongly affect translation quality at smaller model sizes, while performance gaps narrow as parameter counts increase. The study also finds that causal masking and language-modeling objectives applied to the source sequence can hurt translation quality, highlighting the importance of how the source is processed.

With fully visible masking for the source sequence, language models can match encoder-decoder performance on supervised bilingual and multilingual translation. They also improve substantially on zero-shot translation directions by helping reduce outputs in the wrong target language. The findings make architectural details and source visibility central to interpreting comparisons between these model families, rather than treating every single-stack language model as equivalent.
summary.tldr: Translation experiments show that source-sequence visibility and model scale strongly influence whether single-stack language models match encoder-decoder systems.

title: Examining Scaling and Transfer of Language Model Architectures for Machine Translation

abstract: Deep learning models have achieved great success in many fields, yet they are vulnerable to adversarial examples. This paper follows a causal perspective to look into the adversarial vulnerability and proposes Causal Intervention by Semantic Smoothing (CISS), a novel framework towards robustness against natural language attacks. Instead of merely fitting observational data, CISS learns causal effects p(y|do(x)) by smoothing in the latent semantic space to make robust predictions, which scales to deep architectures and avoids tedious construction of noise customized for specific attacks. CISS is provably robust against word substitution attacks, as well as empirically robust even when perturbations are strengthened by unknown attack algorithms. For example, on YELP, CISS surpasses the runner-up by 6.8% in terms of certified robustness against word substitutions, and achieves 80.7% empirical robustness when syntactic attacks are integrated.

paragraphs: Natural language models can be vulnerable to deliberately modified inputs. This paper approaches that vulnerability through causal reasoning and introduces Causal Intervention by Semantic Smoothing, or CISS. The framework aims to learn the effect of intervening on an input, expressed as p(y|do(x)), rather than relying solely on associations in observed examples.

CISS performs smoothing in a latent semantic space, where text is represented in terms of learned meaning. This supplies the mechanism for making robust predictions. The authors describe the framework as scalable to deep architectures and as avoiding the need to construct a separate, customized noise process for each particular attack.

The paper provides a robustness proof for word substitution attacks and empirical evidence under stronger perturbations involving previously unknown attack algorithms. On YELP, it reports a 6.8% advantage over the runner-up in certified robustness to word substitutions and 80.7% empirical robustness when syntactic attacks are included. The distinction matters: the word substitution result has a formal guarantee, while the broader attack result is supported by experiments.
summary.tldr: CISS uses causal intervention through semantic smoothing to provide certified robustness to word substitutions and empirical robustness to broader language attacks.

title: Certified Robustness Against Natural Language Attacks by Causal Intervention

abstract: Theoretical guarantees in reinforcement learning (RL) are known to suffer multiplicative blow-up factors with respect to the misspecification error of function approximation. Yet, the nature of such approximation factors —especially their optimal form in a given learning problem—is poorly understood. In this paper we study this question in linear off-policy value function estimation, where many open questions remain. We study the approximation factor in a broad spectrum of settings, such as presence vs. absence of state aliasing and full vs. partial coverage of the state space. Our core results include instance-dependent upper bounds on the approximation factors with respect to both the weighted $L_2$-norm (where the weighting is the offline state distribution) and the $L_\infty$ norm. We show that these approximation factors are optimal (in an instance-dependent sense) for a number of these settings. In other cases, we show that the instance-dependent parameters which appear in the upper bounds are necessary, and that the finiteness of either alone cannot guarantee a finite approximation factor even in the limit of infinite data.

paragraphs: A restricted function class may be unable to represent the true value function in reinforcement learning. The resulting misspecification error can be multiplied by an approximation factor in learning guarantees. This paper investigates the best possible form of those factors for linear off-policy value estimation, where the available data and the policy being evaluated need not match.

The authors examine settings with and without state aliasing and with full or partial state-space coverage. They derive instance-dependent upper bounds under two error measures: a weighted L2 norm based on the offline state distribution and the L-infinity norm. Making the bounds instance-dependent exposes how properties of the particular estimation problem affect error amplification.

For several settings, the paper proves that the approximation factors are optimal in an instance-dependent sense. In other settings, it shows that parameters appearing in the bounds are necessary, and that either parameter being finite alone cannot ensure a finite approximation factor. This failure can persist with infinite data, identifying a structural obstacle that additional observations by themselves cannot remove.
summary.tldr: Instance-dependent bounds characterize how off-policy value estimation amplifies approximation error and identify structural failures that can persist with infinite data.

title: The Optimal Approximation Factors in Misspecified Off-Policy Value Function Estimation

abstract: Particle gradient descent, which uses particles to represent a probability measure and performs gradient descent on particles in parallel, is widely used to optimize functions of probability measures. This paper considers particle gradient descent with a finite number of particles and establishes its theoretical guarantees to optimize functions that are displacement convex in measures. Concretely, for Lipschitz displacement convex functions defined on probability over $R^d$, we prove that $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ particles and $O(d/\epsilon^4)$ iterations are sufficient to find the $\epsilon$-optimal solutions. We further provide improved complexity bounds for optimizing smooth displacement convex functions. An application of our results proves the conjecture of no optimization-barrier up to permutation invariance , proposed by Entezari et al. (2022), for specific two-layer neural networks with two-dimensional inputs uniformly drawn from unit circle.

paragraphs: Particle gradient descent optimizes a probability distribution by representing it with a collection of particles and updating their positions in parallel. This paper asks what a finite collection can provably accomplish. It focuses on objectives that are displacement convex, a form of convexity defined for probability measures as their mass is moved between distributions.

For Lipschitz displacement-convex objectives over distributions in d dimensions, the authors prove that O(1/epsilon²) particles and O(d/epsilon⁴) iterations are sufficient to reach an epsilon-optimal solution. These bounds connect the desired accuracy to both the size of the representation and the number of optimization steps. The paper also supplies improved complexity bounds when the displacement-convex objective is smooth.

An application concerns the conjecture that neural-network optimization barriers disappear after accounting for permutations. The authors prove this conjecture for specific two-layer networks whose two-dimensional inputs are uniformly distributed on the unit circle. This is a concrete application of the distribution-level optimization results, with the network conclusion tied to that particular architecture and input setting.
summary.tldr: Finite-particle gradient descent receives explicit accuracy guarantees for displacement-convex objectives, with an application to a specific neural-network optimization conjecture.

title: Efficient displacement convex optimization with particle gradient descent

abstract: We study the Stochastic Shortest Path (SSP) problem with a linear mixture transition kernel, where an agent repeatedly interacts with a stochastic environment and seeks to reach certain goal state while minimizing the cumulative cost. Existing works often assume a strictly positive lower bound of the cost function or an upper bound of the expected length for the optimal policy. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm to eliminate these restrictive assumptions. Our algorithm is based on extended value iteration with a fine-grained variance-aware confidence set, where the variance is estimated recursively from high-order moments. Our algorithm achieves an $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(dB_*\sqrt{K})$ regret bound, where $d$ is the dimension of the feature mapping in the linear transition kernel, $B_*$ is the upper bound of the total cumulative cost for the optimal policy, and $K$ is the number of episodes. Our regret upper bound matches the $\Omega(dB_*\sqrt{K})$ lower bound of linear mixture SSPs in Min et al. (2022), which suggests that our algorithm is nearly minimax optimal.

paragraphs: The stochastic shortest path problem asks an agent to reach a goal while minimizing accumulated cost in an uncertain environment. This paper studies repeated episodes when transitions have a linear mixture structure. Earlier approaches often require either a strictly positive minimum cost or a bound on the optimal policy’s expected episode length; the proposed algorithm removes those requirements.

The method combines extended value iteration with confidence sets that account carefully for variance. It estimates variance recursively using higher-order moments. This uncertainty treatment is central to the algorithm’s ability to obtain its guarantee without the two restrictive assumptions identified in earlier work.

The regret bound scales as d times B-star times the square root of K, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is the transition-feature dimension, B-star bounds the optimal policy’s cumulative cost, and K counts episodes. Regret measures the excess cost associated with learning. The bound matches the stated lower bound apart from logarithmic factors, supporting the claim of nearly minimax-optimal performance for this problem class.
summary.tldr: A variance-aware algorithm achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret for linear mixture shortest-path learning without minimum-cost or optimal-episode-length assumptions.

title: Nearly Minimax Optimal Regret for Learning Linear Mixture Stochastic Shortest Path

abstract: Recently, remarkable progress has been made by approximating Nash equilibrium (NE), correlated equilibrium (CE), and coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) through function approximation that trains a neural network to predict equilibria from game representations. Furthermore, equivariant architectures are widely adopted in designing such equilibrium approximators in normal-form games. In this paper, we theoretically characterize the benefits and limitations of equivariant equilibrium approximators. For the benefits, we show that they enjoy better generalizability than general ones and can achieve better approximations when the payoff distribution is permutation-invariant. For the limitations, we discuss their drawbacks in terms of equilibrium selection and social welfare. Together, our results help to understand the role of equivariance in equilibrium approximators.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn to predict game-theoretic equilibria from representations of games. A common architectural choice is equivariance: when the game representation is permuted, the prediction changes correspondingly. This paper examines what that structural choice helps achieve and where it can restrict an equilibrium predictor.

The theoretical analysis covers approximators for Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria in normal-form games. The authors show generalization benefits for equivariant approximators compared with general ones. They also show that better approximation is possible when the distribution of game payoffs is permutation-invariant, so this additional advantage comes with an explicit condition on the games being modeled.

The analysis also identifies drawbacks involving equilibrium selection and social welfare. Predicting an equilibrium and choosing a socially desirable equilibrium are distinct concerns, and the architectural symmetry does not remove that distinction. Taken together, the results explain why equivariance can be a useful inductive bias while still limiting which equilibrium outcomes an approximator can favor. Its value therefore depends on the prediction objective and the payoff distribution.
summary.tldr: Equivariant equilibrium predictors have theoretical generalization benefits but also limitations in equilibrium selection and social welfare.

title: Are Equivariant Equilibrium Approximators Beneficial?

abstract: How can agents learn internal models that veridically represent interactions with the real world is a largely open question. As machine learning is moving towards representations containing not just observational but also interventional knowledge, we study this problem using tools from representation learning and group theory. We propose methods enabling an agent acting upon the world to learn internal representations of sensory information that are consistent with actions that modify it. We use an autoencoder equipped with a group representation acting on its latent space, trained using an equivariance-derived loss in order to enforce a suitable homomorphism property on the group representation. In contrast to existing work, our approach does not require prior knowledge of the group and does not restrict the set of actions the agent can perform. We motivate our method theoretically, and show empirically that it can learn a group representation of the actions, thereby capturing the structure of the set of transformations applied to the environment. We further show that this allows agents to predict the effect of sequences of future actions with improved accuracy.

paragraphs: An agent’s internal representation should describe both what it observes and how its actions change those observations. This paper investigates that relationship using representation learning and group theory. The aim is to learn a representation of sensory information whose transformations remain consistent with the actions applied to the environment.

The proposed autoencoder includes a group representation operating in its latent space. Its training loss encourages equivariance: changes caused by actions in the world should correspond to changes in the internal representation. The loss also enforces a suitable homomorphism property, so combining actions is reflected consistently in their latent transformations. The method requires neither prior knowledge of the group nor a restriction on the actions available to the agent.

The authors provide theoretical motivation and empirical evidence that the method can learn the transformation structure of the actions. They further show improved accuracy when predicting the effects of future action sequences. This makes the learned representation useful for anticipating interventions, extending its role beyond describing individual observations.
summary.tldr: An autoencoder learns action-consistent group structure in its latent space and improves predictions of future action sequences.

title: Homomorphism AutoEncoder -- Learning Group Structured Representations from Observed Transitions

abstract: Zero-order (ZO) optimization is a powerful tool for dealing with realistic constraints. On the other hand, the gradient-tracking (GT) technique proved to be an efficient method for distributed optimization aiming to achieve consensus. However, it is a first-order (FO) method that requires knowledge of the gradient, which is not always possible in practice. In this work, we introduce a zero-order distributed optimization method based on a one-point estimate of the gradient tracking technique. We prove that this new technique converges with a single noisy function query at a time in the non-convex setting. We then establish a convergence rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{K}})$ after a number of iterations K, which competes with that of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{K}})$ of its centralized counterparts. Finally, a numerical example validates our theoretical results.

On the other hand, the gradient-tracking (GT) technique proved to be an efficient method for distributed optimization aiming to achieve consensus. However, it is a first-order (FO) method that requires knowledge of the gradient, which is not always possible in practice. paragraphs: Distributed optimization often uses gradient tracking to help networked participants coordinate their updates. Standard gradient tracking requires access to gradients, which may be unavailable in practice. Zeroth-order optimization instead works with function evaluations, making it relevant when only noisy measurements of an objective can be obtained.

The paper introduces a distributed method that adapts gradient tracking using a one-point gradient estimate. Each step needs a single noisy function query. The authors prove convergence for a stochastic, nonconvex objective, extending the tracking approach to a setting where direct derivative information is absent.

Their convergence rate is O(K^(-1/3)) after K iterations, compared with the O(K^(-1/4)) rate cited for centralized counterparts. These exponents describe how the respective convergence bounds shrink as iterations increase; they do not by themselves establish a wall-clock speed advantage. A numerical example validates the theoretical results. The contribution combines distributed coordination, noisy function-only feedback, and a convergence guarantee within one method.
summary.tldr: A distributed gradient-tracking method converges for nonconvex stochastic objectives using one noisy function evaluation per step.

title: Single Point-Based Distributed Zeroth-Order Optimization with a Non-Convex Stochastic Objective Function

abstract: In this work, we investigate the implicit regularization induced by teacher-student learning dynamics in self-distillation. To isolate its effect, we describe a simple experiment where we consider teachers at random initialization instead of trained teachers. Surprisingly, when distilling a student into such a random teacher, we observe that the resulting model and its representations already possess very interesting characteristics; (1) we observe a strong improvement of the distilled student over its teacher in terms of probing accuracy. (2) The learned representations are data-dependent and transferable between different tasks but deteriorate strongly if trained on random inputs. (3) The student checkpoint contains sparse subnetworks, so-called lottery tickets, and lies on the border of linear basins in the supervised loss landscape. These observations have interesting consequences for several important areas in machine learning: (1) Self-distillation can work solely based on the implicit regularization present in the gradient dynamics without relying on any dark knowledge, (2) self-supervised learning can learn features even in the absence of data augmentation and (3) training dynamics during the early phase of supervised training do not necessarily require label information. Finally, we shed light on an intriguing local property of the loss landscape: the process of feature learning is strongly amplified if the student is initialized closely to the teacher. These results raise interesting questions about the nature of the landscape that have remained unexplored so far. Code is available at https://github.com/safelix/dinopl.

summary.tldr: Students trained against randomly initialized teachers can learn useful transferable features, revealing a role for training dynamics in self-distillation.

title: Random Teachers are Good Teachers

abstract: Given a matrix $A\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ and a vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^n$, we consider the regression problem with $\ell_\infty$ guarantees: finding a vector $x’\in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that $||x’-x^* ||_\infty \leq \frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{d}}\cdot ||Ax^*-b||_2\cdot ||A^\dagger||$ with $x^*$ being the optimal solution to the regression $||Ax-b||_2$. One popular approach for solving $\ell_2$ regression problem is via sketching: picking a structured random matrix $S\in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ with $m\ll n$ and $SA$ can be quickly computed, solve the “sketched” regression problem $x’=\mathrm{argmin} ||SAx-Sb||_2$. In this paper, we show that in order to obtain such $\ell_\infty$ guarantee for $\ell_2$ regression, one has to use sketching matrices that are dense . To the best of our knowledge, this is the first user case in which dense sketching matrices are necessary. On the algorithmic side, we prove that, there exists a distribution of dense sketching matrices with $m=\epsilon^{-2}d\log^3(n/\delta)$ such that solving the sketched regression problem gives the $\ell_\infty$ guarantee, with probability at least $1-\delta$. Moreover, the matrix $SA$ can be computed in time $O(nd\log n)$. Our row count is nearly-optimal up to logarithmic factors, and significantly improves the result in [Price, Song and Woodruff, ICALP’17], in which $m=\Omega(\epsilon^{-2}d^{1+\gamma})$ for $\gamma\in (0, 1)$ is required. Moreover, we develop a novel analytical framework for $\ell_\infty$ guarantee regression that utilizes the Oblivious Coordinate-wise Embedding (OCE) property introduced in [Song and Yu, ICML’21]. Our analysis is much simpler and more general than that of [Price, Song and Woodruff, ICALP’17]. Leveraging this framework, we extend the $\ell_\infty$ guarantee regression result to dense sketching matrices for computing fast tensor product of vectors.

paragraphs: This paper studies fast least-squares regression with a stronger requirement than obtaining a good overall fit: every coordinate of the computed solution must stay close to the corresponding coordinate of the optimal solution. The permitted error depends on the optimal residual, the matrix pseudoinverse norm, the number of coordinates, and an accuracy parameter.

The usual sketching strategy compresses the regression problem using a random matrix before solving it. The authors show that obtaining their coordinate-wise guarantee requires dense sketching matrices. They also establish a suitable distribution of dense sketches using ε⁻²d log³(n/δ) rows, with success probability at least 1−δ. Despite their density, these sketches permit computing the compressed matrix in O(nd log n) time.

The required row count is nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors and improves the earlier bound described in the abstract. A framework based on Oblivious Coordinate-wise Embedding makes the analysis simpler and more general, and extends the result to dense sketches for fast tensor products of vectors.
summary.tldr: Dense but efficiently computable sketches enable nearly optimal compression for regression with coordinate-wise error guarantees.

title: A Nearly-Optimal Bound for Fast Regression with $\ell_∞$ Guarantee

abstract: We introduce EM-Network, a novel self-distillation approach that effectively leverages target information for supervised sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) learning. In contrast to conventional methods, it is trained with oracle guidance, which is derived from the target sequence. Since the oracle guidance compactly represents the target-side context that can assist the sequence model in solving the task, the EM-Network achieves a better prediction compared to using only the source input. To allow the sequence model to inherit the promising capability of the EM-Network, we propose a new self-distillation strategy, where the original sequence model can benefit from the knowledge of the EM-Network in a one-stage manner. We conduct comprehensive experiments on two types of seq2seq models: connectionist temporal classification (CTC) for speech recognition and attention-based encoder-decoder (AED) for machine translation. Experimental results demonstrate that the EM-Network significantly advances the current state-of-the-art approaches, improving over the best prior work on speech recognition and establishing state-of-the-art performance on WMT’14 and IWSLT’14.

paragraphs: Supervised sequence learning provides both an input sequence and a desired output during training. EM-Network uses that target information to create compact oracle guidance representing context from the output side. With access to this guidance, the network makes better predictions than a model relying only on the source input.

The central challenge is passing that advantage to the original sequence model. The paper introduces a one-stage self-distillation strategy through which the model learns from EM-Network’s stronger predictions. This makes target-derived guidance a way to improve training, with knowledge transferred into the sequence model rather than leaving the benefit confined to the guided network.

The authors evaluate the approach with connectionist temporal classification models for speech recognition and attention-based encoder-decoder models for machine translation. They report improvements over the best prior speech-recognition work and state-of-the-art results on WMT’14 and IWSLT’14. These findings support the usefulness of oracle-guided self-distillation across the two different sequence-modeling settings examined.
summary.tldr: EM-Network transfers the benefits of target-derived oracle guidance into sequence models through one-stage self-distillation.

title: EM-Network: Oracle Guided Self-distillation for Sequence Learning

abstract: This paper aims to explain how a deep neural network (DNN) gradually extracts new knowledge and forgets noisy features through layers in forward propagation. Up to now, although how to define knowledge encoded by the DNN has not reached a consensus so far, previous studies have derived a series of mathematical evidences to take interactions as symbolic primitive inference patterns encoded by a DNN. We extend the definition of interactions and, for the first time, extract interactions encoded by intermediate layers. We quantify and track the newly emerged interactions and the forgotten interactions in each layer during the forward propagation, which shed new light on the learning behavior of DNNs. The layer-wise change of interactions also reveals the change of the generalization capacity and instability of feature representations of a DNN.

paragraphs: This paper examines how a deep neural network changes its representation as an input passes through successive layers. The authors want to track both newly extracted knowledge and the removal of noisy features. Their starting point is that there is no agreed definition of knowledge inside a network, so they adopt an interaction-based perspective supported by earlier mathematical evidence.

In this perspective, interactions serve as symbolic building blocks for inference patterns encoded by the model. The paper extends their definition so that interactions can be extracted from intermediate layers. This makes it possible to quantify which interactions newly appear and which disappear at each stage of forward propagation.

The resulting analysis connects layer-by-layer interaction changes with changes in generalization capacity and the instability of feature representations. Its contribution is a way to examine how internal information develops across depth, using an explicit mathematical representation of inference patterns. The conclusions concern knowledge as captured by these interactions, rather than resolving the broader question of how all neural-network knowledge should be defined.
summary.tldr: An extended interaction framework tracks which inference patterns emerge and disappear across a neural network’s layers.

title: Layerwise Change of Knowledge in Neural Networks

abstract: We study the problem of online unweighted bipartite matching with $n$ offline vertices and $n$ online vertices where one wishes to be competitive against the optimal offline algorithm. While the classic RANKING algorithm of (Karp et al., 1990) provably attains competitive ratio of $1-1/e > 1/2$, we show that no learning-augmented method can be both 1-consistent and strictly better than 1/2-robust under the adversarial arrival model. Meanwhile, under the random arrival model, we show how one can utilize methods from distribution testing to design an algorithm that takes in external advice about the online vertices and provably achieves competitive ratio interpolating between any ratio attainable by advice-free methods and the optimal ratio of 1, depending on the advice quality.

Meanwhile, under the random arrival model, we show how one can utilize methods from distribution testing to design an algorithm that takes in external advice about the online vertices and provably achieves competitive ratio interpolating between any ratio attainable by advice-free methods and the optimal ratio of 1, depending on the advice quality.

paragraphs: Online bipartite matching pairs arriving vertices with available vertices on the other side of a graph. Decisions are judged against an optimal algorithm that sees the entire instance beforehand. This paper studies whether external advice can improve performance while preserving protection against bad advice, for unweighted matching with equally sized vertex sets.

Under adversarial arrival order, the authors prove a sharp incompatibility: no learning-augmented method can be both 1-consistent and more than 1/2-robust. Here, 1-consistency means matching the offline optimum with correct advice, while robustness describes the guarantee when advice is unreliable. This tradeoff holds even though the advice-free RANKING algorithm guarantees 1−1/e, exceeding one half.

Random arrival order permits a more favorable result. Using distribution-testing methods, the authors design an algorithm whose competitive guarantee varies with advice quality, interpolating between any ratio attainable without advice and the optimal ratio of one. The contrast shows that arrival assumptions fundamentally affect how much an algorithm can benefit from predictions while retaining a fallback guarantee.
summary.tldr: Advice faces a consistency–robustness barrier under adversarial arrivals, but random arrivals permit guarantees that improve with advice quality.

title: Online bipartite matching with imperfect advice

abstract: Decentralized learning recently has received increasing attention in machine learning due to its advantages in implementation simplicity and system robustness, data privacy. Meanwhile, the adaptive gradient methods show superior performances in many machine learning tasks such as training neural networks. Although some works focus on studying decentralized optimization algorithms with adaptive learning rates, these adaptive decentralized algorithms still suffer from high sample complexity. To fill these gaps, we propose a class of faster adaptive decentralized algorithms (i.e., AdaMDOS and AdaMDOF) for distributed nonconvex stochastic and finite-sum optimization, respectively. Moreover, we provide a solid convergence analysis framework for our methods. In particular, we prove that our AdaMDOS obtains a near-optimal sample complexity of $\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary solution of nonconvex stochastic optimization. Meanwhile, our AdaMDOF obtains a near-optimal sample complexity of $O(\sqrt{n}\epsilon^{-2})$ for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary solution of for nonconvex finite-sum optimization, where $n$ denotes the sample size. To the best of our knowledge, our AdaMDOF algorithm is the first adaptive decentralized algorithm for nonconvex finite-sum optimization. Some experimental results demonstrate efficiency of our algorithms.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning distributes optimization across participants, while adaptive gradient methods adjust learning rates during training. Combining these ideas is attractive, but existing adaptive decentralized algorithms can require many samples. This paper proposes two algorithms intended to reduce that cost for nonconvex objectives, where the optimization landscape need not have a single simple minimum.

AdaMDOS handles stochastic optimization, and AdaMDOF handles objectives formed from a finite collection of samples. The authors develop a convergence-analysis framework for both. They prove near-optimal sample complexity of approximately epsilon to the power minus three, up to logarithmic factors, for AdaMDOS. For AdaMDOF, the bound is proportional to the square root of the sample count times epsilon to the power minus two.

These guarantees concern reaching an epsilon-stationary solution, where the gradient is sufficiently small; they do not assert finding a global optimum. The authors identify AdaMDOF as the first adaptive decentralized method for the nonconvex finite-sum setting, to their knowledge. Reported experiments also demonstrate the algorithms' efficiency.
summary.tldr: AdaMDOS and AdaMDOF provide near-optimal sample-complexity guarantees for adaptive decentralized nonconvex optimization.

title: Faster Adaptive Decentralized Learning Algorithms

abstract: Metallic Glasses (MGs) are widely used materials that are stronger than steel while being shapeable as plastic. While understanding the structure-property relationship of MGs remains a challenge in materials science, studying their energy barriers (EBs) as an intermediary step shows promise. In this work, we utilize Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to model MGs and study EBs. We contribute a new dataset for EB prediction and a novel Symmetrized GNN (SymGNN) model that is E(3)-invariant in expectation. SymGNN handles invariance by aggregating over orthogonal transformations of the graph structure. When applied to EB prediction, SymGNN are more accurate than molecular dynamics (MD) local-sampling methods and other machine-learning models. Compared to precise MD simulations, SymGNN reduces the inference time on new MGs from roughly 41 days to less than one second. We apply explanation algorithms to reveal the relationship between structures and EBs. The structures that we identify through explanations match the medium-range order (MRO) hypothesis and possess unique topological properties. Our work enables effective prediction and interpretation of MG EBs, bolstering material science research.

SymGNN aggregates over orthogonal transformations of the graph structure. title: Predicting and Interpreting Energy Barriers of Metallic Glasses with Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Algorithmic predictions are emerging as a promising solution concept for efficiently allocating societal resources. Fueling their use is an underlying assumption that such systems are necessary to identify individuals for interventions. We propose a principled framework for assessing this assumption: Using a simple mathematical model, we evaluate the efficacy of prediction-based allocations in settings where individuals belong to larger units such as hospitals, neighborhoods, or schools. We find that prediction-based allocations outperform baseline methods using aggregate unit-level statistics only when between-unit inequality is low and the intervention budget is high. Our results hold for a wide range of settings for the price of prediction, treatment effect heterogeneity, and unit-level statistics’ learnability. Combined, we highlight the potential limits to improving the efficacy of interventions through prediction.

paragraphs: Deciding who should receive a limited intervention often seems to require predictions about individual people. This paper examines that assumption when people belong to larger units, such as schools, hospitals, or neighborhoods. It asks whether individual predictions improve allocation compared with decisions based on summary statistics for those units.

The authors develop a simple mathematical framework that compares these allocation strategies. Within their model, prediction-based allocation beats the aggregate-statistics alternatives only when inequality between units is low and the intervention budget is high. These are necessary conditions for the reported advantage, rather than a promise that prediction always helps whenever both conditions hold.

The results extend across a wide range of prediction costs, differences in treatment effects, and possibilities for learning unit-level statistics. The practical implication is that the value of prediction depends on the allocation setting itself. Differences between groups and the available intervention budget can constrain how much more effective an intervention becomes through individual prediction.
summary.tldr: A mathematical model finds that individual prediction improves allocation over unit-level statistics only when between-unit inequality is low and intervention budgets are high.

title: Allocation Requires Prediction Only if Inequality Is Low

abstract: Existing studies on constrained reinforcement learning (RL) may obtain a well-performing policy in the training environment. However, when deployed in a real environment, it may easily violate constraints that were originally satisfied during training because there might be model mismatch between the training and real environments. To address this challenge, we formulate the problem as constrained RL under model uncertainty, where the goal is to learn a policy that optimizes the reward and at the same time satisfies the constraint under model mismatch. We develop a Robust Constrained Policy Optimization (RCPO) algorithm, which is the first algorithm that applies to large/continuous state space and has theoretical guarantees on worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation at each iteration during the training. We show the effectiveness of our algorithm on a set of RL tasks with constraints.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning policy can satisfy its constraints during training and still violate them after deployment. The problem arises when the real environment behaves differently from the training environment. This paper treats that mismatch as a central part of learning, rather than judging a policy only by its performance under the training model.

The authors formulate constrained reinforcement learning under model uncertainty. The objective combines earning rewards with satisfying a constraint despite differences in environment dynamics. They develop Robust Constrained Policy Optimization, or RCPO, to address this formulation in large or continuous state spaces. That scope matters because the method is intended to handle settings beyond small, explicitly enumerated collections of states.

RCPO comes with theoretical guarantees concerning worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation at each training iteration. These guarantees address how learning progresses under the paper’s uncertainty formulation; they should not be read as an unrestricted promise about every deployment environment. Experiments on reinforcement learning tasks with constraints demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution brings model mismatch into both policy optimization and its accompanying theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: RCPO learns constrained policies under model uncertainty, with per-iteration guarantees on worst-case reward improvement and constraint violation.

title: Constrained Reinforcement Learning Under Model Mismatch

abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLM) have revolutionized the NLP landscape, achieving stellar performances across diverse tasks. These models, while benefiting from vast training data, often require fine-tuning on specific data to cater to distinct downstream tasks. However, this data adaptation process has inherent security and privacy concerns, primarily when leveraging user-generated, device-residing data. Federated learning (FL) provides a solution, allowing collaborative model fine-tuning without centralized data collection. However, applying FL to finetune PLMs is hampered by challenges, including restricted model parameter access due to the high encapsulation, high computational requirements, and communication overheads. This paper introduces Federated Black-box Prompt Tuning (FedBPT), a framework designed to address these challenges. FedBPT allows the clients to treat the model as a black-box inference API. By focusing on training optimal prompts and utilizing gradient-free optimization methods, FedBPT reduces the number of exchanged variables, boosts communication efficiency, and minimizes computational and storage costs. Experiments highlight the framework’s ability to drastically cut communication and memory costs while maintaining competitive performance. Ultimately, FedBPT presents a promising solution for efficient, privacy-preserving fine-tuning of PLM in the age of large language models.

paragraphs: FedBPT addresses adapting pretrained language models using data held by different clients. Federated learning allows collaboration without collecting that data in one central location, but ordinary model fine-tuning can require expensive computation, substantial communication, and access to model parameters. These requirements become difficult when a model is available only through an inference interface.

The framework trains prompts while allowing clients to treat the language model as a black-box API. It uses gradient-free optimization, so adaptation does not depend on obtaining gradients from the underlying model. Focusing on prompts also reduces the number of variables exchanged during collaboration, targeting communication, computation, and storage costs together.

Experiments report substantial reductions in communication and memory use while retaining competitive task performance. This makes the result relevant to settings where client resources and model access are both constrained. Its privacy-oriented contribution is collaborative adaptation without centralized data collection, combined with a lightweight optimization target. The findings support prompt tuning as a practical route to federated language-model adaptation under the tested conditions.
summary.tldr: FedBPT combines federated learning with gradient-free prompt tuning to adapt API-accessible language models with substantially lower communication and memory costs.

title: FedBPT: Efficient Federated Black-box Prompt Tuning for Large Language Models

abstract: Modern computer vision offers a great variety of models to practitioners, and selecting a model from multiple options for specific applications can be challenging. Conventionally, competing model architectures and training protocols are compared by their classification accuracy on ImageNet. However, this single metric does not fully capture performance nuances critical for specialized tasks. In this work, we conduct an in-depth comparative analysis of model behaviors beyond ImageNet accuracy, for both ConvNet and Vision Transformer architectures, each across supervised and CLIP training paradigms. Although our selected models have similar ImageNet accuracies and compute requirements, we find that they differ in many other aspects: types of mistakes, output calibration, transferability, and feature invariance, among others. This diversity in model characteristics, not captured by traditional metrics, highlights the need for more nuanced analysis when choosing among different models.

paragraphs: Choosing a vision model often starts with comparing ImageNet classification accuracy. This paper asks how much that familiar score leaves out when a model is intended for a specific application. The authors compare convolutional networks and vision transformers under both supervised and CLIP training, examining behavior beyond a single benchmark result.

The selected models have similar ImageNet accuracy and computational requirements. That makes their other differences especially relevant to model selection: comparable headline scores and compute needs do not imply interchangeable behavior. The analysis examines the kinds of mistakes models make, how well their confidence matches their correctness, how they transfer, and the invariances of their learned features.

The study finds differences across these dimensions despite the matched headline characteristics. Its contribution is therefore a more detailed account of the choices practitioners face, rather than a universal ranking of architectures or training approaches. summary.tldr: Vision models with similar ImageNet accuracy and compute can differ substantially in mistakes, confidence, transferability, and feature invariance.

title: ConvNet vs Transformer, Supervised vs CLIP: Beyond ImageNet Accuracy

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential across numerous applications and have shown an emergent ability to tackle complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical computations. However, even for the simplest arithmetic calculations, the intrinsic mechanisms behind LLMs remains mysterious, making it challenging to ensure reliability. In this work, we delve into uncovering a specific mechanism by which LLMs execute calculations. Through comprehensive experiments, we find that LLMs frequently involve a small fraction ($<$5%) of attention heads, which play a pivotal role in focusing on operands and operators during calculation processes. Subsequently, the information from these operands is processed through multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), progressively leading to the final solution. These pivotal heads/MLPs, though identified on a specific dataset, exhibit transferability across different datasets and even distinct tasks. This insight prompted us to investigate the potential benefits of selectively fine-tuning these essential heads/MLPs to boost the LLMs’ computational performance. We empirically find that such precise tuning can yield notable enhancements on mathematical prowess, without compromising the performance on non-mathematical tasks. Our work serves as a preliminary exploration into the arithmetic calculation abilities inherent in LLMs, laying a solid foundation to reveal more intricate mathematical tasks.

title: Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation

abstract: Discrete Graph Diffusion Models (DGDMs) mark a pivotal advancement in graph generation, effectively preserving sparsity and structural integrity, thereby enhancing the learning of graph data distributions for diverse generative applications. Despite their potential, DGDMs are computationally intensive due to the numerous low-parameter yet high-computation operations, thereby increasing the need of inference acceleration. A promising solution to mitigate this issue is model quantization. However, existing quantization techniques for Image Diffusion Models (IDMs) face limitations in DGDMs due to differing diffusion processes, while Large Language Model (LLM) quantization focuses on reducing memory access latency of loading large parameters, unlike DGDMs, where inference bottlenecks are computations due to smaller model sizes. To fill this gap, we introduce Bit-DGDM, a post-training quantization framework for DGDMs which incorporates two novel ideas: (i) sparse-dense activation quantization sparsely modeling the activation outliers through adaptively selected, data-free thresholds in full-precision and quantizing the remaining to low-bit, and (ii) ill-conditioned low-rank decomposition decomposing the weights into low-rank component enable faster inference and an $\alpha$-sparsity matrix that models outliers. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Bit-DGDM not only reducing the memory usage from the FP32 baseline by up to $2.8\times$ and achieve up to $2.5\times$ speedup, but also achieve comparable performance to ultra-low precision of up to 4-bit.

paragraphs: Discrete graph diffusion models generate graphs while preserving sparsity and structural integrity, but their many computations make inference expensive. Their bottleneck differs from that of large language models: relatively small parameter counts leave computation, rather than loading large weights, as the main issue. Quantization methods for image diffusion also do not transfer straightforwardly because the diffusion processes differ.

Bit-DGDM is a post-training quantization framework designed for these models. It separates activation outliers using adaptively selected, data-free thresholds, retaining those sparse outliers in full precision while quantizing the remaining activations. For weights, it combines a low-rank component intended to accelerate inference with an α-sparse matrix that represents outliers.

These two mechanisms preserve exceptional values separately while reducing the cost of the remaining computation and storage. Experiments report memory reductions of up to 2.8 times relative to FP32 and speedups of up to 2.5 times. The framework also maintains comparable performance at precision as low as 4 bits, demonstrating benefits from quantization tailored to graph diffusion.
summary.tldr: Bit-DGDM handles outliers separately to accelerate and compress discrete graph diffusion models while retaining comparable performance at low precision.

title: Outlier-Aware Post-Training Quantization for Discrete Graph Diffusion Models

abstract: Modern code completion engines, powered by large language models (LLMs), assist millions of developers with their strong capabilities to generate functionally correct code. Due to this popularity, it is crucial to investigate the security implications of relying on LLM-based code completion. In this work, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art black-box LLM-based code completion engines can be stealthily biased by adversaries to significantly increase their rate of insecure code generation. We present the first attack, named INSEC, that achieves this goal. INSEC works by injecting an attack string as a short comment in the completion input. The attack string is crafted through a query-based optimization procedure starting from a set of carefully designed initialization schemes. We demonstrate INSEC’s broad applicability and effectiveness by evaluating it on various state-of-the-art open-source models and black-box commercial services (e.g., OpenAI API and GitHub Copilot). On a diverse set of security-critical test cases, covering 16 CWEs across 5 programming languages, INSEC increases the rate of generated insecure code by more than 50%, while maintaining the functional correctness of generated code. We consider INSEC practical - it requires low resources and costs less than 10 US dollars to develop on commodity hardware. Moreover, we showcase the attack’s real-world deployability, by developing an IDE plug-in that stealthily injects INSEC into the GitHub Copilot extension.

The attack operates through black-box access, showing that this manipulation can work against services whose internal models are unavailable to the attacker.

This separates two properties developers might otherwise conflate: code can perform its intended function and still be insecure. The authors also report development costs below 10 US dollars on commodity hardware and demonstrate an IDE plug-in that covertly inserts the attack into Copilot.
summary.tldr: INSEC uses short injected comments to steer code-completion engines toward insecure code while preserving functionality in the reported tests.

title: Black-Box Adversarial Attacks on LLM-Based Code Completion

abstract: Latent generative models have emerged as a leading approach for high-quality image synthesis. These models rely on an autoencoder to compress images into a latent space, followed by a generative model to learn the latent distribution. We identify that existing autoencoders lack equivariance to semantic-preserving transformations like scaling and rotation, resulting in complex latent spaces that hinder generative performance. To address this, we propose EQ-VAE, a simple regularization approach that enforces equivariance in the latent space, reducing its complexity without degrading reconstruction quality. By finetuning pre-trained autoencoders with EQ-VAE, we enhance the performance of several state-of-the-art generative models, including DiT, SiT, REPA and MaskGIT, achieving a $\times$7 speedup on DiT-XL/2 with only five epochs of SD-VAE fine-tuning. EQ-VAE is compatible with both continuous and discrete autoencoders, thus offering a versatile enhancement for a wide range of latent generative models.

paragraphs: Latent image generators first compress images with an autoencoder, then learn to generate within that compressed space. This paper identifies a problem with existing autoencoders: transformations such as rotation or scaling do not produce corresponding, consistent changes in their latent representations. The resulting latent space becomes more complex for the generative model to learn.

EQ-VAE adds regularization that encourages this transformation consistency, known as equivariance. The authors fine-tune pretrained autoencoders so that their latent representations respond more predictably to transformations that preserve semantic content. They report that this reduces latent-space complexity without degrading reconstruction quality, addressing the representation used by the generator rather than only modifying the generator itself.

The approach improves several generative models, including DiT, SiT, REPA, and MaskGIT. The abstract reports a sevenfold speedup for DiT-XL/2 after just five epochs of SD-VAE fine-tuning. EQ-VAE also works with continuous and discrete autoencoders. Together, these findings show that improving the organization of the compressed representation can benefit multiple kinds of latent image generation.
summary.tldr: EQ-VAE regularizes autoencoder representations to transform consistently with images, improving latent generation without degrading reconstruction quality.

title: EQ-VAE: Equivariance Regularized Latent Space for Improved Generative Image Modeling

abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of variational inference in latent variable models for survival analysis, emphasizing the distinctive challenges associated with applying variational methods to survival data. We identify a critical weakness in the existing methodology, demonstrating how a poorly designed variational distribution may hinder the objective of survival analysis tasks—modeling time-to-event distributions. We prove that the optimal variational distribution, which perfectly bounds the log-likelihood, may depend on the censoring mechanism. To address this issue, we propose censor-dependent variational inference (CDVI), tailored for latent variable models in survival analysis. More practically, we introduce CD-CVAE, a V-structure Variational Autoencoder (VAE) designed for the scalable implementation of CDVI. Further discussion extends some existing theories and training techniques to survival analysis. Extensive experiments validate our analysis and demonstrate significant improvements in the estimation of individual survival distributions.

paragraphs: Survival analysis models when an event will happen, using data that can include censored observations whose event times are not fully observed. This paper examines how variational inference behaves in latent-variable models for that setting. Its concern is that an unsuitable approximation can interfere with learning the time-to-event distribution itself.

The authors prove that the optimal variational distribution, which makes the likelihood bound exact, may depend on the censoring mechanism. This is a conditional finding: it identifies censoring as something the inference design may need to accommodate. Their proposed censor-dependent variational inference, or CDVI, explicitly tailors the approximation to survival analysis.

For scalable implementation, the paper introduces CD-CVAE, a variational autoencoder with a V-shaped dependency structure. It also extends existing theory and training techniques to this setting. Experiments support the analysis and show significant improvements in estimating individual survival distributions. The contribution therefore connects the design of approximate inference directly to the quality of the event-time distributions that survival models are meant to learn.
summary.tldr: CDVI accounts for possible censoring dependence in variational inference to improve individual survival-distribution estimates.

title: Censor Dependent Variational Inference

abstract: Despite the growing popularity of graph attention mechanisms, their theoretical understanding remains limited. This paper aims to explore the conditions under which these mechanisms are effective in node classification tasks through the lens of Contextual Stochastic Block Models (CSBMs). Our theoretical analysis reveals that incorporating graph attention mechanisms is not universally beneficial. Specifically, by appropriately defining structure noise and feature noise in graphs, we show that graph attention mechanisms can enhance classification performance when structure noise exceeds feature noise. Conversely, when feature noise predominates, simpler graph convolution operations are more effective. Furthermore, we examine the over-smoothing phenomenon and show that, in the high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) regime, graph convolutional networks suffer from over-smoothing, whereas graph attention mechanisms can effectively resolve this issue. Building on these insights, we propose a novel multi-layer Graph Attention Network (GAT) architecture that significantly outperforms single-layer GATs in achieving perfect node classification in CSBMs, relaxing the SNR requirement from $\omega(\sqrt{\log n})$ to $\omega(\sqrt{\log n} / \sqrt[3]{n})$. To our knowledge, this is the first study to delineate the conditions for perfect node classification using multi-layer GATs. Our theoretical contributions are corroborated by extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, highlighting the practical implications of our findings.

paragraphs: Graph attention lets a model vary how strongly it uses information from different neighbors. This paper asks when that flexibility helps node classification. Its theoretical analysis uses contextual stochastic block models and distinguishes noise in the graph’s connections from noise in the features attached to its nodes.

Within this framework, attention can improve classification when structural noise exceeds feature noise. When feature noise dominates, simpler graph convolutions are more effective. The paper also studies over-smoothing, where repeated processing makes node representations insufficiently distinct. The central implication is conditional: attention’s value depends on the graph’s noise structure and the operating regime.
summary.tldr: The analysis shows that graph attention’s benefits depend on structural versus feature noise and derives improved classification conditions for a multi-layer architecture.

title: Graph Attention is Not Always Beneficial: A Theoretical Analysis of Graph Attention Mechanisms via Contextual Stochastic Block Models

abstract: We introduce a Riemannian optimistic online learning algorithm for Hadamard manifolds based on inexact implicit updates. Unlike prior work, our method can handle in-manifold constraints, and matches the best known regret bounds in the Euclidean setting with no dependence on geometric constants, like the minimum curvature. Building on this, we develop algorithms for g-convex, g-concave smooth min-max problems on Hadamard manifolds. Notably, one method nearly matches the gradient oracle complexity of the lower bound for Euclidean problems, for the first time.

paragraphs: This paper develops an optimistic online learning algorithm for Hadamard manifolds, a setting in which optimization takes place on a curved space. The algorithm uses inexact implicit updates and can accommodate constraints within the manifold. Handling those constraints is a stated advance over earlier work and expands the optimization problems the method can address.

The authors establish regret bounds matching the best known bounds in Euclidean space, with no dependence on geometric constants such as minimum curvature. Regret measures the learner’s accumulated performance relative to a comparator. The result shows that the stated guarantee avoids an additional factor tied to those geometric constants despite working in the manifold setting.

The paper then builds algorithms for smooth min-max problems that are geodesically convex in one variable and geodesically concave in the other. One method nearly matches the Euclidean lower bound on gradient-oracle complexity, which measures the required gradient queries. This is presented as a first such result, bringing the efficiency guarantee close to that reference bound under the specified geometric and problem assumptions.
summary.tldr: An implicit optimistic method handles constraints on Hadamard manifolds with Euclidean-matching regret bounds and nearly optimal gradient complexity for a min-max method.

title: Implicit Riemannian Optimism with Applications to Min-Max Problems

abstract: Existing works on general time series forecasting build foundation models with heavy model parameters through large-scale multi-source pretraining. These models achieve superior generalization ability across various datasets at the cost of significant computational burdens and limitations in resource-constrained scenarios. This paper introduces LightGTS, a lightweight general time series forecasting model designed from the perspective of consistent periodical modeling. To handle diverse scales and intrinsic periods in multi-source pre-training, we introduce Periodical Tokenization, which extracts consistent periodic patterns across different datasets with varying scales. To better utilize the periodicity in the decoding process, we further introduce Periodical Parallel Decoding, which leverage historical tokens to improve forecasting. Based on the two techniques above which fully leverage the inductive bias of periods inherent in time series, LightGTS uses a lightweight model to achieve outstanding performance on general time series forecasting. It achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance on 9 real-world benchmarks in both zero-shot and full-shot setting with much better efficiency compared with existing time series foundation models
