paragraphs: LightGTS explores how a general forecasting model can work efficiently across different time-series datasets. The paper identifies a cost of existing foundation-model approaches: large pretrained models can generalize well but impose substantial computational demands. Its alternative builds a lightweight model around recurring patterns already present in time series.

The first component, Periodical Tokenization, extracts consistent periodic patterns from datasets with different scales and intrinsic periods. This gives multi-source pretraining a way to handle variation while retaining recurring structure. The second component, Periodical Parallel Decoding, uses historical tokens during prediction so that periodic information also informs the decoding stage.

Together, these components make periodicity an explicit design principle for both representing the past and forecasting the future. Across nine real-world benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art forecasting performance in zero-shot and full-shot settings, with substantially better efficiency than existing time-series foundation models. The results support periodic modeling as a useful route to strong general forecasting with a smaller computational burden.
summary.tldr: LightGTS uses periodic tokenization and decoding to deliver strong general forecasting with a lightweight, computationally efficient model.

title: LightGTS: A Lightweight General Time Series Forecasting Model

abstract: Looped Transformers provide advantages in parameter efficiency, computational capabilities, and generalization for reasoning tasks. However, their expressive power regarding function approximation remains underexplored. In this paper, we establish the approximation rate of Looped Transformers by defining the modulus of continuity for sequence-to-sequence functions. This reveals a limitation specific to the looped architecture. That is, the analysis prompts the incorporation of scaling parameters for each loop, conditioned on timestep encoding. Experiments validate the theoretical results, showing that increasing the number of loops enhances performance, with further gains achieved through the timestep encoding.

paragraphs: Looped Transformers repeatedly apply a Transformer computation, offering benefits in parameter efficiency and reasoning. This paper investigates their ability to approximate sequence-to-sequence functions. The central question is how the looped architecture affects the accuracy with which it can represent a desired mapping between input and output sequences.

The authors establish an approximation rate using a modulus of continuity, which characterizes how a function’s outputs change when its inputs change. Their analysis reveals a limitation specific to the looped architecture. That finding motivates adding scaling parameters for each loop, with those parameters conditioned on an encoding of the current timestep.

The modification gives successive iterations information about their position in the repeated computation. Experiments support the theoretical analysis: increasing the number of loops improves performance, and timestep encoding produces further gains. The paper thus connects an expressiveness analysis to an architectural enhancement, showing empirical benefits from both additional iterations and making the repeated computation sensitive to the iteration index.
summary.tldr: An approximation analysis motivates timestep-conditioned scaling in looped Transformers, which improves performance in the reported experiments.

title: On Expressive Power of Looped Transformers: Theoretical Analysis and Enhancement via Timestep Encoding

abstract: Generative image steganography (GIS) is an emerging technique that conceals secret messages in the generation of images. Compared to GAN-based or flow-based GIS schemes, diffusion model-based solutions can provide high-quality and more diverse images, thus receiving considerable attention recently. However, previous GIS schemes still face challenges in terms of extraction accuracy, controllability, and practicality. To address the above issues, this paper proposes a practical message-driven GIS framework based on diffusion models, called MDDM. Specifically, by utilizing the Cardan grille, we encode messages into Gaussian noise, which serves as the initial input for image generation, enabling users to generate diverse images via controllable prompts without additional training. During the information extraction process, receivers only need to use the pre-shared Cardan grille to perform diffusion inversion and recover the messages without requiring the image generation seeds or prompts. Experimental results demonstrate that MDDM offers notable advantages in terms of accuracy, controllability, practicality, and security. With flexible strategies, MDDM can achieve accuracy close to 100% under appropriate settings. Additionally, MDDM demonstrates certain robustness and potential for application in watermarking tasks.

paragraphs: MDDM hides messages within the process of generating images with diffusion models. The paper targets practical difficulties in earlier generative steganography methods, including accurate message recovery and control over the resulting image. Its approach allows the message to influence image generation while users retain the ability to guide image content through prompts.

During recovery, the receiver uses the pre-shared grille and diffusion inversion to recover the message without needing the original generation prompt or random seed.

Experiments report advantages in recovery accuracy, controllability, practicality, and security. With suitable strategies and settings, message-recovery accuracy can approach 100%; the claim is explicitly conditional on those settings. The authors also report some robustness and potential use in watermarking. The practical contribution is a generation-and-recovery workflow that reduces what sender and receiver must share.
summary.tldr: MDDM encodes messages into diffusion-model noise and recovers them using a shared grille, with near-perfect accuracy under appropriate settings.

title: MDDM: Practical Message-Driven Generative Image Steganography Based on Diffusion Models

abstract: Recent advances in generative models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in producing high-quality images, but their reliance on large-scale unlabeled data has raised significant safety and copyright concerns. Efforts to address these issues by erasing unwanted concepts have shown promise. However, many existing erasure methods involve excessive modifications that compromise the overall utility of the model. In this work, we address these issues by formulating a novel minimalist concept erasure objective based only on the distributional distance of final generation outputs. Building on our formulation, we derive a tractable loss for differentiable optimization that leverages backpropagation through all generation steps in an end-to-end manner. We also conduct extensive analysis to show theoretical connections with other models and methods. To improve the robustness of the erasure, we incorporate neuron masking as an alternative to model fine-tuning. Empirical evaluations on state-of-the-art flow-matching models demonstrate that our method robustly erases concepts without degrading overall model performance, paving the way for safer and more responsible generative models.

title: Minimalist Concept Erasure in Generative Models

abstract: This paper introduces EasyInv, an easy yet novel approach that significantly advances the field of DDIM Inversion by addressing the inherent inefficiencies and performance limitations of traditional iterative optimization methods. At the core of our EasyInv is a refined strategy for approximating inversion noise, which is pivotal for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of the inversion process. By prioritizing the initial latent state, which encapsulates rich information about the original images, EasyInv steers clear of the iterative refinement of noise items. Instead, we introduce a methodical aggregation of the latent state from the preceding time step with the current state, effectively increasing the influence of the initial latent state and mitigating the impact of noise. We illustrate that EasyInv is capable of delivering results that are either on par with or exceed those of the conventional DDIM Inversion approach, especially under conditions where the model’s precision is limited or computational resources are scarce. Concurrently, our EasyInv offers an approximate threefold enhancement regarding inference efficiency over off-the-shelf iterative optimization techniques. It can be easily combined with most existing inversion methods by only four lines of code. See code at https://github.com/potato-kitty/EasyInv.

Existing iterative optimization techniques spend computation repeatedly refining that approximation. EasyInv targets this cost by giving greater influence to the initial latent representation, which contains substantial information about the original image.

The method combines the latent state from the preceding time step with the current state in a systematic way. This aggregation strengthens the influence of the initial image information and reduces the impact of noise, avoiding iterative refinement of the noise terms. The approach therefore changes how inversion information is combined rather than relying on repeated correction of each noise estimate.

The authors report inversion results comparable to or better than conventional DDIM inversion, particularly when model precision or computational resources are limited. Relative to off-the-shelf iterative optimization techniques, they report approximately threefold higher inference efficiency. They also state that EasyInv can be combined with most existing inversion methods using four lines of code, suggesting a lightweight route to adopting the aggregation strategy.
summary.tldr: EasyInv aggregates successive latent states to improve diffusion inversion efficiency, reporting roughly threefold gains over iterative optimization techniques.

title: EasyInv: Toward Fast and Better DDIM Inversion

abstract: Scattering characteristics of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) targets are typically related to observed azimuth and depression angles. However, in practice, it is difficult to obtain adequate training samples at all observation angles, which probably leads to poor robustness of deep networks. In this paper, we first propose a Gamma-Distribution Principal Component Analysis ($\Gamma$PCA) model that fully accounts for the statistical characteristics of SAR data. The $\Gamma$PCA derives consistent convolution kernels to effectively capture the angle-invariant features of the same target at various attitude angles, thus alleviating deep models’ sensitivity to angle changes in SAR target recognition task. We validate $\Gamma$PCA model based on two commonly used backbones, ResNet and ViT, and conduct multiple robustness experiments on the MSTAR benchmark dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that $\Gamma$PCA effectively enables the model to withstand substantial distributional discrepancy caused by angle changes. Additionally, $\Gamma$PCA convolution kernel is designed to require no parameter updates, introducing no extra computational burden to the network. The source code is available at https://github.com/ChGrey/GammaPCA.

paragraphs: A target’s appearance in synthetic aperture radar data depends on the angle from which it is observed. Training examples covering every azimuth and depression angle are difficult to obtain, which can make recognition networks sensitive to viewpoint changes. This paper develops Gamma-Distribution Principal Component Analysis, or ΓPCA, to address that problem through feature extraction.

ΓPCA accounts for the statistical characteristics of SAR data and derives consistent convolution kernels. These kernels are designed to capture features of a target that remain stable across different attitudes. The aim is to give a recognition model information that is less affected by observation angle, reducing the impact of the resulting distribution changes.

The authors integrate the method with ResNet and Vision Transformer backbones and conduct robustness experiments on MSTAR. The results show improved ability to withstand substantial distribution discrepancies caused by angle changes. The ΓPCA kernel requires no parameter updates and is reported to introduce no additional computational burden, making fixed statistical feature extraction central to the approach.
summary.tldr: ΓPCA derives fixed, statistically informed filters that improve SAR target recognition robustness to changes in observation angle.

title: Gamma Distribution PCA-Enhanced Feature Learning for Angle-Robust SAR Target Recognition

abstract: Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) are widely recognised as computationally intractable for neural networks, since they induce an exponential search space over the input features. In this work, we take a first step towards scaling exact SHAP computation to larger search spaces by introducing an algorithm that leverages recent advances in neural network verification to compute arbitrarily tight exact lower and upper bounds on SHAP values for neural networks, ultimately recovering the exact SHAP values. We demonstrate that our approach scales to orders of magnitude larger search spaces than state-of-the-art exact methods. This provides an important first step towards exact SHAP computation and establishes a principled cornerstone for evaluating statistical approximation methods on larger search spaces.

paragraphs: SHAP explains predictions by assigning contributions to input features, but exact computation for neural networks involves an exponentially growing search space over those features. This makes precise explanations computationally difficult as the space expands. Verified SHAP takes a step toward larger exact computations by drawing on advances in neural network verification.

The proposed algorithm computes guaranteed lower and upper bounds on each SHAP value. These bounds can become arbitrarily tight and ultimately recover the exact values. This provides a way to narrow uncertainty about an explanation while preserving mathematical guarantees about where the true contribution lies throughout the bounding process.

The authors demonstrate search spaces orders of magnitude larger than those handled by state-of-the-art exact methods. They present this as an initial step toward scaling exact SHAP, rather than a general removal of its computational difficulty. The resulting bounds and exact values also provide a principled reference for evaluating statistical approximation methods on larger spaces, helping assess how faithfully approximate explanations reflect the quantities they seek to estimate.
summary.tldr: Verified SHAP uses neural network verification to tighten provable attribution bounds and recover exact values on substantially larger search spaces.

title: Verified SHAP: Provable Bounds for Exact Shapley Values of Neural Networks

abstract: Protein function is often controlled by ligands that bias the direction of state transitions, such as agonists and antagonists, rather than stabilizing a single conformation. This is especially important for clinically relevant G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), where therapeutic efficacy depends on functional directionality. Structure-based design methods optimize binding to static conformations and cannot represent non-reversible, directional effects or systematically distinguish agonist from antagonist behavior. To address this gap, we introduce Transition-Directed Discrete Diffusion for allostericBinder design (TD3B), a sequence-based generative framework that designs binders with specified agonist or antagonist behavior via a directional transition control objective. TD3B combines a target-aware Direction Oracle, a soft binding-affinity gate, and amortized fine-tuning of a pre-trained discrete diffusion model, enabling targeted agonist and antagonist generation decoupled from binding affinity and unattainable by equilibrium-based or inference-only guidance baselines. The code and checkpoints are available at https://huggingface.co/ChatterjeeLab/TD3B.

paragraphs: A molecule’s effect on a protein can depend on how it changes transitions between protein states, beyond how strongly it binds one structure. The paper argues that optimizing static conformations does not capture the directional, non-reversible effects needed to distinguish these behaviors.

summary.tldr: TD3B generates binder sequences by targeting directional protein-state transitions, separating desired agonist or antagonist behavior from binding affinity.

title: TD3B: Transition-Directed Discrete Diffusion for Allosteric Binder Generation

abstract: Multi-instance partial-label learning (MIPL) is a recently proposed dual weakly supervised learning framework where each training bag is annotated with a candidate label set containing one true label and several false positives. The key challange of MIPL problem is that the relations between the key instances and the ground-truth labels are much more covered due to the false positive labels. Existing methods usually rely on the model’s own predictions and roughly aggregate instance features according to the learned attention weights, which is easily misled by false positives and lets key instances be overlooked. Here, we propose Average Gradient Outer Product based Multi-instance Partial-Label Learning (AGOPMIPL) method, where the average gradient outer product (AGOP) is directly calculated from the bag-level features and the model prediction, then it is integrated in an attention module to amplify discriminative feature directions and thereby helps key-instance identification. Moreover, the feature prototypes and a progressive disambiguation strategy are introduced to further suppress noisy candidates. The experimental studies on four MIPL benchmarks and the real-world CRC-MIPL dataset are performed and AGOPMIPL consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines, with up to $25.9%$ relative gain on CRC-MIPL-KMeansSeg.

paragraphs: In multi-instance partial-label learning, each training example is a bag of instances paired with several candidate labels, only one of which is correct. The learner must identify both the relevant instances and the true label. Incorrect candidates can mislead attention mechanisms, causing them to emphasize unhelpful instances and overlook the evidence that actually distinguishes the class.

AGOPMIPL uses an average gradient outer product computed from bag-level features and the model’s prediction. This quantity provides information about feature directions associated with changes in the prediction. Incorporating it into attention amplifies discriminative directions, helping the network identify key instances. Feature prototypes and a progressive label-disambiguation strategy further suppress misleading candidate labels.

The method consistently outperforms five state-of-the-art baselines across four MIPL benchmarks and the real-world CRC-MIPL dataset. Its largest reported relative gain is 25.9% on CRC-MIPL-KMeansSeg. The results support using gradient-derived feature information alongside attention and label refinement to address the intertwined uncertainty about which instances matter and which candidate label is correct.
summary.tldr: AGOPMIPL uses gradient-informed attention and progressive label refinement to identify useful instances despite ambiguous candidate labels.

title: Enhanced Multi-Instance Partial Label Learning via Average Gradient Outer Product

abstract: Recent advances in 3D molecular modeling have achieved high-fidelity structural synthesis, yet these models often lack an explicit and manipulable representation space. To address this, MolFLAE introduced a fixed-dimensional, E(3)-equivariant latent space, providing a novel framework for molecular editing independent of atom counts. However, because its latent space was primarily optimized for geometric reconstruction, it remains semantically shallow and inadequate for comprehensive representation learning. In this work, we propose MolAlign3D, which evolves this architecture into a unified semantic-generative engine. By anchoring MolFLAE’s manipulable latents with embeddings from a pre-trained molecular encoder, we yield a manifold that is both semantically dense and geometrically precise. Experiments show that MolAlign3D achieves high-fidelity molecular reconstruction and attains comparable performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks. Notably, the integration of rich semantic priors significantly enhances zero-shot molecular manipulation, including atom-number editing and latent-space interpolation, outperforming prior fixed-dimensional equivariant latent baseline.

paragraphs: MolAlign3D aims to make three-dimensional molecular representations useful for both structural generation and meaningful editing. Its starting point, MolFLAE, provides a fixed-dimensional, E(3)-equivariant latent space that can represent molecules independently of atom count. However, optimizing that space mainly for geometric reconstruction leaves it relatively weak in molecular semantics.

The proposed method anchors these editable latent representations to embeddings from a pretrained molecular encoder. This introduces semantic information while retaining the geometric precision and manipulability of the original architecture. The resulting space is intended to connect what a molecule means in representation learning with how its three-dimensional structure can be reconstructed and changed.

Experiments show high-fidelity reconstruction and comparable performance on molecular property prediction benchmarks. The added semantic priors also improve zero-shot manipulation, including changing atom counts and interpolating between latent representations, outperforming the prior fixed-dimensional equivariant baseline. These findings suggest that semantic alignment can strengthen molecular editing while preserving a compact representation suitable for geometric generation.
summary.tldr: MolAlign3D adds pretrained molecular semantics to an editable geometric latent space, improving zero-shot molecular manipulation.

title: MolAlign3D: Enhancing Fixed-Dimensional E(3)-Equivariant Latent Space for High-Fidelity 3D Molecular Reconstruction and Editing

abstract: Sampling equilibrium molecular configurations from the Boltzmann distribution is a longstanding challenge. Boltzmann Generators (BGs) address this by combining exact-likelihood generative models with importance sampling, but practical scalability is limited. Meanwhile, coarse-grained surrogates enable the modeling of larger systems by reducing effective dimensionality, yet often lack a reweighting procedure required to ensure asymptotically correct statistics. In this work, we propose Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators (CG-BGs), a framework for reduced-order generative modeling with importance sampling in coarse-grained coordinate space. CG-BGs generate samples using a flow-based model and reweight them using a learned potential of mean force (PMF). We show that the PMF can be learned from rapidly converged trajectories via enhanced sampling force matching. Experiments demonstrate that CG-BGs capture solvent-mediated interactions in highly reduced representations while substantially reducing computational cost relative to atomistic BGs, providing a practical route toward equilibrium sampling of larger molecular systems.

Boltzmann Generators combine generative models with importance sampling, but their practical scalability is limited. A flow-based model produces configurations, and a learned potential of mean force supplies the basis for reweighting them. It also substantially lowers computational cost relative to atomistic Boltzmann Generators. The contribution is a framework that combines dimensionality reduction with a reweighting procedure, providing a practical route toward equilibrium sampling for larger molecular systems.
summary.tldr: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators combine reduced-coordinate generation with learned reweighting to make molecular equilibrium sampling less costly.

title: Coarse-Grained Boltzmann Generators

abstract: The Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distance enables comparison across different spaces but remains fragile to structural noise due to its global quadratic coupling. Existing robust extensions primarily rely on node-centric mass relaxation. However, we argue that this strategy is far from sufficient: it only addresses node-induced structural noise (outliers) while neglecting edge-induced distortions where spurious connections exist between valid nodes. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Structurally Robust Gromov-Wasserstein (SRGW) distance, a novel formulation that adaptively filters geometric distortions during optimization. By introducing a structure-aware dual-mask mechanism, our method effectively isolates these stubborn structural outliers while preserving strict marginal constraints for balanced transport. We solve this objective using a Mask-Guided GW Algorithm, which jointly optimizes the transport plan and the structural noise filters. We provide a rigorous theoretical analysis proving that our algorithm converges to a critical point under the Kurdyka-{Ł}ojasiewicz framework. Extensive experiments on synthetic geometric matching and real-world subgraph alignment benchmarks demonstrate that Mask-Guided GW achieves superior alignment quality, particularly under severe structural noise.

paragraphs: Gromov-Wasserstein distance compares structures across different spaces by considering their internal relationships. Its global coupling also makes it sensitive to corrupted structure. The paper distinguishes noise caused by outlier nodes from noise caused by false connections between otherwise valid nodes, arguing that methods focused on adjusting node mass do not adequately handle the latter.

The proposed Structurally Robust Gromov-Wasserstein formulation introduces an adaptive dual-mask mechanism that filters geometric distortions during optimization. It preserves the strict marginal constraints of balanced transport while isolating problematic structure. The contribution is a way to address corrupted relationships without treating all affected nodes as outliers.
summary.tldr: Adaptive structural masks make Gromov-Wasserstein alignment more robust to false connections while preserving balanced transport constraints.

title: Achieving Structurally Robust Gromov Wasserstein Distance via Adaptive Dual-Mask

abstract: Weight-space learning studies neural architectures that operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. Motivated by the growing availability of pretrained models, recent work has demonstrated the effectiveness of weight-space networks across a wide range of tasks. SOTA weight-space networks rely on permutation-equivariant designs to improve generalization. However, this may negatively affect expressive power, warranting theoretical investigation. Importantly, unlike other structured domains, weight-space learning targets maps operating on both weight and function spaces, making expressivity analysis particularly subtle. While a few prior works provide partial expressivity results, a comprehensive characterization is still missing. In this work, we address this gap by developing a systematic theory for expressivity of weight-space networks. We first prove that all prominent permutation-equivariant networks are equivalent in expressive power. We then establish universality in both weight- and function-space settings under mild, natural assumptions on the input weights, and characterize the edge-case regimes where universality no longer holds. Guided by our theoretical results, we show that slight modifications to existing weight-space models yield a 34% improvement over prior SOTA, demonstrating the practical relevance of our framework.

paragraphs: Weight-space networks take the parameters of other neural networks as their inputs. Leading designs respect permutations of those parameters, an architectural choice intended to improve generalization. This paper examines whether that symmetry restricts what they can represent. The analysis must account for both operations on the numerical weights and operations on the functions those weights describe.

The authors develop a systematic expressivity theory and prove that all prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space networks have equivalent expressive power. Under mild, natural assumptions on the input weights, they establish universality in both weight-space and function-space settings. They also characterize exceptional regimes where universality fails, making the assumptions part of the expressivity result.

The theory guides small modifications to existing models that produce a reported 34% improvement over prior state-of-the-art performance. That empirical finding demonstrates practical relevance for the analysis without making universality itself a performance guarantee. Together, the results clarify the representational capabilities shared by prominent architectures and show how understanding their boundaries can inform changes to working weight-space models.
summary.tldr: A unified theory establishes equivalent expressivity and conditional universality for prominent permutation-equivariant weight-space networks, guiding effective architectural changes.

title: On the Expressive Power of Permutation-Equivariant Weight-Space Networks

abstract: Sign-based and LMO-inspired optimizers have recently attracted substantial attention in deep learning due to their strong performance and low memory footprint. However, their fixed-magnitude updates can hurt terminal convergence: they decouple update mechanisms from gradient magnitudes and fail to account for parameter heterogeneity, often leading to oscillation rather than convergence. We propose SoftSignum, a smooth relaxation of sign-based optimization that replaces the hard sign map with a temperature-controlled soft-sign transformation, enabling a parameter-wise transition from sign-like updates to magnitude-sensitive SGD-like steps. We complement it with an adaptive quantile-based temperature schedule and extend the same principle to matrix-valued optimizers, obtaining SoftMuon. We also develop a generalized geometry-relaxation framework based on strongly convex regularizers and Fenchel conjugates, proving convergence in stochastic non-convex setting. Experiments on diverse deep learning tasks, including LLM pretraining, show that SoftSignum and SoftMuon consistently improve over their hard sign-based counterparts and standard AdamW.

We complement it with an adaptive quantile-based temperature schedule and extend the same principle to matrix-valued optimizers, obtaining SoftMuon. We also develop a generalized geometry-relaxation framework based on strongly convex regularizers and Fenchel conjugates, proving convergence in stochastic non-convex setting. Experiments on diverse deep learning tasks, including LLM pretraining, show that SoftSignum and SoftMuon consistently improve over their hard sign-based counterparts and standard AdamW.

paragraphs: Sign-based optimizers can deliver strong performance with a small memory footprint, but fixed-magnitude updates discard gradient-size information. That can become problematic near convergence, particularly when parameters behave differently: updates may continue oscillating instead of settling. SoftSignum addresses this issue by replacing the hard sign operation with a smooth, temperature-controlled transformation.

The transformation allows individual parameters to move between sign-like updates and magnitude-sensitive steps resembling stochastic gradient descent. An adaptive schedule based on quantiles controls the temperature. The authors extend the same principle to matrix-valued optimization in SoftMuon, making smooth relaxation applicable beyond individual scalar updates.

The paper also develops a general geometry-relaxation framework using strongly convex regularizers and Fenchel conjugates, and proves convergence in a stochastic non-convex setting. Experiments across diverse deep-learning tasks, including language-model pretraining, show consistent improvements over the evaluated hard-sign counterparts and AdamW. Together, the analysis and experiments support restoring sensitivity to gradient magnitude as a way to handle parameter heterogeneity more effectively.
summary.tldr: SoftSignum and SoftMuon smooth fixed-magnitude optimizer updates, improving reported training results while supporting stochastic non-convex convergence analysis.

title: Softsign: Smooth Sign in Your Optimizer For Better Parameter Heterogeneity Handling

abstract: The LogSumExp function, dual to the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence, plays a central role in many important optimization problems, including entropy-regularized optimal transport (OT) and distributionally robust optimization (DRO). In practice, when the number of exponential terms inside the logarithm is large or infinite, optimization becomes challenging since computing the gradient requires differentiating every term. We propose a novel convexity- and smoothness-preserving approximation to LogSumExp that can be efficiently optimized using stochastic gradient methods. This approximation is rooted in a sound modification of the KL divergence in the dual, resulting in a new $f$-divergence called the Safe KL divergence. Our experiments and theoretical analysis of the LogSumExp-based stochastic optimization, arising in DRO and continuous OT, demonstrate the advantages of our approach over existing baselines.

Its computational difficulty grows when the logarithm contains very many exponential terms, or an infinite collection of them. The paper introduces an approximation designed for efficient stochastic gradient optimization while preserving convexity and smoothness. The authors provide theory and experiments for applications in distributionally robust optimization and continuous optimal transport, reporting advantages over existing baselines. The work offers a mathematically structured route to making large LogSumExp-based problems accessible to stochastic methods.
summary.tldr: A Safe KL-based approximation preserves LogSumExp’s convexity and smoothness while enabling efficient stochastic optimization.

title: Improved Stochastic Optimization of LogSumExp

abstract: Recent work shows that vision encoders capture ordinal attributes along linear axes, which can be recovered from as few as two labeled images. However, in the zero-shot setting, the text-driven rank axis for Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP remains suboptimal. In this work, we study the embeddings of Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs). We hypothesize that MLLMs can overcome this limitation due to three potential advantages: their inherent ordinal understanding, capacity for conditional embeddings, and a small cross-modal gap. We show that MLLMs are rankable using only text prompts. Experiments demonstrate that a text-driven rank axis for MLLM embeddings achieves 90% of the performance of the supervised linear rank axis, significantly outperforming the 61% observed in VLM embeddings. We validate that this capability stems from MLLMs’ conditional embeddings and a smaller modality gap than VLMs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this property generalizes to the audio domain. Our findings suggest that language provides a direct interface for probing latent ordinal structures in MLLMs. Code and prompts are available at https://github.com/kaist-ami/prompt-probing

paragraphs: A representation can encode an ordered attribute along a direction, allowing examples to be ranked by where they fall on that axis. Prior work recovers such directions in vision encoders with very few labeled images, but text-only directions in vision-language models remain suboptimal. This paper examines whether multimodal language models offer a better language interface.

The authors hypothesize three possible advantages: ordinal understanding, embeddings that depend on conditioning, and a smaller gap between text and other modalities. They show that text prompts alone can reveal ranking directions in multimodal language-model embeddings, enabling zero-shot ranking without labeled examples to define the axis.

In the experiments, text-derived directions achieve 90% of the performance of supervised linear ranking directions, compared with 61% for vision-language-model embeddings. These figures describe relative performance, not absolute ranking accuracy. The analysis attributes the capability to conditional embeddings and a smaller modality gap, and demonstrates extension to audio. The findings suggest that language can directly probe ordered structure already present in multimodal representations.
summary.tldr: Text prompts reveal ranking directions in multimodal language-model embeddings that reach 90% of supervised-axis performance in the reported experiments.

title: Zero-Shot Rankability: Revealing Latent Ordinal Structure in Multimodal Large Language Models via Language

abstract: Structure-Based Drug Design (SBDD) aims to discover bioactive ligands. Conventional approaches construct probability paths separately in Euclidean and probabilistic spaces for continuous atomic coordinates and discrete chemical categories, leading to a mismatch with the underlying statistical manifolds. We address this issue by representing molecules using composite exponential-family distributions, where coordinates and categories are represented within a unified natural parameter space to evolve synchronously along exponential geodesics under the Fisher-Rao metric. To avoid the instantaneous trajectory collapse induced by geodesics directly targeting Dirac distributions, we propose Evolving Exponential Geodesic Flow for SBDD (EvoEGF-Mol), which replaces static Dirac targets with dynamically concentrating distributions and is trained with a progressive-parameter-refinement architecture. Our model approaches a reference-level PoseBusters passing rate (93.4%) on CrossDock, demonstrating remarkable geometric precision and interaction fidelity, while achieving superior performance over baseline methods on real-world MolGenBench tasks for bioactive scaffold recovery. Code is available at https://github.com/BLEACH366/EvoEGF-Mol.

paragraphs: Molecular generation must coordinate continuous atom positions with discrete chemical categories. Conventional approaches evolve these quantities in separate spaces, which the authors identify as a mismatch with their underlying statistical geometry. EvoEGF-Mol represents both through composite exponential-family distributions, putting coordinates and categories into a shared natural-parameter space.

Within that representation, the two kinds of information evolve together along exponential geodesics under the Fisher-Rao metric. Directly targeting a perfectly concentrated Dirac distribution would cause instantaneous trajectory collapse. The proposed method avoids this by using target distributions that become concentrated dynamically, together with a training architecture that progressively refines parameters.

On CrossDock, the model achieves a 93.4% PoseBusters passing rate, approaching the reference level reported by the authors. It also outperforms baseline methods on MolGenBench tasks involving recovery of bioactive scaffolds. These results support the approach’s geometric precision and interaction fidelity in the evaluated tasks. The contribution ties those outcomes to a unified probabilistic treatment of molecular position and chemical identity.
summary.tldr: EvoEGF-Mol jointly evolves atom positions and chemical categories in a unified probabilistic geometry, improving evaluated molecular generation quality.

title: EvoEGF-Mol: Evolving Exponential Geodesic Flow for Structure-based Drug Design

abstract: With diffusion and flow matching models achieving state-of-the-art generating performance, the interest of the community now turned to reducing the inference time without sacrificing sample quality. Consistency Models (CMs), which are trained to be consistent on diffusion or probability flow ordinary differential equation (PF-ODE) trajectories, enable one or two-step flow or diffusion sampling. However, CMs typically require prolonged training with large batch sizes to obtain competitive sample quality. In this paper, we examine the training dynamics of CMs near convergence and discover that CM trajectory tangents – CM output update directions – are quite oscillatory, in the sense that they move parallel to the data manifold, not towards the manifold. To mitigate oscillatory trajectory tangents, we propose a new loss function, called the manifold feature distance (MFD), which provides manifold-aligned trajectory tangents that point toward the data manifold. Consequently, our method – dubbed Align Your Trajectory Tangent (AYT) – can accelerate CM training by orders of magnitude and even out-perform the learned perceptual image patch similarity metric (LPIPS). Furthermore, we find that our loss enables training with extremely small batch sizes without compromising sample quality. Code is available at https://github.com/1202kbs/AYT

paragraphs: Consistency models can generate samples in one or two steps, but obtaining competitive quality often requires lengthy training and large batches. This paper investigates what happens near convergence, focusing on trajectory tangents: the directions in which the model's outputs change along the underlying generation trajectory.

The authors find that these directions can oscillate along the data manifold, the structure occupied by realistic data, instead of pointing toward it. They introduce manifold feature distance, a loss designed to redirect these changes toward the manifold. Their method, Align Your Trajectory Tangent, therefore targets the geometry of the learning signal rather than simply extending training.

The reported results show that this loss can accelerate consistency-model training by orders of magnitude and outperform the LPIPS perceptual metric. It also permits extremely small training batches without sacrificing sample quality in the reported experiments. The central implication is that the direction supplied by a training objective can be a major obstacle to efficient consistency learning, and adjusting that direction can improve both training speed and batch-size flexibility.
summary.tldr: AYT redirects consistency-model updates toward the data manifold, enabling substantially faster training and much smaller batches in reported experiments.

title: Align Your Trajectory Tangent: Training Better Consistency Models via Manifold-Aligned Tangents

abstract: We investigate learning dynamics in competitive newsvendor games, a class of continuous-action games with strategic substitutes. Despite established equilibrium properties, convergence of independent learning algorithms in repeated general-sum play remains uncertain. We analyze structural properties under complete and incomplete information, deriving closed-form equilibria for a symmetric complete-information benchmark with perfect substitution. Our main theoretical contribution proves strict monotonicity in both complete-information and Bayesian models with private costs, ensuring equilibrium uniqueness and ruling out unstable dynamics. This provides convergence guarantees for variational-inequality-based algorithms. Numerical experiments using deep reinforcement learning agents with Proximal Policy Optimization empirically demonstrate convergence to Nash and Bayesian Nash equilibria, verified by equilibrium checks. These results establish a foundation for applying deep reinforcement learning in competitive inventory management.

paragraphs: Competitive newsvendor games model inventory decisions made by competing sellers. Actions are continuous, and the strategic-substitute structure means competitors’ choices influence which inventory decisions are attractive. Although equilibria in these games have established properties, that does not by itself settle whether independently learning agents will approach an equilibrium through repeated interaction.

The paper studies both complete information and private-cost settings. It derives explicit equilibrium formulas for a symmetric complete-information benchmark with perfect substitution. Its main theoretical result establishes strict monotonicity in the analyzed complete-information and Bayesian models. This structure ensures a unique equilibrium, rules out unstable dynamics in the analysis, and supports convergence guarantees for algorithms based on variational inequalities.

The authors separately test deep reinforcement learning agents trained with Proximal Policy Optimization. Numerical experiments show convergence to Nash and Bayesian Nash equilibria, with equilibrium checks used to verify the outcomes. The distinction matters: the theoretical convergence guarantees concern variational-inequality-based algorithms, while the PPO evidence is empirical. Together, the results support using deep reinforcement learning for competitive inventory decisions.
summary.tldr: The paper proves equilibrium uniqueness for competitive inventory games and empirically shows PPO agents converging to Nash and Bayesian Nash equilibria.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning Finds Bayes-Nash Equilibrium in Competitive Newsvendor Problems

abstract: Modality translation is inherently under-constrained, as multiple cross-modal mappings may yield the same marginals. Recent work has shown that diffusion bridges are effective for this task. However, most existing approaches rely on fully paired datasets, thereby imposing a single data-driven constraint. We propose a diffusion-bridge framework that characterizes the space of admissible solutions and restricts it via alignment constraints, treating paired supervision as an optional heuristic rather than a prerequisite. We validate our method on synthetic and real modality translation benchmarks across unpaired, semi-paired, and paired regimes, showing consistent performance across supervision levels. Notably, it achieves near fully-paired quality with a substantial relaxation in pairing requirements, and remaining applicable in the unpaired regime. These results highlight diffusion bridges as a flexible foundation for modality translation beyond fully paired data.

paragraphs: Translating between modalities is ambiguous because different mappings can produce the same distributions on either side. Matching those distributions alone therefore does not identify which cross-modal relationships should be learned. Existing diffusion-bridge approaches commonly resolve this ambiguity with fully paired examples, making the pairing itself the main constraint on the mapping.

This paper develops a diffusion-bridge framework that explicitly characterizes the possible solutions and narrows them through alignment constraints. Paired supervision becomes an optional heuristic within that framework instead of a prerequisite. The approach places the desired relationship between modalities at the center of the problem, providing structure even when complete example-by-example correspondences are unavailable.

The authors test synthetic and real modality-translation benchmarks with unpaired, partially paired, and fully paired data. They report consistent performance across supervision levels and near fully paired quality with substantially fewer pairing requirements, while retaining applicability without pairs. These findings support diffusion bridges as a flexible basis for translation when supervision varies, with alignment constraints helping restrict an otherwise underdetermined mapping.
summary.tldr: Structured diffusion bridges use alignment constraints to support modality translation with fewer paired examples and remain applicable when no pairs are available.

title: Structured Diffusion Bridges: Inductive Bias for Denoising Diffusion Bridges

abstract: Policies learned via continuous actor-critic methods often exhibit erratic, high-frequency oscillations, making them unsuitable for physical deployment. Current approaches attempt to enforce smoothness by directly regularizing the policy’s output. We argue that this approach treats the symptom rather than the cause. In this work, we theoretically establish that policy non-smoothness is fundamentally governed by the differential geometry of the critic. By applying implicit differentiation to the actor-critic objective, we prove that the sensitivity of the optimal policy is bounded by the ratio of the Q-function’s mixed-partial derivative (noise sensitivity) to its action-space curvature (signal distinctness). To empirically validate this theoretical insight, we introduce PAVE (Policy-Aware Value-field Equalization), a critic-centric regularization framework that treats the critic as a scalar field and stabilizes its induced action-gradient field. PAVE rectifies the learning signal by minimizing the Q-gradient volatility while preserving local curvature. Experimental results demonstrate that PAVE achieves smoothness comparable to policy-side smoothness regularization methods, while maintaining competitive task performance, without modifying the actor.

paragraphs: Continuous actor-critic policies can produce rapid, erratic changes in actions that make physical deployment difficult. Common remedies penalize roughness directly in the policy’s output. This paper instead examines the critic, whose Q-function evaluates actions and supplies the learning signal that shapes the policy.

Using implicit differentiation, the authors bound the sensitivity of the optimal policy by a ratio involving two properties of the Q-function. The numerator captures mixed-derivative sensitivity, described as sensitivity to noise, while the denominator captures curvature over actions, or how distinctly the critic favors actions. This links policy smoothness to the geometry of the critic’s learning signal.

PAVE applies that insight by treating the critic as a scalar field and stabilizing the action gradients it induces. It minimizes gradient volatility while preserving local curvature, leaving the actor unchanged. Experiments achieve smoothness comparable to methods that regularize the policy directly while maintaining competitive task performance. The results support critic regularization as an effective route to smoother control.
summary.tldr: PAVE smooths actor-critic policies by stabilizing the critic’s action gradients while preserving curvature and leaving the actor unchanged.

title: Stabilizing the Q-Gradient Field for Policy Smoothness in Actor-Critic Methods

abstract: When designing interventions to promote desired actions, two-stage agent heterogeneity – encompassing both engagement with the intervention and completion of the desired action – creates significant challenges in identifying optimal intervention policies. While this two-dimensional heterogeneity creates distinct agent response types with varying marginal policy returns, existing literature typically falls short in full identification of all agent types, leading to inefficient intervention allocations. To address the challenge of learning optimal policies that account for two-stage outcomes, we propose a minimax approach within a counterfactual principal strata framework. A value function, accommodating varying policy returns across six potentially non-identifiable principal strata, is designed and partially identified to minimize the worst-case value loss relative to three benchmark policies: never-treat, always-treat, and oracle. We introduce three estimators for optimal policy learning: Principal Outcome Regression (P-OR), Principal Inverse Propensity Scoring (P-IPS), and Principal Doubly Robust (P-DR), providing theoretical guarantees for their unbiasedness, robustness, and regret upper bounds. Extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: An intervention can affect whether someone engages with it and whether they ultimately complete the desired action. These two stages create different kinds of responses, so allocating interventions based on a single outcome can miss important differences in their benefits. This paper studies policy learning when those response types cannot all be fully identified.

The authors use counterfactual principal strata: groups defined by how agents would respond under different intervention choices. Their framework accommodates six potentially unidentifiable groups with different policy returns. Rather than requiring complete identification, it partially identifies policy value and uses a minimax objective to limit worst-case value loss relative to never intervening, always intervening, or an oracle policy.

The paper introduces regression, inverse-propensity, and doubly robust estimators adapted to this framework. It supplies theoretical guarantees concerning unbiasedness, robustness, and regret bounds, alongside numerical experiments reporting superior performance. The contribution is a way to make intervention decisions while explicitly accounting for uncertainty about two-stage responses, rather than assuming every relevant response type can be recovered.
summary.tldr: A minimax framework learns intervention policies that account for uncertain differences in both engagement and eventual action.

title: A Minimax Approach for Optimal Intervention Policy Learning with Two-Stage Outcomes

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have emerged as powerful decision-makers across a wide range of single-agent and stationary environments, fewer efforts have been devoted to settings where LLMs must engage in repeated and strategic interactions with unknown or dynamic opponents. In such settings, recipes built upon offline pre-training or fine-tuning, though robust against worst-case adversaries, do not fully exploit the capability of LLMs to adapt online based on interaction feedback. Instead, we explore the more natural perspective of scaling inference-time computation as a mechanism for adaptation, embedding the principles of a classical game-theoretical learning dynamic, smooth Fictitious Play (sFP), into LLM inference: (i) for belief formation, we employ an auxiliary opponent model that in-context learns to imitate the time-averaged behavior of the opponent; (ii) for best response, we advance best-of-$N$ (BoN) sampling by simulating against the opponent model. Empirical evaluations on two distinct forms of repeated negotiation games demonstrate that our method enables significant performance improvement over online interaction compared to various baselines, offering a scalable and principled approach to strategic decision-making without any parameter updates.

paragraphs: Repeated negotiation gives an agent opportunities to learn from an opponent’s behavior as interactions unfold. This paper investigates how language models can use those opportunities when opponents are unknown or changing. Its approach spends additional computation during inference to adapt strategy, without updating model parameters.

The method brings two elements of smooth Fictitious Play into language-model inference. First, an auxiliary opponent model learns in context to imitate the opponent’s time-averaged behavior, forming a working belief about likely responses. Second, the decision-maker samples multiple candidate responses and evaluates them through simulations against that opponent model. This extends best-of-N selection with an explicit model of the other participant.

Evaluations on two forms of repeated negotiation report significant improvements over the course of online interaction compared with various baselines. The results show that accumulated feedback can guide strategic adaptation through contextual modeling and simulation. The demonstrated benefit is specific to the evaluated negotiation settings, with time-averaged opponent behavior providing the method’s stated basis for forming beliefs.
summary.tldr: An LLM adapts during repeated negotiation by modeling its opponent and simulating candidate responses without parameter updates.

title: Scaling Inference-Time Computation via Opponent Simulation: Enabling Online Strategic Adaptation in Repeated Negotiation

abstract: Modern diffusion/flow-based models for image generation typically exhibit two core characteristics: (i) using multi-step sampling, and (ii) operating in a latent space. Recent advances have made encouraging progress on each aspect individually, paving the way toward one-step diffusion/flow without latents. In this work, we take a further step towards this goal and propose "pixel MeanFlow" (pMF). Our core guideline is to formulate the network output space and the loss space separately. The network target is designed to be on a presumed low-dimensional image manifold (i.e., x-prediction), while the loss is defined via MeanFlow in the velocity space. We introduce a simple transformation between the image manifold and the average velocity field. In experiments, pMF achieves strong results for one-step latent-free generation on ImageNet at 256$\times$256 resolution (2.22 FID) and 512$\times$512 resolution (2.48 FID), filling a key missing piece in this regime. We hope that our study will further advance the boundaries of diffusion/flow-based generative models.

paragraphs: Diffusion and flow models commonly generate images through repeated sampling steps and operate in a latent representation. Pixel MeanFlow, or pMF, brings together two departures from that setup: producing an image in one step and working directly without a latent space. The paper’s main design choice concerns what the network predicts and where its error is measured.

The network predicts an image, following the assumption that images lie on a low-dimensional manifold. Its loss, however, is defined in velocity space through MeanFlow. A transformation connects the image prediction to the average velocity field, allowing the output representation and training objective to be designed separately while remaining linked.

On ImageNet, the method reports FID scores of 2.22 at 256-by-256 resolution and 2.48 at 512-by-512 resolution for one-step, latent-free generation. These results support the feasibility of combining direct pixel generation with one-step sampling. The contribution is the formulation that makes those choices work together, especially the separation between an image-shaped prediction target and a velocity-based learning signal.
summary.tldr: Pixel MeanFlow enables one-step image generation without latents by combining image prediction with a MeanFlow loss in velocity space.

title: One-step Latent-free Image Generation with Pixel Mean Flows

abstract: While self-consistency methods have emerged as a promising approach to enhance the correctness of large language model (LLM) outputs by aggregating multiple stochastic samples, they suffer from two critical limitations, resulting in high computation cost. First, they evaluate output consistency monolithically, failing to efficiently combine partially correct answers across multiple samples. Second, they use static stopping criteria that cannot adapt to varying task complexities and model capabilities, resulting in suboptimal computational efficiency.In this work, we present Task-and-Model-Aware Fractal-Consistency (TMAFC), a novel self-consistency framework that addresses these limitations through two key innovations: (1) Fractal-Consistency, which evaluates output consistency at the granularity of output components to effectively combine partial correct answers across samples, and (2) Adaptive Stopping Criteria Calibration (ASCC), which dynamically adjusts sampling stopping criteria based on real-time assessment of both task difficulty and LLM capability. Through extensive experiments on diverse question-answering benchmarks, we demonstrate that TMAFC achieves superior efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, reducing sample cost by up to 55% while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
originalAbstract: While self-consistency methods have emerged as a promising approach to enhance the correctness of large language model (LLM) outputs by aggregating multiple stochastic samples, they suffer from two critical limitations, resulting in high computation cost. First, they evaluate output consistency monolithically, failing to efficiently combine partially correct answers across multiple samples. Second, they use static stopping criteria that cannot adapt to varying task complexities and model capabilities, resulting in suboptimal computational efficiency.In this work, we present Task-and-Model-Aware Fractal-Consistency (TMAFC), a novel self-consistency framework that addresses these limitations through two key innovations: (1) Fractal-Consistency, which evaluates output consistency at the granularity of output components to effectively combine partial correct answers across samples, and (2) Adaptive Stopping Criteria Calibration (ASCC), which dynamically adjusts sampling stopping criteria based on real-time assessment of both task difficulty and LLM capability. Through extensive experiments on diverse question-answering benchmarks, we demonstrate that TMAFC achieves superior efficiency-accuracy trade-offs, reducing sample cost by up to 55% while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Self-consistency improves language-model answers by generating multiple samples and combining their results. This can be computationally expensive, especially when entire answers are compared as indivisible units and sampling ends according to a fixed rule. TMAFC addresses both issues by changing how agreement is measured and how the system decides whether to generate another sample.

Fractal-Consistency examines individual components of outputs, allowing partially correct material from different samples to be combined. This makes useful agreement within answers available to the aggregation process. Adaptive Stopping Criteria Calibration then adjusts the stopping rule using real-time assessments of task difficulty and model capability. The framework can therefore vary its sampling effort with both the problem and the model attempting it.

Experiments across diverse question-answering benchmarks show a better balance between sampling cost and accuracy. The authors report sample-cost reductions of up to 55% while retaining competitive accuracy against state-of-the-art baselines. The result supports extracting more value from each sampled answer and calibrating when to stop, without claiming that every task receives the maximum reported saving.
summary.tldr: TMAFC combines agreement among answer components with adaptive stopping to reduce reasoning sample costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: Task-and-Model-Aware Fractal-Consistency for Efficient LLM Reasoning

abstract: The paradigm of visual generation is rapidly shifting from single-image conditioning toward multi-image conditioning, making the ability to synthesize and edit images based on multiple visual references a critical capability. Despite this trend, existing benchmarks remain largely limited to single-reference scenarios or narrowly defined tasks, leaving model behavior under complex multi-concept composition insufficiently explored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MICE-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark for Multi-reference Image Creation and Editing. The benchmark is designed around three core principles: 1) heterogeneous concept composition across seven visual dimensions; 2) varying levels of constraint density, ranging from dual-concept to seven-concept configurations; 3) concept-centric data construction and benchmark evaluation, enabling fine-grained analysis of interactions among multiple concepts. MICE-Bench consists of 3,119 high-quality test cases within a unified concept space. Using an 8-dimensional evaluation metric, we systematically evaluate 13 state-of-the-art models. Our results show that although closed-source models maintain a clear performance advantage, all models experience notable degradation in concept consistency and physical realism as concept complexity increases.This indicates that current models rely on superficial composition rather than genuine multi-concept synthesis, highlighting substantial room for future improvement.

paragraphs: MICE-Bench evaluates image creation and editing when a model must combine information from several visual references. Existing evaluations often emphasize a single reference or a narrow task, leaving complex combinations underexamined. This benchmark makes the interaction among concepts central, testing whether models can preserve multiple requested properties while producing a coherent image.

The benchmark contains 3,119 test cases organized within one concept space. Its design spans seven visual dimensions and increases constraint density from two concepts to seven. Both data construction and evaluation are concept-centered, allowing analysis of how different requirements interact. The authors assess 13 models using an eight-dimensional evaluation metric, examining performance beyond a single overall measure of image quality.

The authors interpret this pattern as evidence of superficial composition rather than genuine synthesis of multiple concepts. The benchmark therefore exposes a shared difficulty: satisfying increasingly many visual requirements together, even when individual outputs may otherwise look capable.
summary.tldr: MICE-Bench finds that image models struggle to preserve concept consistency and physical realism as multi-reference requirements become more complex.

title: MICE-Bench: A Challenging and Comprehensive Benchmark for Multi-Reference Image Creation and Editing

abstract: Semi-supervised imitation learning (SSIL) consists in learning a policy from a small dataset of action-labeled trajectories and a much larger dataset of action-free trajectories. Some SSIL methods learn an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to predict the action from the current state and the next state. An IDM can act as a policy when paired with a video model (VM-IDM) or as a label generator to perform behavior cloning on action-free data (IDM labeling). In this work, we first show that VM-IDM and IDM labeling learn the same policy in a limit case, which we call the IDM-based policy. We then argue that the previously observed advantage of IDM-based policies over behavior cloning is due to the superior sample efficiency of IDM learning, which we attribute to two causes: (i) the ground-truth IDM tends to be contained in a lower complexity hypothesis class relative to the expert policy, and (ii) the ground-truth IDM is often less stochastic than the expert policy. We argue these claims based on insights from statistical learning theory and novel experiments, including a study of IDM-based policies using recent architectures for unified video-action prediction (UVA). Motivated by these insights, we finally propose an improved version of the existing LAPO algorithm for latent action policy learning. We experiment on the Procgen, Push-T and LIBERO benchmarks.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised imitation learning combines a small collection of trajectories with action labels and a much larger collection without them. An inverse dynamics model predicts which action connects a current state to the next state. It can supply missing labels for behavior cloning or work alongside a video model to produce a policy.

The authors show that these two uses learn the same policy in a limiting case. They then argue that previously observed advantages over behavior cloning arise from the sample efficiency of learning inverse dynamics. Their explanation has two parts: the true inverse dynamics model tends to belong to a less complex hypothesis class, and it is often less stochastic than the expert policy.

It also motivates an improved version of LAPO for learning latent action policies. Experiments use Procgen, Push-T, and LIBERO. The paper thus connects different inverse-dynamics approaches through a common limiting policy and explains why inferring actions from state transitions can require fewer labeled examples.
summary.tldr: Inverse dynamics can make imitation learning more sample-efficient because predicting actions from transitions may be simpler and less stochastic than learning the expert policy.

title: On the Sample Efficiency of Inverse Dynamics Models for Semi-Supervised Imitation Learning

abstract: Modern database workloads are highly predictable: query streams are dominated by recurring jobs and templates, even when their arrival order is not known in advance. This motivates a learning-augmented view of online differentially private (DP) analytics: can algorithms utilize predictions about which queries will occur to improve utility under a single global privacy budget, while remaining robust when predictions are wrong? We study online DP query answering, where a curator must answer a stream $Q$ of $S$ linear queries arriving in uniformly random order under privacy budget $(\epsilon,\delta)$. We present LAPRAS, which assumes access to an oracle that outputs a prediction set of queries likely to appear in the stream and uses it to guide privacy spending. LAPRAS answers predicted queries using the offline-optimal Matrix Mechanism and answers the remaining queries online from a residual budget. To pace spending across an unknown number of unpredicted queries, we introduce Smooth Allocation, which forms an unbiased stopping-time estimate $\widehat{B}$ from the first $T=\Theta(\log^2 S)$ unpredicted queries and continuously recalibrates per-query expenditure. Empirically, over two real datasets, we validate the intended consistency–robustness trade-off: LAPRAS achieves near-offline utility under high overlap and degrades gracefully to baseline-level performance when overlap is low.

paragraphs: LAPRAS studies how predictions about future database queries can improve differentially private answers under one global privacy budget. Recurring jobs make query identities potentially predictable even when their arrival order is unknown. The formal setting assumes a stream of linear queries arriving in uniformly random order and an oracle supplying a predicted query set.

The algorithm allocates privacy spending through two routes. Predicted queries use the offline-optimal Matrix Mechanism, while unexpected queries draw on a residual budget through online answering. This division lets useful predictions inform the overall allocation while retaining resources for queries that the oracle missed.

To handle the unknown number of unexpected queries, Smooth Allocation builds an unbiased stopping-time estimate from the first number of such queries proportional to the squared logarithm of stream size. It then continually adjusts per-query expenditure. Experiments on two real datasets show near-offline utility when predictions overlap strongly with the stream and graceful degradation toward baseline performance when overlap is low.
summary.tldr: LAPRAS uses predicted query sets to allocate a global privacy budget while adapting spending to unexpected queries.

title: LAPRAS : Learning-Augmented PRivate Answering for linear query Streams.

abstract: Incorporating group symmetries via equivariance into neural networks has emerged as a robust approach for improving efficiency and overcoming the data requirements of modern deep learning. While most existing approaches, such as group convolutions and averaging-based methods, focus on compact, finite, or low-dimensional groups with linear actions, this work explores how equivariance can be extended to infinite-dimensional groups. We propose a strategy designed to induce diffeomorphism equivariance in pre-trained neural networks via energy-based canonicalization. Formulating equivariance as an optimization problem allows us to access the rich toolbox of already established differentiable image registration methods. Empirical results on segmentation and classification tasks confirm that our approach achieves approximate equivariance and generalizes to unseen transformations without relying on extensive data augmentation or retraining.

paragraphs: Equivariant neural networks aim to respond consistently when their inputs undergo transformations. Many existing methods handle transformation groups that are finite, compact, or low-dimensional with linear actions. This paper explores diffeomorphisms, a much richer family of smooth, invertible deformations belonging to an infinite-dimensional group.

The proposed strategy adds energy-based canonicalization to pretrained networks. It formulates the equivariance problem as an optimization task, allowing established differentiable image-registration methods to be used. Canonicalization provides a way to handle transformations through this optimization process, extending the available machinery beyond the groups commonly addressed by convolution or averaging methods.

Experiments on segmentation and classification show approximate equivariance and generalization to transformations not seen previously. These results are achieved without relying on extensive data augmentation or retraining. The empirical finding is approximate consistency under deformation, supporting canonicalization as a practical route toward applying pretrained networks to a broader range of transformations while reusing existing image-registration tools.
summary.tldr: Energy-based canonicalization gives pretrained networks approximate equivariance to smooth deformations and generalization to unseen transformations.

title: Towards Diffeomorphism-Equivariant Neural Networks via Canonicalization

abstract: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) extends standard RL by optimizing policies with respect to multiple, often conflicting, objectives. While max-min MORL has emerged as an effective approach for promoting fairness, its applicability remains limited, particularly when constraints must be incorporated. In this paper, we propose a MORL framework that integrates the max-min criterion with explicit constraint satisfaction. We establish a theoretical foundation for the proposed framework and validate the resulting algorithm through convergence analysis and experiments in tabular settings. We further demonstrate the practical relevance of our approach in simulated building thermal control, multi-objective locomotion control, and greenhouse-gas-emission-aware traffic management. Across these domains, our method effectively balances fairness and constraint satisfaction in multi-objective decision-making.
originalAbstract: Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (MORL) extends standard RL by optimizing policies with respect to multiple, often conflicting, objectives. While max-min MORL has emerged as an effective approach for promoting fairness, its applicability remains limited, particularly when constraints must be incorporated. In this paper, we propose a MORL framework that integrates the max-min criterion with explicit constraint satisfaction. We establish a theoretical foundation for the proposed framework and validate the resulting algorithm through convergence analysis and experiments in tabular settings. We further demonstrate the practical relevance of our approach in simulated building thermal control, multi-objective locomotion control, and greenhouse-gas-emission-aware traffic management. paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning asks a policy to handle several goals that may conflict. A max-min criterion promotes fairness by focusing on the worst-performing objective, rather than allowing strong results on some objectives to overshadow weak results on others. This paper addresses how to combine that criterion with explicit constraints on acceptable behavior.

The proposed framework makes constraint satisfaction part of the multi-objective learning problem. That matters because balancing objectives and respecting constraints are distinct requirements: a fair balance alone does not establish that a policy meets its restrictions. The authors develop a theoretical foundation and analyze convergence of the resulting algorithm, alongside experiments in tabular settings.

They also evaluate the approach in simulated building thermal control, multi-objective locomotion, and traffic management that accounts for greenhouse-gas emissions. Across these domains, the reported results show effective balancing of fairness and constraint satisfaction. The contribution connects a fairness-oriented objective to constrained decision-making, with theoretical support in the analyzed setting and practical demonstrations across several types of control problem.
summary.tldr: This framework combines max-min fairness with explicit constraints in multi-objective reinforcement learning.

title: Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning with Max-Min Criterion

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning systems often suffer from unstable training dynamics due to non-stationarity, where learning objectives and data distributions evolve over time. We show that under non-stationary targets, isotropic Gaussian embeddings are provably advantageous. In particular, they induce stable tracking of time-varying targets for linear readouts, achieve maximal entropy under a fixed variance budget, and encourage a balanced use of all representational dimensions–all of which enable agents to be more adaptive and stable. Building on this insight, we propose the use of Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization for shaping representations toward an isotropic Gaussian distribution during training. We demonstrate empirically, over a variety of domains, that this simple and computationally inexpensive method improves performance under non-stationarity while reducing representation collapse, neuron dormancy, and training instability.
