paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents train against objectives and data distributions that change over time. Their internal representations can become unstable or underused as learning proceeds. This paper investigates whether shaping the geometry and distribution of those representations can help agents adapt to changing targets.

The authors establish advantages of isotropic Gaussian embeddings, whose variation is balanced across directions. Under nonstationary targets, these embeddings support stable tracking by linear readouts. They also maximize entropy under a fixed variance budget and encourage balanced use of representational dimensions. The linear-readout setting is an explicit part of the stated tracking result.

Building on these properties, Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization pushes learned representations toward an isotropic Gaussian distribution during training. The method is described as simple and computationally inexpensive. Across multiple domains, experiments show improved performance under nonstationarity and reductions in representation collapse, dormant neurons, and training instability. Together, the theory and experiments motivate representation shaping as a practical way to support more stable adaptation.
summary.tldr: Regularizing representations toward an isotropic Gaussian improves reported reinforcement-learning stability and adaptation to changing targets.

title: Stable Deep Reinforcement Learning via Isotropic Gaussian Representations

abstract: Late-interaction retrievers like ColBERT achieve high quality but suffer from large multi-vector indices. Standard compression minimizes token reconstruction error, while ranking depends critically on preserving scores of sparse "winner" tokens. We introduce CrossQ, which adaptively improves effective token fidelity within documents by conditioning token codes on lightweight document context computed at indexing time (but not stored). CrossQ is trained with ranking-aligned objectives that preserve candidate score distributions and protect hard-negative margins. At 2 B/token, CrossQ improves MRR@10 by +0.010 over the strongest strictly footprint-matched quantization baseline and by +0.012 over the strongest candidate-matched system reference. On the nine-dataset BEIR subset reported in Appendix G.1, CrossQ improves average nDCG@10 by +0.009 at 4 B/token over the strongest candidate-matched system reference. At 4 B/token, CrossQ achieves $64\times$ raw token-storage reduction, approximately $61\times$ including metadata and approximately $58\times$ under conservative padding/alignment accounting. At 8 B/token, CrossQ + light fine-tuning retains approximately 98% of full-precision ColBERT MRR@10, improving the footprint-quality tradeoff for memory-constrained late-interaction retrieval.

paragraphs: Late-interaction retrieval systems store multiple token vectors per document, making their indexes expensive. Compressing each vector to minimize reconstruction error can miss what matters for ranking: a small set of winning token matches may determine a document's score. CrossQ instead makes compression sensitive to document context and trains it to preserve retrieval behavior.

Its token codes depend on lightweight context computed during indexing, without storing that context. Training objectives preserve candidate score distributions and protect score margins against hard negatives. At two bytes per token, CrossQ improves MRR@10 by 0.010 over the strongest strictly footprint-matched quantization baseline and by 0.012 over the strongest candidate-matched system reference.

At four bytes per token, it improves average nDCG@10 by 0.009 on the reported nine-dataset BEIR subset. Storage reduction is 64-fold for raw tokens, approximately 61-fold with metadata, and approximately 58-fold with conservative padding and alignment. At eight bytes per token, light fine-tuning retains approximately 98% of full-precision ColBERT MRR@10. These results show how ranking-aware compression can improve the trade-off between index size and retrieval quality.
summary.tldr: CrossQ compresses retrieval token vectors using document context and ranking-aware training to improve quality at small index sizes.

title: CrossQ: Task-Aligned Cross-Token Conditional Quantization for Late Interaction Retrieval

abstract: Artificial and biological systems may converge on similar computational strategies despite different architectures and learning mechanisms—a form of convergent evolution. We test this at scale by comparing internal representations of 630 AI models (language and vision; 1.33M–72B parameters) against fMRI from the Natural Scenes Dataset, producing over 60 million alignment measurements. Within each modality, higher-performing models spontaneously develop stronger brain correspondence (language: r = 0.89; vision: r = 0.53); because the inputs are image-evoked, the language results reflect visual-semantic alignment rather than a direct cross-modal comparison. Longitudinal analysis combined with bidirectional Granger tests further shows that past alignment predicts future performance more reliably than the reverse, identifying brain-like representations as a robust early-emerging correlate of learning. Modality-specific organization also emerges: language models align with limbic and integrative regions, vision models with visual cortical hierarchies.

paragraphs: This study asks whether artificial models and biological brains develop similar internal representations despite their different architectures and learning mechanisms. The authors compare 630 language and vision models, spanning 1.33 million to 72 billion parameters, with brain activity measured by fMRI in the Natural Scenes Dataset. Their analysis produces more than 60 million alignment measurements.

Within each modality, better-performing models tend to show stronger correspondence with brain activity. The reported correlations are 0.89 for language models and 0.53 for vision models. Because the brain responses were evoked by images, the language-model result concerns visual-semantic correspondence; it is not a direct comparison of language and vision processing under equivalent inputs.

Tracking training over time, the authors find that earlier brain alignment predicts later performance more reliably than the reverse in bidirectional Granger tests. This identifies alignment as an early correlate of learning, without establishing that it causes improvement. The regional patterns also differ: language models correspond more with limbic and integrative regions, while vision models align with visual cortical hierarchies.
summary.tldr: Across 630 AI models, stronger performance correlates with greater brain alignment, which also emerges as an early predictor of learning progress.

title: Alignment between Brains and AI: Evidence for Convergent Evolution across Modalities, Scales and Training Trajectories

abstract: Generalized Bayesian Inference (GBI) tempers a loss with a temperature $\beta>0$ to mitigate overconfidence and improve robustness under model misspecification, but existing GBI methods typically rely on costly MCMC or SDE-based samplers and must be re-run for each new dataset and each $\beta$-value. We give the first fully amortized variational approximation for the specific case of the tempered posterior family $p_\beta(\theta\mid x) \propto \pi(\theta)p(x \mid\theta)^\beta$ by training a single $(x,\beta)$-conditioned neural posterior estimator $q_\phi(\theta \mid x, \beta)$ that enables sampling in a single forward pass, without simulator calls or inference-time MCMC. We introduce two complementary training routes: (i) synthesizes off-manifold samples $(\theta, x) \sim \pi(\theta)p(x \mid \theta)^\beta$ and (ii) reweights a fixed base dataset $\pi(\theta)p(x \mid \theta)$ using self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS), where we show that the SNIS-weighted objective provides a consistent forward-KL fit to the tempered posterior with finite weight variance. Across four standard simulation-based inference (SBI) benchmarks—including the chaotic Lorenz–96 system—our $\beta$-amortized estimator achieves competitive posterior approximations, in standard two-sample metrics, with non-amortized MCMC-based power-posterior samplers over a wide range of temperatures.

paragraphs: Generalized Bayesian inference can adjust how strongly observations influence an inference, helping address overconfidence when a model does not fully match reality. Existing methods often repeat expensive sampling for every new dataset and temperature setting. This paper targets the specific posterior family formed by raising the likelihood to a positive power, beta, and combining it with the prior.

The authors train one neural posterior estimator that takes both observations and beta as inputs. Once trained, it produces samples in a single forward pass without further simulator calls or inference-time MCMC. They offer two training routes: generating samples for the tempered setting, or reweighting an existing dataset using self-normalized importance sampling.

For the reweighting route, the authors establish a consistent forward-KL fitting objective under finite importance-weight variance. Across four simulation-based inference benchmarks, including Lorenz–96, the estimator produces posterior approximations competitive with non-amortized MCMC methods across a wide temperature range. The contribution is reusable inference across datasets and temperatures within this particular posterior family.
summary.tldr: A single neural estimator learns tempered Bayesian posteriors across observations and temperatures, enabling sampling without inference-time simulation or MCMC.

title: Amortized Simulation-Based Inference in Generalized Bayes via Neural Posterior Estimation

abstract: Modeling the bidirectional correspondence between external sensory stimuli and internal neural activity has emerged as a critical frontier in neuroscience. However, existing approaches predominantly treat brain encoding and decoding as isolated tasks, relying heavily on unimodal alignment and external priors while overlooking the brain’s intrinsic nature as a multimodal integration system. To address these limitations, we propose BrainJanus, the first unified brain model that integrates brain, vision, and language within a single framework. Specifically, we introduce a Unified Brain Tokenizer to quantize continuous neural dynamics into discrete tokens aligned with visual and linguistic representations in a shared Omni space. Building on this, we utilize an All-in-One autoregressive architecture that leverages next-token prediction to enable seamless any-to-any generation, which encompasses image-to-brain and text-to-brain encoding, and brain-to-image and brain-to-text decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BrainJanus achieves superior performance across diverse benchmarks. Furthermore, our framework exhibits zero-shot generalization and preserves interpretable biological topography, highlighting its potential as a general-purpose brain modeling paradigm. The code is available at https://github.com/HaitaoWuTJU/BrainJanus.

paragraphs: BrainJanus brings two directions of brain modeling into one system: predicting neural activity from sensory inputs, and reconstructing images or language from neural activity. The paper argues that treating these as separate tasks overlooks the brain's integration of multiple kinds of information. Its approach instead connects brain signals, images, and language within a shared framework.

A Unified Brain Tokenizer converts continuous neural activity into discrete tokens aligned with visual and linguistic representations in a common space. An autoregressive model then predicts successive tokens across these representations. This supports image-to-brain and text-to-brain encoding, alongside brain-to-image and brain-to-text decoding, using the same overall modeling approach.

The authors report superior performance across diverse benchmarks, together with zero-shot generalization and preservation of interpretable biological topography. The latter finding means the representation retains meaningful biological organization alongside its predictive capabilities. These results support the framework's potential for general-purpose brain modeling, with the central contribution being a shared representation and prediction mechanism for tasks previously handled separately.
summary.tldr: BrainJanus uses a shared token representation to model both directions of correspondence among brain activity, images, and language.

title: BrainJanus: A Unified Model for Understanding and Generation across Brain, Vision, and Language

abstract: Inference-time scaling offers a flexible way to align visual generative models with downstream objectives without updating model parameters. In modern image generation models, a natural way to do this is to optimize the random noise from which generation starts. However, searching in this high-dimensional noise space is highly inefficient, because many directions have little effect on the final image. We trace this inefficiency to a spectral bias in generative dynamics: model sensitivity to initial perturbations decays rapidly as frequency increases. Based on this insight, we propose Spectral Evolution Search (SES), a plug-and-play framework for initial noise optimization that performs gradient-free evolutionary search in a low-frequency subspace. Theoretically, we derive the Spectral Scaling Prediction from perturbation propagation dynamics, which explains the frequency-dependent impact of perturbations. Extensive experiments across diverse settings show that SES substantially improves the trade-off between generation quality and computational cost, consistently outperforming strong baselines under the same compute budget.

paragraphs: Image generators can be steered toward a downstream objective by searching for better initial noise while keeping model parameters fixed. The difficulty is that the noise space is large, and many changes to it have little effect on the final image. This paper examines why some search directions are more influential than others.

The authors identify a spectral bias: the generator’s sensitivity to initial perturbations falls rapidly as their frequency increases. Spectral Evolution Search uses that observation to restrict gradient-free evolutionary search to a low-frequency subspace. This concentrates the search on variations that the analysis indicates have greater influence on the generated result.

The paper derives a Spectral Scaling Prediction from the dynamics of perturbation propagation, explaining the frequency-dependent effect theoretically. Experiments across diverse settings report a substantially better trade-off between generation quality and computation, with consistent improvements over strong baselines at equal compute budgets. The findings support using the generator’s sensitivity structure to allocate inference-time search effort more effectively.
summary.tldr: Spectral Evolution Search improves reward-aligned image generation by focusing initial-noise search on influential low-frequency directions.

title: Spectral Evolution Search: Efficient Inference-Time Scaling for Reward-Aligned Image Generation

abstract: Semantic caching has emerged as a pivotal technique for scaling LLM applications, widely adopted by providers including AWS and Microsoft. By utilizing embedding vectors as cache keys, this mechanism effectively minimizes latency and redundant computation for semantically similar queries. In this work, we conceptualize semantic cache keys as a form of fuzzy hashes. We demonstrate that the locality required to maximize cache hit rates fundamentally conflicts with the cryptographic avalanche effect necessary for collision resistance. Our conceptual analysis formalizes this inherent trade-off between performance (locality) and security (collision resilience), revealing that semantic caching is inherently vulnerable to key collision attacks. While prior research has focused on side-channel and privacy risks, we present the first systematic study of integrity risks arising from cache collisions. We introduce CacheAttack, an automated framework for launching black-box collision attacks. We evaluate CacheAttack in security-critical tasks and agentic workflows. It achieves a hit rate of 86% in LLM response hijacking and can induce malicious behaviors in LLM agent, while preserving strong transferability across different embedding models. A case study on a financial agent further illustrates the real-world impact. Finally, we discuss mitigation strategies, highlighting a persistent trade-off between cache efficiency and robustness.

paragraphs: Semantic caches reuse responses when a new query has an embedding similar to a stored query. That similarity improves efficiency, but it also makes the cache’s matching behavior relevant to answer integrity. This paper treats embedding-based keys as fuzzy hashes and analyzes how their useful locality conflicts with cryptographic collision resistance.

The authors formalize a trade-off between keeping related inputs close together and resisting key collisions. They then introduce CacheAttack, an automated black-box framework for studying those collisions. The focus is whether a cache can return an attacker-influenced response or affect an agent’s behavior, extending the analysis beyond previously studied privacy and side-channel concerns.

In the evaluated settings, CacheAttack achieves an 86% hit rate for response hijacking and can induce malicious agent behavior. The authors also report strong transferability across embedding models and present a financial-agent case study. These findings connect the conceptual trade-off to observed integrity failures. The paper discusses mitigations while emphasizing that improving robustness retains a persistent tension with the efficiency gained from semantic reuse.
summary.tldr: CacheAttack demonstrates how the similarity matching that makes semantic caches efficient can enable response hijacking and harmful agent behavior.

title: From Similarity to Vulnerability: Key Collision Attack on LLM Semantic Caching

abstract: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) are promising alternatives to autoregressive large language models (AR-LLMs), as they potentially allow higher inference throughput. Reinforcement learning (RL) is crucial to enabling dLLMs to achieve performance comparable to that of AR-LLMs on important tasks, such as reasoning. However, RL algorithms well-suited to dLLMs’ unique characteristics have yet to be developed. This paper proposes Distribution Matching Policy Optimization (DMPO), a principled and theoretically grounded RL fine-tuning method specifically designed to enhance the reasoning capabilities of dLLMs by matching the dLLM policy distribution to the optimal, reward-tilted one through cross-entropy optimization. We identify a key implementation challenge with small training batch sizes and propose several effective solutions based on a novel weight baseline subtraction technique. DMPO exhibits superior performance on multiple reasoning benchmarks without supervised fine-tuning, achieving up to a $39.63$ percentage-point improvement in accuracy over prior non-DMPO RL baselines and $67.97$ percentage points over the base model, underscoring the effectiveness of the distribution-matching framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/yuchen-zhu-zyc/DMPO.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models offer the possibility of higher generation throughput, but improving their reasoning requires reinforcement-learning methods suited to their structure. This paper introduces Distribution Matching Policy Optimization, or DMPO, as a theoretically grounded way to fine-tune these models using rewards.

DMPO trains the model to match an optimal reward-tilted distribution: a target distribution that favors outputs according to their rewards. It performs this matching through cross-entropy optimization. The authors identify a practical difficulty when training batches are small and develop several remedies using a new weight baseline subtraction technique. Addressing that implementation issue is part of making the distribution-matching objective usable in practice.

Across multiple reasoning benchmarks, DMPO improves performance without supervised fine-tuning. The largest reported accuracy gains are 39.63 percentage points over earlier non-DMPO reinforcement-learning baselines and 67.97 percentage points over the base model. These are maximum gains across the reported evaluations, rather than a uniform improvement on every task. The results support distribution matching as an effective approach to strengthening diffusion-model reasoning.
summary.tldr: DMPO improves diffusion language-model reasoning by matching a reward-favored target distribution, with large reported gains without supervised fine-tuning.

title: Enhancing Reasoning for Diffusion LLMs via Distribution Matching Policy Optimization

abstract: Linear prediction methods, such as least squares for regression, logistic regression and support vector machines for classification, have been extensively used in statistics and machine learning. In this paper, we study stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithms on regularized forms of linear prediction methods. This class of methods, related to online algorithms such as perceptron, are both efficient and very simple to implement. We obtain numerical rate of convergence for such algorithms, and discuss its implications. Experiments on text data will be provided to demonstrate numerical and statistical consequences of our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: The paper studies stochastic gradient descent for regularized linear prediction methods. The setting includes least-squares regression, logistic regression, and support vector machines, bringing several established prediction approaches into the same optimization discussion. Its focus is how to solve these learning problems efficiently when their scale makes computation an important concern.

The algorithms are described as both efficient and simple to implement, with connections to online methods such as the perceptron. Beyond proposing a practical procedure, the authors obtain a numerical convergence rate and discuss its implications. Such a rate gives a quantitative account of progress toward the optimization solution, adding theoretical substance to the efficiency claim.

Experiments on text data examine numerical and statistical consequences of the theoretical findings. This connects the analysis of optimization progress with the behavior of the resulting prediction methods. The contribution is therefore a combined computational and statistical study of SGD for regularized linear learning, with the experiments used to illustrate implications of the convergence analysis.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes convergence rates of simple SGD algorithms for regularized linear prediction and examines their consequences on text data.

title: Solving large scale linear prediction problems using stochastic gradient descent algorithms

abstract: Learning algorithms often obtain relatively low average payoffs in repeated general-sum games between other learning agents due to a focus on myopic best-response and one-shot Nash equilibrium (NE) strategies. A less myopic approach places focus on NEs of the repeated game, which suggests that (at the least) a learning agent should possess two properties. First, an agent should never learn to play a strategy that produces average payoffs less than the minimax value of the game. Second, an agent should learn to cooperate/compromise when beneficial. No learning algorithm from the literature is known to possess both of these properties. We present a reinforcement learning algorithm (M-Qubed) that provably satisfies the first property and empirically displays (in self play) the second property in a wide range of games.

First, an agent should never learn to play a strategy that produces average payoffs less than the minimax value of the game. Second, an agent should learn to cooperate/compromise when beneficial. paragraphs: The paper examines repeated general-sum games in which agents learn while interacting. It argues that focusing on immediate best responses or equilibria of a single round can lead to relatively low average payoffs. Looking instead at equilibria of the repeated interaction motivates a learner that considers both protection against poor outcomes and opportunities for mutually beneficial behavior.

The authors identify two desired properties. An agent should never learn a strategy whose average payoff falls below the game’s minimax value. It should also learn to cooperate or compromise when doing so is beneficial. The abstract states that no existing learning algorithm was known to possess both properties.

The proposed reinforcement learning algorithm, M-Qubed, addresses these goals with different kinds of evidence. The payoff-protection property is proved. Cooperation and compromise are observed empirically in self-play across a wide range of games. This distinction matters: the paper provides a formal guarantee for the first goal and experimental support, specifically in self-play, for the second.
summary.tldr: M-Qubed guarantees minimax payoff protection and empirically learns beneficial cooperation or compromise in self-play.

title: Learning to compete, compromise, and cooperate in repeated general-sum games

abstract: The proliferation of text documents on the web as well as within institutions necessitates their convenient organization to enable efficient retrieval of information. Although text corpora are frequently organized into concept hierarchies or taxonomies, the classification of the documents into the hierarchy is expensive in terms human effort. We present a novel and simple hierarchical Dirichlet generative model for text corpora and derive an efficient algorithm for the estimation of model parameters and the unsupervised classification of text documents into a given hierarchy. The class conditional feature means are assumed to be inter-related due to the hierarchical Bayesian structure of the model. We show that the algorithm provides robust estimates of the classification parameters by performing smoothing or regularization. We present experimental evidence on real web data that our algorithm achieves significant gains in accuracy over simpler models.

We show that the algorithm provides robust estimates of the classification parameters by performing smoothing or regularization. paragraphs: Document collections are often organized into taxonomies, but assigning documents to that structure requires substantial human effort. This paper proposes a hierarchical Dirichlet generative model for classifying text into a given hierarchy without supervised document assignments. It also derives an efficient algorithm for estimating the model’s parameters and carrying out the classification.

The model assumes that class-conditional feature means are related through a hierarchical Bayesian structure. In plain language, the statistical description of one category is connected to the descriptions of related categories. This dependence lets the hierarchy participate in estimation, rather than functioning only as a set of destinations for completed classifications.

The authors show that the estimation procedure performs smoothing, or regularization, producing robust estimates of classification parameters. Experiments on real web data report significant accuracy gains over simpler models. The findings support using the supplied hierarchy as a source of statistical structure: relationships among categories help stabilize the model and improve classification in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical Dirichlet model uses relationships among categories to regularize unsupervised document classification into a supplied taxonomy.

title: Hierarchical Dirichlet model for document classification

abstract: Although each iteration of the popular kMeans clustering heuristic scales well to larger problem sizes, it often requires an unacceptably-high number of iterations to converge to a solution. This paper introduces an enhancement of k-Means in which local search is used to accelerate convergence without greatly increasing the average computational cost of the iterations. The local search involves a carefully-controlled number of swap operations resembling those of the more robust k-Medoids clustering heuristic. We show empirically that the proposed method improves convergence results when compared to standard k-Means.
originalAbstract: Although each iteration of the popular kMeans clustering heuristic scales well to larger problem sizes, it often requires an unacceptably-high number of iterations to converge to a solution. This paper introduces an enhancement of k-Means in which local search is used to accelerate convergence without greatly increasing the average computational cost of the iterations. The local search involves a carefully-controlled number of swap operations resembling those of the more robust k-Medoids clustering heuristic. We show empirically that the proposed method improves convergence results when compared to standard k-Means.

paragraphs: K-means can process large clustering problems efficiently within each iteration, yet reaching a solution may require too many iterations. This paper addresses that distinction between the cost of a single step and the cost of finishing the clustering process. Its goal is to accelerate convergence while retaining much of the computational economy of K-means.

The proposed enhancement adds local search using swap operations resembling those in K-medoids, a clustering heuristic described as more robust. The method carefully limits the number of swaps. That control is central to the design: additional search is intended to make useful progress without greatly raising the average computational cost of an iteration.

The authors report empirical improvements in convergence compared with standard K-means. These results support the proposed combination of inexpensive K-means iterations and a controlled amount of more exploratory local search. The method remains a heuristic, and the stated finding concerns its observed convergence behavior. Its practical contribution is a way to improve progress per iteration while keeping the extra work limited.
summary.tldr: Adding a controlled number of K-medoids-like swaps empirically improves K-means convergence without greatly increasing average iteration cost.

title: Best of both: a hybridized centroid-medoid clustering heuristic

abstract: Most studies of online learning measure the performance of a learner by classification accuracy, which is inappropriate for applications where the data are unevenly distributed among different classes. We address this limitation by developing online learning algorithm for maximizing Area Under the ROC curve (AUC), a metric that is widely used for measuring the classification performance for imbalanced data distributions. The key challenge of online AUC maximization is that it needs to optimize the pairwise loss between two instances from different classes. This is in contrast to the classical setup of online learning where the overall loss is a sum of losses over individual training examples. We address this challenge by exploiting the reservoir sampling technique, and present two algorithms for online AUC maximization with theoretic performance guarantee. Extensive experimental studies confirm the effectiveness and the efficiency of the proposed algorithms for maximizing AUC.

The key challenge of online AUC maximization is that it needs to optimize the pairwise loss between two instances from different classes. We address this challenge by exploiting the reservoir sampling technique, and present two algorithms for online AUC maximization with theoretic performance guarantee. Extensive experimental studies confirm the effectiveness and the efficiency of the proposed algorithms for maximizing AUC.

paragraphs: Online learning updates a model as training examples arrive. Many approaches judge success through classification accuracy, but that measure can be inappropriate when classes occur at very different frequencies. This paper instead targets the area under the ROC curve, or AUC, a measure widely used to evaluate classification with imbalanced data.

Optimizing AUC creates a different learning problem because the loss compares pairs of examples from different classes. An update therefore depends on relationships between examples, rather than only on the newly arriving example. The authors use reservoir sampling to address this obstacle and construct two online algorithms that can work with the pairwise objective.

Both algorithms come with theoretical performance guarantees, and extensive experiments support their effectiveness and efficiency at maximizing AUC. The contribution is a way to align an online learner’s optimization target with an evaluation measure suited to class imbalance. It also shows how sampling can help bridge the gap between learning from individual arrivals and optimizing comparisons across examples.
summary.tldr: Two online algorithms use reservoir sampling to optimize pairwise AUC losses, with theoretical guarantees and supportive experiments.

title: Online AUC Maximization

abstract: This paper analyzes the problem of Gaussian process (GP) bandits with deterministic observations. The analysis uses a branch and bound algorithm that is related to the UCB algorithm of (Srinivas et al, 2010). For GPs with Gaussian observation noise, with variance strictly greater than zero, Srinivas et al proved that the regret vanishes at the approximate rate of O(1/√ t ) , where t is the number of observations. To complement their result, we attack the deterministic case and attain a much faster exponential convergence rate. Under some regularity assumptions, we show that the regret decreases asymptotically according to O(e^{-τ t/(ln t)^{d/4}}) with high probability. Here, d is the dimension of the search space and tau is a constant that depends on the behaviour of the objective function near its global maximum.
originalAbstract: This paper analyzes the problem of Gaussian process (GP) bandits with deterministic observations. The analysis uses a branch and bound algorithm that is related to the UCB algorithm of (Srinivas et al, 2010). For GPs with Gaussian observation noise, with variance strictly greater than zero, Srinivas et al proved that the regret vanishes at the approximate rate of O(1/√ t ) , where t is the number of observations. To complement their result, we attack the deterministic case and attain a much faster exponential convergence rate. Under some regularity assumptions, we show that the regret decreases asymptotically according to O(e^{-τ t/(ln t)^{d/4}}) with high probability. Here, d is the dimension of the search space and tau is a constant that depends on the behaviour of the objective function near its global maximum.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Gaussian process bandit optimization when function evaluations are deterministic. The learner searches for a global maximum using observations of an unknown objective. Its performance is expressed through regret, which measures the shortfall associated with the search relative to the optimum.

The analysis uses a branch-and-bound algorithm related to upper-confidence-bound optimization. It complements an earlier result for observations with strictly positive Gaussian noise, where regret decreases at approximately the inverse square root of the number of observations. By focusing on the deterministic setting, the authors obtain a substantially faster asymptotic rate.

Under regularity assumptions, they prove with high probability that regret decreases as O(exp(-τt/(ln t)^(d/4))). Here, t is the observation count, d is the search-space dimension, and τ depends on the objective's behavior near its global maximum. The expression describes exponential decay modified by a logarithmic factor. The result highlights how much stronger convergence guarantees can become without observation noise, while retaining explicit dependence on dimension, local objective behavior, and the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: For deterministic Gaussian process observations, a branch-and-bound analysis gives a high-probability, near-exponential regret decay rate under regularity assumptions.

title: Exponential Regret Bounds for Gaussian Process Bandits with Deterministic Observations

abstract: We present local discriminative Gaussian (LDG) dimensionality reduction, a supervised linear dimensionality reduction technique that acts locally to each training point in order to find a mapping where similar data can be discriminated from dissimilar data. We focus on the classification setting; however, our algorithm can be applied whenever training data is accompanied with similarity or dissimilarity constraints. Our experiments show that LDG is superior to other state-of-the-art linear dimensionality reduction techniques when the number of features in the original data is large. We also adapt LDG to the transfer learning setting, and show that it achieves good performance when the test data distribution differs from that of the training data.

We focus on the classification setting; however, our algorithm can be applied whenever training data is accompanied with similarity or dissimilarity constraints. Our experiments show that LDG is superior to other state-of-the-art linear dimensionality reduction techniques when the number of features in the original data is large. We also adapt LDG to the transfer learning setting, and show that it achieves good performance when the test data distribution differs from that of the training data.

paragraphs: Reducing the number of features can make data easier to work with, but the resulting representation still needs to preserve distinctions relevant to prediction. This paper introduces local discriminative Gaussian dimensionality reduction, or LDG, a supervised method that learns a linear mapping using information local to each training point.

The mapping is chosen so that similar examples can be distinguished from dissimilar ones. Although classification is the main setting studied, the method can also use training data supplied with similarity or dissimilarity constraints. Its local perspective guides the construction of a single linear representation, connecting neighborhood-level distinctions to the overall reduction in dimensionality.

Experiments show that LDG outperforms the compared state-of-the-art linear reduction techniques when the original data has many features. The authors also adapt it to transfer learning and report good performance when training and test distributions differ. These findings support its usefulness for high-dimensional supervised problems and for the distribution-shift settings examined in the paper.
summary.tldr: LDG learns a linear low-dimensional representation from local similarity information and performs well on high-dimensional classification and transfer-learning tasks.

title: Dimensionality Reduction by Local Discriminative Gaussians
